a) Letters

Of the many letters concerning the Servant of God, sent by various figures mostly to the Foundress Mother, the 12 most significant are reproduced here.

Among the "Letters," arranged in chronological order, one stands out as a "postulatory letter" presented to Card. Michelangelo Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, for the opening of the Informative Process.

1. Letter from Canon Ignazio Zuccaro, secretary of the Archbishop of Palermo Card. Michelangelo Celesia, to the Foundress, of 9 June 1885 (Proc. p. 484).

He is deeply moved and still incredulous at the loss of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Not only the Sisters, but the whole city of Palermo and Cardinal Archbishop Celesia are grieved.

The last moments of the Servant of God's life.

Palermo, 9 June 1885

Most Reverend Mother,

I meant to write to you yesterday itself, but try as I might, I was not able to. It is plain to see that our plans are fallible, for while we reason with human prudence, divine Providence, with its infinite Wisdom, works in a way different from our expectations.

The loss of Sister Anna Salvatore is truly like a dream. I can tell you that the whole city is deeply grieved over it, and my own Most Eminent Lord too showed himself profoundly moved, and was touched when, on my return to the Palace, I found him already informed of the sorrowful event.

All the Sisters are inconsolable; care was taken, however, to avoid excessive displays, by exhorting them to resignation, and they conducted themselves wisely.

Even the less devout people recognize that the loss was irreparable, and they are right, for one does not often find so many graces in a single creature, nourished moreover by so faithful a correspondence to them.

Nothing was omitted of what was due, either in her illness or in the procession to the Cemetery, where she was accompanied by all the Sisters, as far as possible, and by four Priests. Care was taken to place in a small crystal vial an inscription, signed by several Priests, for whatever the Lord may wish.

She remained fully present to herself until the last moment, and died as she had lived, a true saint. A few moments before expiring, the sisters wished to ask her forgiveness, and, through the Confessor, asked for some remembrance, and she said: I wish you to be lovers of the holy rules, to be good, and to stand firm in the holy vocation. They asked for her blessing, and she, as much as she could, raised her hand to bless them, turning her gaze to them all with a smile, and, fixing her eyes on the Crucifix held between her own joined hands, went to find her well-earned reward.

Forgive me if you find no coherence in this letter, but yesterday I summoned all the strength I could to encourage the poor sisters; today, however, I feel more wretched. Last night Sister A. Gualberta also died at the Fernandez Infirmary, and tonight she will be buried beside Sister A. Salvatore. Sister A. Alberica is better.

I close for now, but will write to you again. I remain, with my usual regard

most obliged and devoted

Canon I. Zuccaro

2. Letter from Canon Ignazio Zuccaro, secretary of the Archbishop of Palermo Card. Celesia, to the Foundress, of 16 June 1885 (Proc. p. 507).

The solemn Requiem Mass for Sister Anna del Salvatore has been celebrated, with great attendance. Enclosed is the newspaper "La Sicilia Cattolica," which spontaneously reported on it. In the evening the sisters carried to the grave the numerous wreaths of flowers.

Palermo, 16 June 1885

Most Reverend Mother,

Yesterday I had no time to write to you, but I hastened to send you word at once by telegraph of the flawless success of the funeral you ordered, and which found an echo in everyone who knew Sister Anna del Salvatore. I am sending you the newspaper La Sicilia Cattolica, which spontaneously reported on it.

The Superiors of the Houses of Palermo, most pleased with the outcome, expressed to me their keen wish to contribute to the expenses. Sister A. Salvatore, even after death, provides for everything, but I had to promise them that, once the accounts were settled, I would not fail, with the sole aim of giving them the satisfaction of having contributed, to invite them to give something towards it. And in itself the thought is a dear one, that all should spontaneously offer to do so…

The whole assistance came from the Cathedral, even the voices for the singing. They wanted me to sing the mass, and my not-very-fortunate voice too took part in the service. From 6 in the morning until 12, two altars were never without Masses, and everyone contributed voluntarily to pray for that blessed soul.

The catafalque was adorned with many most beautiful and splendid wreaths of flowers, which in the evening were brought by the Sisters to the grave of the deceased, and I myself went to the cemetery together with the House Chaplain to receive them.

However much more one might have wished to do, nothing further could have been managed; but in the city what was done made an excellent impression, and it is spoken of with satisfaction.

The outcome, then, was that Sister A. Alberiga, the sad ceremony barely over, was declared by the doctor out of danger of death; she still knows nothing, and yesterday, when I visited her, she was so cheerful, and kept the companions around her so happy, that it hardly seemed true. Up to the previous evening she spoke with difficulty, and unintelligibly.

Pray for me, who remains always

Most devoted and obliged

Canon I. Zuccaro

3. Letter from the priest Enrico Filiti, confessor of the Servant of God, to the Foundress, of 7 July 1885, Palermo (Proc. p. 508).

He deserves no thanks, for he has merely done his own duty. He was, for four years, spiritual director of the Servant of God, and to attend her in her final moments of life was for him a privilege.

He affirms that Sister Anna del Salvatore practiced the virtues in heroic degree, although she sought, in vain, to hide herself: whoever drew near her noticed the fragrance of Christ that she gave off. Her life was a continual sacrifice, faced with a manner that was always cheerful.

Even in her final moments of life, concerned above all for others, she was profoundly humble and fully conformed to the Will of God.

Most Reverend Mother,

The flattering words you were kind enough to send me in your letter made my face flush with embarrassment, as I thought that the accounts given of me amid the shared misfortune of the loss of the unforgettable Sister Anna Salvatore were exaggerated. I assure you I did nothing but my duty, that is, to try to bring comfort to those poor daughters who were sunk in desolation.

As for the care I gave to the lamented Superior, I tell you that I would not have yielded to anyone that enviable fortune of attending the last moments of that holy soul, all the more since for more than four years I was, though most unworthily, her director of conscience.

Those solemn moments can never be forgotten! On entering the room where the dying Superior lay on her bed, instead of a feeling of sorrow, a feeling of consolation arose spontaneously. She was not a woman struggling amid the throes of her final pains, but an angel who, shunning the earth, longed to take flight towards the Heaven from which she had come. Her face was sad but gentle, her eyes languid but serene, her body suffering but vigorous; it was a sublime contrast between flesh being martyred and a spirit quickened by virtue. Happy was she! Not a groan, not a complaint, but a continual Fiat was heard from her trembling lips. Her eyes were always turned to Heaven, and if she turned them elsewhere, it was upon her daughters that her serene gaze rested, as if to encourage them in virtue.

But time marched on apace, and unfortunately the final hour drew near. The good daughters surrounded their mother's bed in sorrow, and they longed ardently for some remembrance, some word from their dying mother. I called her by name, told her that the sisters wanted some remembrance, and she, though too weak, gathering her strength, turned her gaze about and, fixing it on her daughters, said to them: Be good and obedient. She wished to say more but could not. I advised her to give them her blessing, and she made a sign to me to bless them.

Holy soul! You were profoundly humble to the very end of your life. This moving scene had not yet ended when she herself told me to commend her soul, and quietly breathed her last.

Reverend Mother, I could not put into words the heroic virtues the lamented Superior possessed; it was a hidden virtue, yet apparent to everyone who came near her, even for the first time; in vain she strove to hide herself, to the point that at certain moments and in certain cases she tried to make herself look foolish; this ingenious device was of no avail, she was the violet spreading the fragrance of its scent while hidden beneath the leaves.

Her life was a continual sacrifice, a continual torment, but her bearing was always cheerful; it seemed she could find consolation nowhere but in the torments she perpetually suffered. And the reward for her sufferings, she has received. God called her to himself, ah! too soon for us, but too late for her, for she desired nothing other than soon to be united to her loving Jesus. May she, from Heaven, implore divine blessings on those who admired her on this earth, on the holy Institute for whose good she would have given her life, and on those (and they are many) who now invoke her to implore the divine Mercy.

And now there remains nothing for me but to thank you for the kind sentiments you hold towards my poor person, asking you at the same time to commend me to the Lord, that he may grant me the grace to carry out the works of my ministry with holy zeal, while, blessing you in the Lord, I remain

Palermo, 7 July 1885

Your most affectionate servant

Fr. Enrico Filiti

4. Letter from the priest Gaetano Gabriele, to the Foundress, of 11 August 1885, Palermo (Proc. p. 510).

He hesitated before having printed (cf. below, p. 409) the funeral eulogy of Sister Anna del Salvatore, but is now glad he did; all who have read it have been filled with admiration for her virtues, and ask whether she is buried in a "provisional" resting place, since one day she may be raised to the honors of the altar.

He knows that the Foundress intends to have the Servant of God's biography written, and he encourages her in this.

Most Reverend Mother General,

I receive this very day Your Most Reverend Ladyship's esteemed letter, in which the goodness of your heart moves you, more than to pity me, to thank me for the humble work I devoted to the blessed memory of the Superior Sister Anna del Salvatore. Oh! how I esteemed the good Superior, whom God wished to have with him in paradise!

In the trepidations of spirit I felt in having that discourse printed, I took comfort in the thought that Sister Anna del Salvatore's merits would excuse the many faults I had fallen into; and so it turned out, for many who have read it have been so filled with admiration for the extraordinary life of the deceased that they wished to know whether she had been buried in a provisional resting place, as one whom the Church's judgment might one day raise to the honor of the altars.

Certainly more and better could have been done; but I trust that the good Superior, from heaven, if on the one hand she took pity on my poor effort, on the other will have welcomed the little bouquet of flowers I laid upon her tomb; for the glory that redounds thereby to God, for every best gift... is from above, coming down from the Father of lights. As I also trust that Your Most Reverend Ladyship will have had compassion for the faults into which I fell, through the smallness of my talent and my still being a stranger to the sanctuary of virtue.

I know Your Ladyship intends to have her life written; and I too urge you to do so with all my heart, for it could not fail to be of universal edification to the faithful, and a protest against the many immoral books that corrupt the young.

I am very sorry for the trouble Your Ladyship has suffered, and I pray the Lord, unworthily indeed, but with all my heart, that he keep you for many years at the helm of your charitable Institute, which God may ever better prosper for the benefit of sufferers. You, in turn, pray also to the Lord for me, for my mother, who is advanced in years and infirm, and I shall be amply repaid for my small effort on behalf of the lovable and holy Superior.

Thanking you, then, for the noble sentiments you expressed to me, which reveal the noble spirit that dictated them, and paying you my respects with deep religious feeling, I remain at your venerated commands.

Palermo, 11 August [18]85.

Most devoted in the Lord

Fr. Gaetano Gabriele

5. Circular letter of the co-founder Father Giovanni Battista Tornatore and the foundress Rosa Gattorno, to the whole Institute, [January 1886] (Proc. p. 511).

The authors report, as a singular grace, the precious death of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, which took place the previous year. They recall her heroic virtues and the particular gifts with which she was enriched, stressing that her reputation for sanctity is such as to give hope that the Lord will glorify her with the honor of the altars.

An Institute is in the flower of observance when the spirit of Jesus Christ reigns within it. The Spirit of Jesus Christ is shown especially in charity, which led him to die for us. Now of this spirit, by God's mercy, the Institute showed itself full also this year.

The Lord afflicted the poor city of Palermo with cholera. While, frightened by so terrible a pestilence, people fled this way and that, and the poor struck down by the disease were left abandoned, our sisters, full of the charity of Jesus Christ, went into the midst of the slaughter, and by night and by day went about the houses and the streets, bringing every kind of comfort, and did not leave the victims except when they were healed, or when they had placed the souls of the dying into God's hands and their bodies in the tomb.

This spirit of evangelical courage, which cheerfully faced the dangers of death to save the lives of their brothers and sisters, filled with wonder not only the good, but also the enemies of our holy religion, and in this way caused Jesus Christ, the source of holy charity, to be glorified both by the good and by the wicked.

Another fine grace the Lord granted also this year. Institutes are schools where one learns to die well. Now this year many showed they had profited greatly within the Institute, for in general all who died there died the precious death of the just, and left a sure hope of having gone to Heaven, as so many luminous gems of the Holy Mother's crown. Among them all, special mention is due to Sister Anna del Salvatore, a truly chosen soul, who both in life and in death was the admiration of all Palermo. She lived as a saint and died as a saint, a saint to the point of giving hope that one day God will glorify her with the honors of the altars.

In her, every virtue shone in a truly heroic degree. In her there was heroic obedience. In the Mother she observed and loved Jesus Christ, so that a mere sign from her was enough for her to be found wherever the Mother called her. As Superior she was a true mother to her sisters, so that with sisterly love she watched over them both in spirit and in body. The affection she bore her mother was so tender, so loving, that to her she revealed all those singular lights with which Heaven had abundantly enriched her — the gift of seeing hidden things, the gift of prophecy, the gift of devout contemplation. She thought of nothing but her mother, lived for nothing but her mother's good. In truth it could be said she lived on the thought of her mother.

Another signal grace is that this year our two great Benefactors brought to completion the house in Rome, a large house, a house that offers every convenience for religious community life. With what disinterestedness, with what care did the aforesaid benefactors oversee it! How much toil, how much sweat, so that at the same time the work might be done to perfection while money was saved! So great were the cares of these two great souls that both of them fell ill, and one is still under the illness, which obliges the whole Institute to pray for them. Since, then, the Generalate House is not fully finished, and since this year's Chapter is a private one, only fifty Superiors will be called, and the rest will be called to the Chapter that will follow.

This year eleven houses were opened, and thirty sisters sent to America. 130 Novices received the habit, and thirty passed to a better life. We ask for the usual suffrages!

May the peace and blessing of the Lord accompany you everywhere

Gio. Batt.a Tornatore

Most affectionate M. Rosa G.

6. Postulatory letter to Card. Pietro Michelangelo Celesia, Archbishop of Palermo, of 8 December 1894 (Proc. p. 513).

Recalling the continual extraordinary graces obtained through the intercession of the Servant of God, numerous ecclesiastical and civil figures address a supplicant petition to the Cardinal for the opening of the Informative Process.

Your Eminence,

The undersigned, with the sole aim of giving greater glory to God, come to beseech Your Most Reverend Eminence as follows.

On 7 June 1885 there died in Palermo the religious Anna del Salvatore Orsi, in the world Marianna, of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, after having led an exemplary and virtuous life, as the unanimous voice of the whole citizenry and of all who had the good fortune to know her attested through public demonstrations on that sorrowful occasion.

Merciful God, who had granted his Servant so many favors in life, continues even after her death to glorify her, granting immense graces through the intercession of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, to such a point that Your Most Reverend Eminence did not disdain to accept the plea of many that her body be placed in a provisional resting place, which took place on 14 February 1887 in the presence of His Most Reverend Excellency Msgr. Giovanni Cirino, Archbishop of Ancyra, and of other most worthy persons.

Through this Servant of God's intercession, extraordinary graces continue to multiply, not only in Palermo but in very many other parts of Italy, and also in America; and so the undersigned, for the purpose stated at the outset, of the greater glory of God, and also to prevent the passing of the years from causing the loss of those persons who today can give precious testimony in favor of the religious Anna del Salvatore Orsi, beseech Your Most Reverend Eminence to be pleased to open the informative process on the life, virtue, and graces obtained through the intercession of the said Servant of God, who will not fail to obtain from God himself favors and blessings.

Confident of the favor, we humbly kiss the hem of the Sacred Purple.
