7. Letter from the priest Luigi Mollo to the Foundress, of 18 October 1895, Naples (Proc. p. 520).

He thanks her for the images of St. Anne, but points out to the Mother the misunderstanding: he wants the images of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, of whom he is devoted and from whose intercession he expects many graces, both for himself and for the souls under his direction.

Naples, 18 October 1895

Most Reverend Mother,

May the Heart of Jesus be with us.

I give many thanks for the two little packets of images of our protectress St. Anne which reached me on Monday by post. I thank you very much for them; but I must tell you that my expectation was disappointed, since, had I wanted images of St. Anne, I would not have troubled you, being able to procure them myself; but I wanted those of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi; so much so that I also added that, if you had some small item, such as from her habit or something else, you should not deprive me of it, since I have become devoted to her, and I hope for fine graces through her mediation, both for myself and for some soul under my direction, with the promise to render due account of it.

Meanwhile, do not fail to pray for me to her who was your daughter, and today is our common advocate. However I learned that Your Charity would be coming here to Naples within a few days; I hope, then, for a very great gift, namely that you let me know of your arrival, so that I may obtain the happiness of seeing you.

I wish you the fullness of every spiritual contentment and, with Heaven's blessing, I remain.

Of Your Maternal Reverence

Most devoted Servant

Fr. Domenico Maria Mollo

8. Letter from the Honorable Angela Gotelli, Undersecretary for Health, to Sister Anna Luisa Bocci, Superior of the community of Lucera, of 21 June 1960, Rome (Proc. p. 530).

The image of Sister Anna del Salvatore is very dear to her, and she wishes to have more to distribute.

The Undersecretary of State for Health

Rome, 21 June 1960

Most Reverend Mother,

Only today, which is your name-day feast, am I writing to send you, with the warmest wishes, my thanks, however belated, for the kind letter you sent me some time ago with your good wishes (pray!), with the welcome image of Sister Anna del Salvatore.

It is very dear to me, and I would like to know where I can obtain a certain quantity to distribute.

How are you? And your sister, whom you mentioned in an earlier letter of yours? With cordial regards and good wishes

Yours in the Lord

Angela Gotelli

9. Letter from Aida Ilari to the Superior of the General House, of 27 May 1961, New York (Proc. p. 531).

She asks for the biography or images of the Servant of God.

New York, 27 May 1961

Dear Mother Superior,

I would be glad to have some little booklet or poster about Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, whose cause of beatification is in process.

If the booklet has a cost, please let me know how much it is, and I will send the necessary money, including the cost of postage or shipping.

I ask you to answer me as soon as possible. I thank you and send you my cordial greetings.

Aida Ilari

10. Letter from Clelia Bosi to the Superior of the Mother House, Sister Anna Ludovica Sommaruga, of 6 August 1966, Albareto (Parma) (Proc. p. 532).

In Albareto they have not forgotten the dear "little saint," Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, and have decided to dedicate the Nursery School to her; she asks for the biography to make her better known to the population.

Albareto, 6-8-66

Reverend Mother,

I am from Albareto di Borgotaro (Parma), the town where Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi was born, who died in Palermo with a reputation for holiness, and who belonged to your order.

We have not forgotten this dear little saint, who also brings honor to our town, and we have thought of naming our nursery school after her. But we would like the people to know a little about her life, and I turn precisely to you to ask (if you have it) for a copy of her life, which was written so many years ago.

With the turnover of so many parish priests, the copy that was kept in the parish house has been lost. If you have only one copy, we will return it promptly afterwards; and if you have two copies, we would be glad to buy one, making whatever offering you think fit. We would be so happy to have Sister Anna's life story!

In the meantime, I thank you and offer my respects

Most devoted

Clelia Bosi

11. Letter from Clelia Gotelli to the Superior of the General House, Sister Anna Augusta Lobraico, of 25 November 1972, Albareto (Parma) (Proc. p. 532).

She asks for the biography of Sister Anna del Salvatore; since childhood she has nourished great devotion to the Servant of God and prays to her every day.

Albareto, 25-11-72

Reverend Mother,

I am from Albareto (Parma), the town where Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi (Provincial of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily) was born.

I, since childhood, have always nourished a lively devotion towards her, and even now I pray to her every day. I even have a relic of hers (a piece of a garment of hers, given to me by a Sister of St. Anne when I was still a girl).

Now I am advanced in years, and a copy of her life story, which I know exists, would be very dear to me. Could you not have the charity and kindness to get a copy to me, which I would pay for at any price? How dear it would be to me! I truly hope you will grant my wish! I would also treasure many images of her, which I would distribute among the women of my town and the neighboring priests, to make her known and loved.

I would so wish that she might rise to the glory of the altars, this glory of our little town. In the meantime, I thank you and offer my respects:

Clelia Gotelli

12. Letter from Oliveto Aldo to the Superior General Sister Anna Goffreda Roberto, of 26 February 1976, Valgreghentino (Como) (Proc. p. 533).

He asks for the biography or anything else concerning Sister Anna del Salvatore on behalf of his mother, Valentina Orsi, a relative of the Servant of God.

Valgreghentino, 26 February 1976

My elderly mother, now eighty-two years old, would like to receive, if possible, the biography or anything else concerning the life of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, first Provincial of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily, born in Albareto (Parma) on 23 February 1842 and died in Palermo on 7 June 1885 with a reputation for Holiness.

The reason for this wish is the fact that my mother, like Sister Anna, was born in Albareto (Parma) in 1894 and is the daughter of Valentina Orsi (called del Salvatore). In all likelihood, my mother is a direct relative of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi.

To receive what I ask would certainly mean, both for you and for us in the family, receiving news on the matter. Should it be necessary to receive books, images, relics, etc., I am prepared to reimburse any necessary expense.

Trusting in the courtesy that will be shown me in replying to this letter, I thank you in advance also on behalf of my mother, and extend my distinguished regards

Oliveto Aldo

b) Written Reports

This heading, in Proc. pp. 534-621 under "Testimonies," consists of 50 reports — mostly in the form of letters — drawn up (at the request of the Foundress herself and of successive Superiors General) between 1886 and 1960 by numerous sisters, priests, and laypeople who knew the Servant of God, who received graces through her intercession, or who likewise witnessed it.

Since most of these reports come from eyewitnesses "de visu" and provide first-hand information about the life, virtue, and reputation for holiness of the Servant of God, they prove particularly valuable, even though they are not strictly part of the judicial process, owing to the well-known interruptions that befell the Process.

They are arranged here in chronological order.

For those that add no new or significant elements, only the summary has been reproduced.

1. Report of Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, of 6 June 1886, written in the form of a letter to the Foundress Rosa Gattorno, in the hand of Sister Anna Oliveto (Proc. p. 534).

She narrates two healings that occurred through the intercession of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi.

Sister A. Battista Cosmano, a novice among the Daughters of St. Anne, had been ill since the very first days after her reception of the habit, with great abdominal pain caused by constipation; she suffered continuous torment. She took a first, a second purgative; a third, which had little effect. Visited by the doctor, he too prescribed another purge and enemas; but, like the first ones, these only gave her momentary relief. The pain kept increasing, and an enteroclysis had to be resorted to. Forced to take a fourth medicine, this proved even more useless than the others. On the doctor's second visit, he gave her a certain purgative water which, instead of helping, only made her feel the pains she was suffering even more, along with a constipation that produced a great swelling of her stomach, so that she could not manage to walk, to sit, or to take food. Only out of obedience did she swallow a few spoonfuls of broth.

More than a month had passed, and the Reverend Superior, seeing that every treatment had proven useless, was most reluctant to have to tell her that, since all remedies had become ineffective, the long illness did not allow the Novice to remain any longer in the Religious life, finding herself unable to do all that the Rules prescribe, and therefore outside regular observance; the best course, if the Mother General so judged, would be to send her back home. But the Superior was grieved by this and still waited before deciding.

Poor Sister A. Battista could not find peace with this news; she wept night and day thinking that, worse than the illness itself, this was the greater evil: having to leave the Institute, and forever. The poor little thing wept and did not know where to turn for help, when one Sister (Sister A. Maffea) suggested she turn in prayer to the late Sister Anna del Salvatore. Further encouraged by her Reverend Mistress, the novice began a Novena; and on the very evening of the first day of that novena she had a bowel movement without taking any purgative and felt a very noticeable improvement, though not free of the usual abdominal pains and swelling. That same night, after so many sleepless nights, she slept and dreamed...

She saw in a dream three nuns she knew, and one of them asked her why she was crying. "I want to see Sister A. del Salvatore, to ask her for a grace (these are her own words)." Sister A. del Salvatore indeed came forward to her; "she asked me why I was so distressed and in tears. I knelt at the sight of her, and told her of the illness I was suffering, and that, more than the illness, it was the extreme sorrow of having to leave Religious life." "No," she answered me, "the Holy Mother does not wish it"; and, touching and pressing on my stomach: "You have nothing wrong," she added. "Be obedient," and, saying this, she vanished. I went on sleeping and woke at the sound of the ejaculatory prayer, together with the other sisters. I got out of bed perfectly healthy; and from that day on I have had no more cause to complain (thus the Novice continues). I am very well; I eat with appetite everything given to me by the Community.

Thanks be given to God and to Sister A. del Salvatore, who obtained for me from Him the instantaneous healing.

Besides, the cook Sr. A. of the Stigmata developed a trouble in one eye; after I had cared for her myself, seeing that it showed no sign of improvement, I had her seen by the doctor, who said it was no small matter and that it would not be hard to lose the eye; indeed, I took her off kitchen duty and had every treatment applied that human art knew and could manage, but all in vain. Finally, weary of always seeing her bandaged and of using so many different remedies, I had every treatment stopped and touched her eye with the photograph of Sr. A. Salvatore. This was in the evening; by the next day she was already much improved, and after two days I put her back in the kitchen perfectly cured. What do you say, Mother, are these not miracles?

Believe me, I have great confidence and I hope she will continue to grant me the graces of which I have written to you; the whole community is witness to this, and still more those who have benefited. Would that God might make us all so many other Sister Anna del Salvatores, then indeed our dear Institute would progress. Enough; let us hope that, through her prayers, we shall become so, and thus be her consolation, and, better still, the joy of the Heart of Jesus.

Meanwhile, O Mother, be pleased to bless me and forgive me for everything, while, kissing your hand, I remain the most unworthy among your daughters, but one who loves you dearly

Trapani, 6/6/86

Sr. A. Costanza Cenni

2. Report of Canon Gaetano Pagliani, of 16 June 1889, to the Secretary General Sister A. Benedetta Carrega (Proc. p. 536).

He narrates a conversion worked by Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, four years after her death, appearing in a dream to a sick woman.

Long live the Precious Blood of Jesus!

I, the undersigned, swearing upon the Holy Gospel, and tacto pectore more sacerdotali, attest as follows:

In the month of October 1888, in a city of Sicily, finding myself engaged in a course of Holy Preaching, a woman tormented by an illness that seriously threatened her health approached me for comfort. Grieved by that harrowing account, I could think of nothing better to suggest than to begin a novena of prayers to the Blessed memory of Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi, first purifying herself in Holy Confession, and approaching the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist. She answered that she would gladly do so, and that for a year she had never missed Holy Communion.

Well, once that novena had begun, it was impossible for this woman to approach Holy Communion: so many and such great obstacles stood in her way each morning. On the last day of the novena, she came to me dissolved in tears of penance, and revealed that she had seen in a dream a little nun, who announced herself by the name of Sister Anna del Salvatore, and who ordered her to open her heart at once in Holy Confession and convert, if she did not wish to be subjected to terrible scourges.

Penitent and moved (granting me leave to draw up this declaration for the glory of that blessed soul), she revealed to me in confession:

1. - that for seven years she had belonged to the Masonic sect,

2. - that she had abjured the Holy Catholic Religion,

3. - that she went to Holy Communion in order to inflict injury on the Most Holy flesh of Jesus Christ,

4. - that she had the mission of corrupting young girls, and especially the Sisters of a Religious Community,

She handed over to me the infamous documents of her oaths, the insignia of Freemasonry, and, her soul washed clean in a general Holy Confession, has returned to the path of truth and salvation.

Thus I attest, under the sanctity of my oath, to the glory of that blessed soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, whom, to my last breath of life, I claim as my sister and special protectress.

Palermo, 16 June 1889

Canon Gaetano Pagliani

Apostolic Missionary of the Precious Blood

3. Excerpt from the Report of Sister Anna Letizia Sordi, of 21 November 1890, written in the form of a letter to the secretary general Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega (Proc. p. 537).

The author stresses her spirit of prayer, of penance, and narrates some facts considered extraordinary.

A. M. F.

Appignano, 21 November 1890

Reverend Sister A. Benedetta,

Now I will go on to something else. Since you asked me to tell you what I know of Sr. A. Salvatore, I do so most willingly. I will say what I remember without searching for fine words, exactly as I saw it with my own eyes, heard it with my own ears, held it in my own hands, in the presence of God, without fear of saying a word that is not true. During the year 1877, when you were superior in Florence, I would often get up from bed after midnight or one o'clock to go and see where she was. I almost always found her kneeling on the floor, leaning against a chair, burning and shedding abundant tears before the Tabernacle. I would beg her to go to bed, but she did not notice that it was already so late and that she had to keep company with Jesus, who was all alone. In the morning, after Holy Communion, she would hide her face in her hands, and one could shake her, call her, all to no avail.

In the same year, while in church at morning prayers, when they were accustomed to recite the "Remember, O Our Lady" and reached the words "we cannot" etc., she would vanish from the sisters' sight. One sister at once ran to catch up with her; she was searched for a long time but was not found until several hours later. Another time, in the year 1878, in the public church of Appignano, shortly after Holy Communion, she got up from the pew saying: "Let's go." The sister next to her, who was Sr. A. Pacifica, run though she did after her, could not catch up with her. It seemed as though she had wings for the stairs... Reaching the nearest room, which belonged to the infirmary sister, she locked herself in, and all this in the blink of an eye, threw herself on her knees, her eyes full of tears turned and fixed on heaven, her arms spread in the form of a cross, speaking a language we could not understand. We could make this out through the keyhole, because the key was turned in such a way that one could see everything. We knocked hard on the door for a long time, we called her, she gave no sign of hearing us. After some time she came out, and seemed ashamed before us, saying she had done one of her usual things, and called herself mad, a mole, without sense.

Whenever she wished to obtain some grace, or the Mother entrusted some need to her, she would at once turn to the prayer of the Filotea, on page 492: "Here I am before you, O great Queen of heaven," etc., and would obtain what she asked, and the next day would tell the sisters: "The Mother," or such a person, "has received the grace." In her talk she always spoke of Jesus's love for us, of Magdalen when she came among the soldiers escorting Jesus to Calvary and how He looked at her and called her by name. She always spoke of Jesus under the figure of a fisherman, and, when she saw fish, would say: "Ah, how I wish I could catch big fish for Jesus!" She would always exclaim: "From the tabernacle there continually comes forth a voice telling us to love Jesus."

In the year 1878, while in Piacenza in the month of April, at the moment of the Elevation at Holy Mass, she heard a voice say to her: "You will go to Appignano and you will see Clementina" (this was my own name in the world). In early May she was sent by the Superior General to Appignano. She herself told me this. In the same year, when the vote for the election of town councilors was to be held in Appignano, the Reverend Provost entrusted the outcome to her prayers. Sr. A. Salvatore, during the voting, said to us in a prophetic tone these exact words: "Be of good cheer, for the thing has gone well." After midday, what she had said came to pass.

At the end of a month, which I do not recall, during the year 1877, being superior in Florence and in great distress at having to pay the baker about two hundred lire, and having no more than a few cents, she shut herself in her room, full of holy confidence in God, where there was a wooden Crucifix on a pedestal (which the sisters said spoke to her), and prayed for a long time. Shortly after, she went out, and a lady handed her the money, and I went with her to pay the baker. Things like this happened often, but I do not remember them all. Suffice it to say that the house in Florence began with two lire, and after a few years was supplied with linens, its own laundry, and every good thing of God's, and the community always numbered about fifty people, including the boarding pupils.

She also obtained another grace for a young woman taken in at the house in Florence, who, over her own troubles, having to pay many months of board, and always putting off the Superior with the promise that money would come to her from afar, one day dissolved many matches in water and drank it. The case was desperate; everyone wept to see the good Superior in such pain over this trouble. She goes to her room and, weeping bitter tears, prays to her crucifix. The grace is obtained, and the woman returns to her former state through simple remedies given her by the Superior. I was not present at the time, but if you wish further details, Sr. A. Stanislaa Vignoli, who I believe is still in Bregnano, may well know them.

In winter, in the harshest cold, she was found wearing only her black habit and a black bodice. Her stockings always torn, with her feet showing through, her shoes worn out, and if one wanted to cause her real distress, enough to make her cry, all one had to do was give her something new. There was no way to get her to wear it. She would give it to another sister. As for food, she ate only once every 24 hours. I myself once forced her to take a small piece of chocolate in the morning. After much suffering, she gave it back. She always ate vegetables and things that had already been rotting for several days, and said it was exquisite food. She told me that, even when at home, she liked to eat coal, ash, raw potato peelings, cabbage stalks and leaves, that she always went looking for things in the garbage, because, as she said (out of humility): "I have always been a little creature, a little animal." She almost always wore the cilice, made like a net, with the inside all of points pressed close together; it was made of iron, but shone like steel from the continuous use she made of it. However much she tried to hide it, we noticed that she suffered greatly when standing up and sitting down. On Fridays she never, ever left it off, this I can attest to myself. She had several, one shorter one to wear on her thighs. In fact, this one she had allowed me to wear during the hours of strict silence, something I was not able to keep up for long.

In Florence, in 1877, she had an abscess on her arm. The sisters, against her will, sent for the doctor. The Superior, before he came in, prayed and begged earnestly to be left alone for a moment. They did not do so, because they suspected she wanted to remove her cilice. And indeed so it was: before the doctor's arrival, the cilice fell to the floor, and was picked up by a sister, to her own great distress.

I myself have experienced the power of her prayers. Some years ago I suffered horrible temptations against Holy Purity. I wrote to the Mother, who told me to make a novena to Sr. A. Salvatore; through that true saint, I was heard. This is all I can tell you, frankly and sincerely, as I would say it were I to die this very instant. I close, commending myself to your prayers. Give my greetings to the dear Mother. If the novice is not the right one, then we shall wait a little longer. I kiss you affectionately, and if through Sr. A. Salvatore there should be things to give to our Institute, a first saint, I would be grateful if you would let me know.

Believe me, with affection, your loving sister

Sr. A. Letizia Sordi

4. News about the life of Sister Anna del Salvatore, written by Don Tommaso Grilli, parish priest of Albareto, of 26 November 1890 (Proc. p. 648).

It provides valuable information about the childhood and youth of the Servant of God.

Biographical notes on Orsi Marianna

Orsi Angelo and Mussi Domenica, a married couple of the Parish of Albareto di Borgotaro, in the municipality of the same name, Diocese of Pontremoli, good Catholics, of landowning status, had nine children, three girls and six boys.

Of these, the firstborn was Orsi Marianna, who was born in the said Parish at about eight o'clock in the evening on the 22nd of February in the year 1842, and on the following day was baptized in the Parish Church of that place by the Very Reverend Master D. Giovanni, its Rector, and was named Marianna Veronica.

She was lifted from the sacred font by Mussi Francesco, who was at that time the Podestà of the said municipality, and by Orsi Giovanna, sister of the aforesaid Angelo, both residing in Albareto itself (so recorded in the Parish Register).

At the age of four, that is, on 25 July 1846, she was confirmed in the Parish Church of Borgotaro, Diocese of Piacenza, by His Most Reverend Excellency Monsignor Michele Angelo Orlandi, Bishop of Pontremoli, who was there together with the elderly Bishop Sanvitale of Piacenza, on the occasion of the inauguration feast of the new Seminary of Bedonia (so recorded in the Parish Archive: Confirmation Records of 1846). Well instructed in the catechism by her devout parents and by the aforesaid Parish Priest, she was admitted to Holy Communion around the age of puberty.

Her father taught her a little to read and a little to write; being the firstborn, she helped her own mother with care and patience in looking after and raising her little brothers and sisters. In this she was certainly always of great help and benefit to her mother.

When her father sent her brothers Giovanni and Luigi to the seminary school of Bedonia as day students, she went there for some time and took care of preparing their food and of the household cleaning. She also spent some time as a servant with her uncles, good priests, Don Antonio Mussi, parish priest of Buzzo, and Don Luigi Mussi, parish priest of Rovinaglia and later of Valmozzola, but her love for her Mother and her own family prevailed, and so for the most part she remained in her father's house.

This parishioner of mine (I say mine, because when she left Albareto I had already been parish priest for seven years) was a young woman of gentle character and calm spirit, with no vanity in her dress or personal conduct. Sincere, cheerful, yet modest in conversing with her companions, obedient, respectful. With devotion she frequented the Most Holy Sacraments, and with devotion said her daily prayers. In the novenas and devotional feasts she never failed to come to Church, and gladly took part in accompanying the Viaticum to the sick and the procession of the dead.

Her parents, in raising their large family, had incurred some debts, and to pay these, and in hope of greater advantage, sold all the property they had in this parish to certain Rovella brothers, and went to live in Centovera, in the territory of Piacenza, in 1863; but their daughter, Orsi Marianna, remained still in Albareto, in the Mussi household, with her godfather-uncle Francesco and her uncle Lorenzo, and with diligence and satisfaction attended to household chores and duties, being well regarded and respected.

Around 1866, she too left Albareto and went to Centovera, to join her family, which, I am told, after a little while went to live in Tuna, a place near Piacenza, from where the aforesaid young woman entered the convent and took the name of Sister Anna del Salvatore.

Before entering the Religious life, she returned to Albareto to greet her relatives and her companions, and had a familiar conversation with Signora Bosi Valentina, her confidante, who assures me with certainty (and is a person worthy of trust) that Orsi also spoke to her of the dances which, in private homes of Albareto, she had occasionally happened to attend, at the invitation and urging of some companions, and told her that, every time, after such amusements, she always found herself regretful and so repentant that she was forced to weep by herself. It was also on this occasion that the said Orsi declared to the aforementioned Signora Bosi that, after leaving Albareto, she had found a match to marry, and that at first she had given him a word of hope, but that after some time (certainly enlightened by a higher grace) she thought of renouncing the world, and told the young man that she no longer wished to take a husband, because she had decided to become a nun, as indeed she later did. Happy was she, I will say, who chose a Bridegroom ever loving, ever young, ever handsome, and never old, for all eternity.

Thus done and written in Albareto di Borgotaro, 26 November 1890.

Priest D. Tommaso Grilli

P.S. There is no record that Orsi Marianna, in Albareto, showed signs of any particular gifts.

5. Report of Sister Anna Consolata Massimelli, provincial superior of Upper Italy, of 30 November 1890, to the secretary general Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega, written in the form of a letter (Proc. p. 540).

She sets forth the life and virtues of the Servant of God, stressing above all her spirit of self-concealment, her love of God, and her spirit of prayer.

A. M. F.

Dear Sister A. Bene.ta,

I beg you to forgive me for not answering your most dear letter at once. We have had so many sick sisters these days that we have had no moment's rest.

Of our dear Saint I will tell you little, because she was very hidden. It is the saints who understand one another without speaking, not the saints with sinners; though the latter admire the saints and feel envy of them. The first time I had the good fortune to know Sr. A. Salvatore was at S. Martinello. Her presence made such an impression on me, so angelic was she. She was very mortified; and I, seeing her so wasted in body, cleverly obliged her to eat the food served to the community, and she too, cleverly, always tried to mortify her appetite. In the house of S. Martinello she would always wake me, and I would always find the sister half-dressed, kneeling at a window that faced the little church of the Marchioness, in the act of adoring Jesus in the Sacrament. I always pretended not to see her, to let her make love with the Lover of Souls.

In Florence I had the good fortune to have her as my superior, and there too she led a most rigorous life, having little health. In Ovada she ate once a day; when she kept watch I would tell her to have a little coffee afterwards. She was always content with everything, and thanked me with such loving kindness that it can never be expressed; but then we realized that she made her coffee with the scrapings (soot) from the pots. At night she slept very little; in the bitter cold of Ovada she kept her window open while praying. Sr. A. Leonilde heard her scourging herself while passing by chance through a corridor; and at other times found her in the sacristy, kneeling with arms outstretched before a crucifix, pouring out her heart in sweet conversation with her beloved Crucified Jesus.

On the eighth of December, the feast of the Immaculate Virgin, it was something wonderful to see her, truly a volcano of love. I remember that, on the night before the feast of the Madonna, it snowed about half a meter deep, and she, after dinner, said: "Take us to the Capuchin church, to pay a visit to the Immaculate Virgin," and I said: "But... with this snow..." and Sr. A. Salvatore: "Oh, take us... yes... yes... good, take us," and some other sister: "yes, let's go..."; then I said: "let's go..."; and we went the whole way outside the town, that is, along the main road, and believe me, dear Sr. A. Benedetta, we did not meet a single person.

As soon as we were outside the hospital, Sr. A. del Salvatore began to laugh and jump about in the snow, and to play the fool, until we reached the church square, and then she grew still. Both going and coming back, we were amazed and laughed a great deal at the leaps she made and the antics she performed. "Poor thing!" I said to myself. "Oh, how much she enjoys and how much she suffers... Oh, how powerful love is."

As for the rest, we can all attest that she was always observant, to the point of scruple, of the Holy Rule. Oh, blessed is she! Happy would I be if I could imitate her.

Dear Sr. A. Benedetta, please present my respectful duty to the Most Reverend Mother, asking her to send us her blessing. To you, my most cordial greetings, with the request that you remember poor me at Holy Communion, as I always do for you. May we see each other again in the chapel before Jesus in the Sacrament.

Ovada, 30 June 1890

Most affectionate Sister

A. Consolata Massimelli

6. Report of the priest Giuseppe Giacopazzi to Don Gaetano Gabriele, Beneficiary of the Metropolitan Church of Palermo, of 4 December 1890, Borgo San Donnino (today Fidenza), written in the form of a letter (Proc. p. 542).

It highlights the goodness and spirit of prayer of the Servant of God, attested by her mother Domenica Mussi.

Borgo S. Donnino, 4 December [18]90

Most Illustrious Sir,

Forgive me if I answer a little late to your most kind letter. I had to write to the parish priest of Albareto, where Sister Anna was born, to learn some news from him, and this has already taken a bit too long. I enclose here what he writes to me, without adding or removing anything.

As for myself, I could not tell you anything in particular; I will only say that she was always a good young woman. Her mother, Domenica Mussi, who still lives in Piacenza, assures me she never had the least displeasure from this daughter. Indeed, she told me that she sometimes found her up at night praying, when she was still very young. Otherwise, even she herself cannot tell me anything that she knows to be heroic.

I offer you my respects, hoping soon to have a copy of Sister Anna's Life, and if I may be of service to you in anything, do not hesitate to ask.

Of Your Most Illustrious Lordship, most devoted

Fr. Giuseppe Giacopazzi

7. Report by an unidentified author, of 18 February 1891, written in the form of a letter to a fellow sister (Proc. p. 618).

She relates episodes from the life of the Servant of God that were told to her by Sister Anna Emanuela, Sister Anna Lodovica, Sister Anna Ermina, and Sister Anna Tranquillina.

A. M. F.

Pisa, 18 February 1891

Dearest Sister,

I called Sr. A. Emanuela and asked her about what she had seen and heard of Sr. A. Salvatore. She told me exactly this:

"I was together with her for six months in the house in Florence, and I always saw her most observant of the Holy Rule, and although she was Superior she acted as laundress, as porter, as infirmarian, and ate only once a day. She was always shown to be affable with everyone and full of charity."

Sr. A. Lodovica says: "I was together with Sr. A. Salvatore for a short time in the House of Sestri Ponente, and I went with her sometimes on the alms round and to the sick; I saw it with my own eyes. Once we went to a poor woman and found her so filthy it was revolting. Sr. A. Salvatore goes up to the bed, embraces her, kisses her, and then, with great charity, washes her all over, and afterwards kissed her again, and we went back home. Another time we were going together on the collection round and we came to the house of some gentlefolk who, as soon as they saw her, heaped scorn on her, and she still kept going there almost every day, as though she had received every kindness. At home, moreover, she always showed herself humble, respectful towards everyone, never asked for anything she might need, and when the Superior would say to her, 'Salvatore, do you need nothing?' she would answer, laughing: 'A little love of God...' These were her very words."

The people she cared for all loved her dearly, and always asked after her.

Sr. A. Erminia says: "I was with her for two years, and I always saw that she ate nothing but already-rotten vegetables, unwashed, and at night she never slept, so much so that she had no bed, and spent the night before Jesus in the Sacrament. With the sisters, however, she was all charity and gentleness. She did the heaviest work of the Community, although she was Superior and Provincial; she also acted as laundress, as the house's infirmarian, and often went out to keep vigil as well, and when I went with her, she never let me do anything, but did everything herself, especially when the sick were repulsive to look at."

When, then, there were sick sisters, she would not leave their bedside, neither by day nor by night. In short, so great was her charity, humility, and gentleness that if ever I found myself troubled by some spiritual anguish, as soon as I went to her I felt consoled at once; I remember one morning I was coming back from vigil and felt uneasy about making my Most Holy Communion. As soon as she saw me, she said: "Wait, the Confessor will come later, and I will have you go to confession; I have already understood, but I don't want to know anything" — and I had told no one anything. I can say nothing else but that her way of acting was truly that of a Saint.

Sr. A. Tranquillina says: "I came to know Sr. A. Salvatore in Piacenza. I was ill, and by order of the Reverend and dear Mother, she took me to Naples. On arriving in Naples, she asked the Mother to take me on to Palermo, and the dear Mother said yes; I felt very ill, so much so that the Superior of the Naples House said to her: 'Sr. A. Salvatore, this sister will die at sea.' She answered: 'Be at ease, she will not die.' We left Naples, and she had me lean on her lap, and made me eat and drink as though nothing were wrong; I felt nothing of my illness; indeed, everyone else felt sick except me, and this was indeed a grace she obtained for me through her prayers. In Palermo I was with her for five years, and I always saw her work and do every task of the Community, as though she were the least of the Sisters."

"Many times I was with her on the alms round; along the way she did nothing but pray; this was her food, while she walked all day without ever eating; she would make me drink and eat, but she, until five o'clock, took nothing, and then ate a little boiled cabbage and nothing else. In short, by day she did not eat and by night she did not sleep, and still she worked more than anyone."

"She was always cheerful, and in the early years, when the House was quite poor, one could see that she suffered (for the Sisters' sake), but even so she always showed herself content, and with her humility and charity she won not only the affection of us Sisters, but the hearts of many people in the City, who all said she was a Saint. A few hours before she died, seeing me somewhat upset, she said to me: 'Sr. A. Tranquillina, what is wrong? Be content' — and yet one could see that she herself suffered greatly, and still remembered and tried to console everyone. The rest I do not recall."

9. Report of Sister Anna Paolina Viani, of 21 April 1891, written in the form of a letter to the secretary general Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega (Proc. p. 543).

She recounts some episodes from the life of the Servant of God of which she was a direct witness, highlighting her fervor, her spirit of charity, and her acceptance of God's will.

A. M. F.

Marradi, 21 April 1891

My good Sr. A. Benedetta,

I will write to you briefly the life of Sr. A. Salvatore, as you wish.

Once, while I was attending a sick woman together with the Superior, and the dying woman no longer showed any sign of life, she had us take a little card of St. Anne; as soon as the dying woman took it, after a quarter of an hour she began to speak, and within a few days she recovered completely.

In the first year we went to Palermo, in the first house we opened, there were 5 of us Sisters; we had gone out to attend to the sick, and on returning home we rang the doorbell many times and no one came to open it, so we went in through another door we never used, where Father Gusman [Cusmano] came to open it for us, and we went in and found the Superior sitting in the dormitory with her work in her hands; and I called her so loudly, several times, that she did not hear; finally the Superior came to with a start, so that she herself was embarrassed to see two Sisters standing before her without knowing how we had come in; from the way we saw her, I can say nothing else but that she was in ecstasy.

Once the Superior had no bed to sleep in; I begged her so much to sleep with me, and she, to please me, got into bed with me, and then, during the night, I awoke from sleep and saw the Superior speaking with Jesus, so much so that she even made the bed shake with the great fervor she had, with the outpourings of love she felt, which so carried her away that I believed she would fall from the bed to the floor; I, having noticed this, pretended to sleep so as not to cause her any distress, because, knowing that this displeased her, I said not a word to anyone, not even to her; as soon as day broke, she got up at once, as though nothing had happened.

Another time she was away visiting the houses as provincial; she arrived home at midnight without warning us, and rang the bell to come in, but we heard nothing at all, since we were all in bed and noticed nothing, and she remained outside the door for 5 hours, and it was winter, and it was very cold, and she, with her patience, waited until daybreak; as soon as we had the wake-up call, I was the one who went to open the door, and I found the Superior all frozen, sitting on her suitcase; I asked her when she had arrived, and she answered that she had arrived at midnight; and I said to the Superior: "Why didn't you ring the bell?..."; she answered that she had rung it, but softly, so as not to wake the gentlefolk living in the building, and so she told me that all night long she thought of St. Francis, when he knocked at the door of his convent and even his friars did not hear him; and I cannot but admire the great patience she had... and then, as soon as she came in, she went straight to bed to shake off the cold she had caught that night, which lasted for several days as she felt the cold she had suffered, but even so I could not hear a single complaint from her lips; she was always cheerful and at ease, so that she let no one know what she herself was suffering; if ever she felt a little unwell and some visitor arrived at the house, she, with the utmost indifference, concealed it all.

Sister A. Romualda having fallen ill with pneumonia, while she, the Superior, had to leave by order of the Mother for Termini Imerese, and I do not know for how many days the Superior was away, Sr. A. Romualda came to die, and the Superior, on her return, no longer found the Sister, who had already been taken to the cemetery; and as soon as the Superior reached the door, she asked the porter when they had taken her, and he answered that they had taken her away in the evening, and as soon as she got home, she sat down at once to weep, out of the sorrow she felt at not having been present at her death; I asked her: "Superior, why didn't you come, when I waited for you so much?..."; and she answered me that she wanted to come, but the sisters at Termini kept her there, but nevertheless she told me that she had seen the sister die, and knew everything; and knowing this, she gave vent to her grief in tears, and then at once resigned herself to the divine Will of God, saying that God had permitted it as her punishment, and would say: "How much you make me suffer, my Jesus..."; and she kept making such exclamations to Jesus, because He mortified her in this way....

When the Superior found herself forced to stay in bed, ill with a fever of 40 degrees, as soon as she received a telegram from the Mother she got up at once and left for Trapani, and returned that evening still fasting, having taken nothing but Communion, though she could have eaten again, since she had had nothing that day; and afterwards she went back to bed never to rise again; I would sometimes ask her: "Superior, don't you wish to get well?..."; she would answer me: "Yes, I would so much wish to get well, for the Mother's sake"; but then she would say: "If the Lord does not wish it, fiat Voluntas tua."

My good Sr. A. Benedetta, if I wished to write everything to you, it would be impossible to describe it all; you told me in your letter to write also of her failings, but of this I cannot do, because I have never been able to understand that the Superior committed any fault; she was so attached to her Jesus that she spent all the free time she had praying before the Most Holy Sacrament, and when the Mother wished for some grace, she commended herself to Salvatore's prayers, and then would go to the Sisters and tell them to pray, because the Mother desired a grace, and likewise, as soon as she had the Mother's answer, she would come to thank the Sisters, saying that the Mother thanked them for the prayers they had made for her, that the grace she had desired had been obtained, and she would say nothing more.

I assure you that I would be ready to make any sacrifice, but I will always say that the Superior is a saint. Once, being with another Superior, and I speaking of Salvatore, she let me understand that she did not hold her in much esteem, because, having heard of that slander innocently imputed to her, she made me feel so mortified that I no longer had the courage to speak of Salvatore; and as long as I live I will always speak well of her, because she always did good.

I close, because time is lacking, and were I to continue, I would never finish saying that Salvatore was a Saint…

Most affectionate Sister

Sr. A. Paolina Viani

9. Report of Sister Anna Macrina Paolini to Sister Anna Celsa Speranza, of 31 July 1912 (Proc. p. 647).

She provides information about the opening of the house known as that of the "nurses" in Palermo, and about the joyful poverty lived alongside the Servant of God.

Genoa, 31-7-912

My dearest Sr. A. Celsina,

I thank you for the comforting news you give me regarding the process of my beloved Mother. Most happy to be able to assist it as best I can, I explain myself:

The Sisters were summoned by Father Don Gasparo Bava and Monsignor Don Ignazio Zuccaro, then secretary to the Archbishop, and we were supported by them for about a year, paying the sum of £200 a month. The Sisters were called in the year 1880, on the 4th of May.

The first sisters were Sr. A. del Salvatore, Sr. A. Primitiva, Sr. A. Albina, Sr. A. Settimia, and Sr. A. Paolina. After 10 months came Sr. A. Pazienza, Sr. A. Placentina, Sr. A. Quirina, Sr. A. Caterina, Sr. A. Antonina, Sr. A. Altaria; those I remember are listed above; the others, afterwards, came and went because they opened other houses; I do not remember their names.

The first house we inhabited was at S. Marco, in a corridor that served as a dormitory and recreation room; in the middle of the corridor there was a window overlooking the Church of S. Marco, where we made our devotions, and we only went down an inner stair to that Church for Holy Communion. There we stayed for a full 18 months, in the company of mice running about the house; with all that, we were as happy as if it were always Easter, so much so that the Superior came to say: "Here we are on Mount Tabor."

Our office was that of home nurses; the sacrifices we made are easier to imagine than to describe; besides keeping watch by night at the bedside of the sick, we were always busy by day too in serving the neediest patients, often in degrading conditions, and we vied with one another to see who could do the most. About two years later the houses of Pignatelli, Sant'Annuzza, and the Asylum were opened, and later, in my time, the Hospital of S. Saverio and Malaspina, S. Martino, and the Royal Home for the Poor of Monreale, leaving the other towns.

When our dear Mother sent us to open the house in Palermo, she spoke these words: "I send you as Jesus Christ sent his Apostles; I hope you will sow good seed." When she later came to see us for the first time, she exclaimed: "Oh! what great consolation you give me, it means I sowed the seed in good soil" — she said this because, though there were only six of us, the work was as if we had been 24; her own words.

If you should also wish to know about the opening of the house in Naples, I too was present; it was opened 3 years before Palermo.

I thank the Reverend Mother who was pleased to send her blessing to this poor wretch, and I embrace you warmly, ever your unworthy but most affectionate daughter

Sr. A. Macrina

10. Report of Sister Anna Guida, of 7 February 1913, written in the form of a letter to the assistant general Sister Anna Camilla Valentini (Proc. p. 545).

She narrates a painful moment in the life of the Servant of God; she highlights her humility, her fortitude under trial, and the esteem a layman held for her.

A. M. F.

Bovino, 7 February 1913

My ever dear Superior Camilla

I gladly answer your most dear letter of yesterday. I knew at once it was you writing to me, and I was not a little surprised: "What could good Superior Camilla want from me? Why would she write to me?" And I read it with enthusiasm. And what can I tell you about that holy soul who was Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi?!

I do remember that the poor Sister suffered a great deal that year — 1878 — and I also recall that she accompanied me to Ferrara. Of the journey there I remember nothing, not even the conversations we had. I remember very well, though, that one day, while in Ferrara, in the work school, she told me that, during the time of that struggle, she was tempted not only internally but also from without, by her relatives. They had come to visit her, and had told her of a dream in which they had seen her suffer greatly (everything she was really suffering), even thrown down the stairs... And seeing her truly suffering, they wanted at all costs for her to come back home, promising that they would leave her free to do as she wished, and, it seems to me, even that they would build her a little chapel at home. It took much effort to persuade them that she was well, and so as not to yield to their enticements, but she won out.

In the two and a half months we were together in Ferrara, I saw her suffer harsh treatment at table — especially once — but she never complained of it and continued her regimen of eating only once a day. It seems to me that sometimes she was obliged to eat supper and that she obeyed, but that afterwards she was forced to bring up the food she had taken. I knew her to be good, humble, and charitable towards everyone.

From Ferrara we set out together as far as Bologna: I went on — alone — to Piacenza, and she continued her journey to Rome. I do not know if on this journey she was tempted again, because I never saw her again.

When she was at Sampierdarena, I learned that at night she worked a great deal: she washed, she carried stones... I remember that once we wanted to give her a little party — I do not remember whether for Christmas or some other occasion — and good Sr. Salvatore, who disliked praise and celebrations, had hidden herself. It took a great deal of effort to find her; and then, to get her to attend the party, we had to catch her unawares, in some random spot. Indeed, she stood there, in the midst of Sisters and girls — also standing — so absorbed that she seemed more in heaven than on earth.

Other details I do not know. — Ah! I recall that, passing through Reggio in 1888, a gentleman — I believe Mr. Ramirez — asked me whether I had known that Sister, and when I answered that I had, he immediately added: "Ah, she was a holy Sister! Her death was a great loss!" And indeed it is so: when good people leave us, it is a great loss.

My Superior, I have written this at school, with the children, so please excuse everything... Give my greetings to Sr. Immacolata and Sr. Predicanda, and tell them I would need their help... I can no longer have it on this earth...

I hope to see you and embrace you soon. Meanwhile, accept a kiss from me and greetings from everyone.

Affectionately,

Sr. A. Guida

11. Report of Sister Anna Elisabetta Veronesi, of 22 February 1913 (Proc. p. 547).

She expresses esteem and admiration for the Servant of God, formed already during the time of the novitiate spent together at the Mother House in Piacenza, highlighting above all the exquisite charity she showed towards the sick and towards her fellow sisters, her profound humility, and her serenity and fortitude under trial.

A. M. F.

Pistoia, 22-2-913

I, the undersigned, Sister A. Elisabetta Veronesi, came to know the Servant of God Sister A. del Salvatore Orsi when, in August 1869, I took the habit of the Daughters of St. Anne at the Mother House of Piacenza, the said Servant of God already being a Sister since the month of March, and I was edified by her humble, recollected bearing, and by her manner full of gentleness and charity towards everyone, and by the exact observance of her religious duties; and from then on I held her in the esteem of a soul truly beautiful and dear to the Lord. This esteem of mine grew when, a few months after taking the habit, I was assigned by the Superior as her companion in attending a poor sick woman. It was then that I was able to admire her exquisite charity, both towards the sick woman and towards me.

We were allowed, if the sick woman was not so seriously ill as to need both sisters attending her at the same time, for one to rest until midnight on the chair, while the other tended to the patient, and after midnight the first would rest while the other served. Now Sister Anna del Salvatore wanted me to rest first, and would tell me to rest easy, that if my help were needed she would call me; and I, so as not to displease her, obeyed; but instead of sleeping, I kept watching, without her noticing, how she served the poor sick woman, for, I repeat, I held her in great esteem and wanted to see with how much love and charity she served the sick.

This poor sick woman was all swollen, I believe from dropsy, and had sores on her legs; Sister Anna del Salvatore, believing I was asleep and so could not see what she was doing, very gently unwrapped the poor woman's ulcerated legs, treated them, and then — what surprised and greatly edified me, and which confirmed ever more to me her sanctity already in those early years — I saw her lick the sores of that poor creature with her tongue, kiss them affectionately, and rebandage them with truly admirable charity. I never said anything of what I had seen, because I was certain that, out of her great humility and the care she took to hide her heroic virtues, she would have been distressed to find herself discovered in so pious and heroic an act; but I could never forget that deed, and my veneration for her grew ever greater.

When I then begged her to rest a little, that I would do the service by the sick woman's side, she knew how to say so much that there was no way to get her to rest, and she continued her care until morning; one could plainly see it was her delight to serve the sick, in whom she truly recognized the adorable person of Jesus, and she always preferred the poorest. I could not enjoy her edifying company for long, since both of us were sent to other houses, but I always kept towards her the greatest esteem and veneration, and I did not see her again until 1878, on the occasion of the Holy Exercises held in Piacenza.

We made the journey together from Loreto to Piacenza; I came from Acquaviva and she from a house near Loreto; here we met and got into the same compartment. In this circumstance too, painful for her, since as was said she had been unjustly accused, or rather slandered, I was able to admire her great virtue and humility.

When we met, she said to me: "This morning I went to confession, I made Holy Communion at the Holy House; let happen what may, I am at peace and wholly abandoned in my Lord." Did she perhaps know what was being said against her? I do not know!... During the journey, it was August and quite hot, and we all felt the need now and then to refresh ourselves; she never took so much as a drop of water, and remained fasting in this way until the next day, until a late hour, and made Holy Communion and heard Holy Mass together with me at the Church of the Capuchin Fathers, since at the Mother House it had already been celebrated earlier, by the time we arrived.

We made the Holy Exercises; it is needless to say with what recollection and devotion she made them. When all was over, word spread that grave accusations had been made against her, and that she would have to undergo a great humiliation; I cannot describe my dismay, for I could not persuade myself that Sr. A. del Salvatore could have done anything that would lead to such a decision; and so, together with other sisters who shared my feeling, we proposed to ask the Superiors, on her behalf, for the grace that such a resolution not be reached; this we did, and it was all obtained.

Her innocence was later recognized. In the meantime, she seemed a little sad, yes, but with a calm and resigned sadness, and ready for anything; yet she said she would always love and pray for the dear Institute; not one word of excuse or defense came from her lips; on the contrary she would say to me: "Ah! if the Lord did not hold his Most Holy Hands upon my head, I could do this and worse"; and, wholly abandoned into the Lord's hands, she entrusted her defense to Him, who, though He may put those dear to him through hard trials, never fails afterwards to make their innocence and holiness shine out all the more; and so he did with this His Servant.

During this time, she having lost the Crucifix we wore at our side, no one knew how, I, at the end of the Exercises, having gone out into the city, was given a Crucifix like our own, and I, knowing she was without hers, wished to give it to her, but she would not accept it without first having the Mother's permission, which was granted her, and only then did she take it; in this too one sees how delicate her conscience was. From that time I never saw her again, and after some years, that is in 1885, she flew up to heaven to receive the reward of her virtues.

All that I have set forth is the plain truth, which I am ready to swear to if asked.

Sister A. Elisabetta Veronesi

12. Report of Sister Anna Camilla Valentini, general counselor, of 26 February 1913, written in the form of memoirs (Proc. p. 549).

She narrates a crucial moment: at the end of the spiritual exercises of 1878, the Servant of God was on the verge of being expelled from the Institute. She highlights her humility and serenity under trial, and the spirit of prayer and penance that accompanied her throughout her life.

Memoirs

In 1878 I was at Borgo S. Donnino; it seems to me that in the month of August the Holy Exercises for the Superiors were held in Piacenza.

I was called, but could go only on the last day — that is, the closing day. On reaching Piacenza, several Superiors told me that on that day they would strip the habit from Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi and send her away from the Institute. Without asking the reason for such a decision, I asked where Sr. Anna Salvatore was: "In the church," I was told; and indeed she was there, wholly absorbed in prayer, calm and serene.

I went down to the garden, where some sisters were; I asked a few questions to find out something, and I met Sr. A. Celsa Speranza, now Secretary General. I asked her whether she knew the reason for what was about to happen, and she answered that she did not. A certain Sr. A. Palmira Grillotti joined us, telling us: "Come along too, let's all go together and ask the Mother's forgiveness for Sr. Anna del Salvatore." We went, and forgiveness was obtained.

Several Superiors went to the chapel to tell her that the Mother had forgiven her, and she, all rejoicing, thanked first the Lord, then the Mother General, and all of us. I was most edified by the bearing of that good soul, which I have never been able to forget; indeed, at the mere memory of what happened I have always been moved.

I remember having heard a sister say (whose name I no longer recall) that on a journey made from Piacenza to Ferrara, or from Ferrara to Rome, Sr. Anna del Salvatore was tempted to leave the institute, and was almost on the point of giving in, when her Guardian Angel appeared visibly to her and told her to obey and continue on her way. At once she asked forgiveness for that weakness of hers and went on with the journey.

The Sisters often told me that Sr. Anna del Salvatore ate only once a day, and if sometimes they made her eat supper, she obeyed, but shortly after was forced to bring it back up. They also told me: "When she was in Palermo, the cook sister had the duty of gathering every morning all the leftover milk, coffee, left in the sisters' cups, as well as the leftover bread — even if only little crumbs — then putting everything in the cup of the Superior, Sr. Anna del Salvatore." And this, most of the time, made up her meal.

In the last years of her life, she spent part of the night in the chapel before Jesus — and part still working at the humblest tasks of the house — or in the laundry, cleaning clothes or doing the housework. All this out of a great spirit of penance. I did not come close to Sr. Anna del Salvatore very often, but I always held her in the highest esteem, having heard told many acts of great virtue she performed; along with the Institute, I too considered her a Saint.

All that I have set forth above is the plain truth, and I am ready to take an oath to it.

Rome, 26-2-13

Sr. A. Camilla Valentini
