15. Report of Sister Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi, of 28 February 1913 (Proc. p. 553).

She stresses her spirit of prayer and mortification, her humility and fortitude under trial, and the esteem the Foundress Rosa Gattorno held for her.

A. M. F.

What I can say of Sr. A. Salvatore.

Her prayer was continuous and fervent. Her charity towards the poor was so great; she attended them with love and comforted them with warm words of God's love.

Once in Genoa I went on night watch with Sr. Anna Salvatore; I felt so sleepy, and she said to me: "Sleep, I will do everything for the sick woman"; and in the moments when nothing was being done for the sick woman, I saw her many times on her knees praying; then she died, and I, filled with fear, had myself placed to one side, and she went on praying.

When she saw an offense against God, she would exclaim: "Either Paradise or the desert," so afire was she with the desire to be united with God. In assisting at Holy Mass and in receiving Jesus in the Sacrament into her heart, she was so recollected. She would come back from her labors always cheerful, the delight of everyone; on her face shone the joy of her heart, always showing herself merry and serene. In Palermo, in the house called "the poor man's morsel," she set her bed in a corridor near a little window, below which was the church, and there she prayed.

I cannot say just how observant she was of the law of fasting; her abstinences were so many; she always ate the humblest things. One day I invited her to dine (at the Pignatelli Institute in Palermo, where the deponent was Superior, a secretary's note); it was the eve of St. Joseph; she did not want to accept, saying that eating made her ill; after much pleading she agreed to stay, but her suffering was so great that I said I would never again make her obey such a request.

I remember once when she came to me; as she drew near I noticed a certain bad odor; I wanted to know what it was, and she was forced to confide in me that she had had a blister plaster on her stomach for many days, without ever having it treated; I ordered her to remove it; she told me she would, but with some reluctance. She took no care of herself at all; when she needed something, she was accustomed to turn to Jesus in the Sacrament and to the Most Holy Virgin. With her speech she kindled such fervor. When she received anything, however small, she showed her full gratitude.

She suffered persecutions and slander. Once, all the Superiors were called to make the Holy Exercises in Piacenza, and dear Sr. A. Salvatore came to me, saying: "Do you know what they're saying? That in these days a Superior is going to be stripped of her habit; who will it be, poor creature? God grant it isn't true; meanwhile, let us pray for her." The next day she came to find me again, as I was in bed; she threw herself upon me, crying: "Crocifissa, it's me, that wretched one! I am innocent, I don't know what this is about." When the holy exercises ended, everyone left, and she remained in Piacenza. After a few months, we saw each other again, and she told me of something that had happened to her, after that storm. Almost immediately she received the obedience to go as Superior to Sermoneta; getting off the train, she felt tempted not to go on, and instead to go to her uncle, a priest, who loved her so much, and to lay aside her habit; she had a fierce struggle between yes and no; suddenly she felt an invisible hand give her a push, and heard a voice telling her: "Go on, continue on your way"; and so she did.

She was most zealous for the worship of God, guarding all the things of the chapel with such care. She always showed such reverence and obedience to her Superiors; she esteemed everyone above herself: she was never heard to utter an offensive word against anyone, and always held herself the last of all. I know that the Venerated Mother, whenever she had some sister to be reformed in spirit, would send her to Sr. Anna Salvatore, for indeed they would come back better and more virtuous.

I also remember that a fellow sister confided to her that she was in great anguish because she did not love the Lord, but she, with an example, managed to set her mind at ease, assuring her too that she did have the love of God.

I pray that my fellow sister may also soon be venerated at the altars.

Sister Anna Crocifissa Fiocchi

Siena, 28 February 1913

16. Report of the priest Petronio Russo, of 28 February 1913, written in the form of a letter to the superior general Sister Anna Benedetta Carrega (Proc. p. 554).

He highlights the heroic fortitude and humility of the Servant of God, witnessed during a visit of hers to the house of Adernò (today Adrano).

I. M. I.

Adernò, 28 February 1913

Most Reverend Mother General,

Having had, in 1882, the good fortune to call the Daughters of St. Anne to direct this municipal hospital and poorhouse, around 1884 I had the good fortune to come to know and appreciate, in passing, in the very few days of her stay in Adernò, the heroic virtue of fortitude and humility of Sister Anna Salvatore Orsi, who had come here as Provincial to inspect her daughters in J.C.

This poorhouse was administered by the confraternity of charity, whose President was Fr. Benedetto Ciancio, of the Friars Minor. He imprudently asked of the Sisters, as a favor, a service that the Mother Provincial neither could nor should grant according to the rules of the Institute. Fr. Ciancio insisted until he heaped insults and abuse upon her. But she did not react at all; rather, she humbly accepted the insults and remained steadfast in upholding the Institute's good name.

It seemed fitting to me, as parish priest, confessor of the Sisters, and one of the leading citizens of Adernò, to apologize to her for the insult she had suffered. She, however, all calm and smiling, kept repeating: "That Father said words that I deserved." Moreover, she added: "Be at ease, Father, it is the Sisters who want to call me Provincial, but I am the servant of the Daughters of St. Anne."

Keep me in your prayers, and believe me yours

Most devoted always in J. Christ

Provost Petronio Russo

17. Report of Sister Anna Nazaria Provera, of 1 March 1913 (Proc. p. 555).

She illustrates the heroic exercise of the virtues practiced by the Servant of God: the theological virtues, prudence, temperance, and humility.

A. M. F.

Fontanella, 1.3.13

I believe it right and a duty to testify, in all conscience, to what I observed in the year 1884 in the city of Palermo regarding the religious virtues practiced by the servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi.

1. - Of her heroic Faith

So great was the servant of God's faith that she prayed at length before the Most Holy Sacrament, spending whole nights there, in any season of the year. She exhorted us, her subjects, to seek in God our only comfort. She heard Holy Mass with deep recollection, as well as the Community prayers, meditation, the Sacraments, etc. She held the Supreme Pontiff, the Prelates, and the other priests in great veneration.

I sometimes saw her pay homage to the Most Eminent Cardinal Celesia with such a sense of faith that she prostrated herself to the ground, kissing his sacred ring, with the greatest veneration. She was most zealous for the dignity of the church, striving to adorn it with great care, as a sign of love for the house of the Lord.

2. - Of her heroic Hope

Standing at the head of a large community, in the city of Palermo, where the Sisters had to live on alms, she was not troubled by temporal matters, but hoped solely in God, exhorting us, her Sisters, not to worry, even in difficult circumstances, confident that the Lord never fails those who trust in Him. Her health was frail, yet she took on any labor, trusting that the Lord would grant her the strength necessary to sustain the duties of the office of Mother Provincial of all Sicily.

3. - Of her heroic Charity towards God

She observed the laws of the Church exactly, even to the point of scrupulousness. She avoided even the smallest offense against God. In her bearing one could sense a heart aflame with love for God. When questioned, she answered with few words, so as not to be drawn away from her deep recollection.

4. - Of her heroic Charity towards her Neighbor

She loved the poor, helping them in all their needs. She was most attentive to the sick poor, spending whole nights lavishing on them all the care their illnesses required. She eased their suffering with the most gracious manner, so much so that word spread that she was a great saint. All the sick wished to be cared for by her, for the relief they felt. She never complained, whatever insult she received. I myself observed that, having received a harsh insult, she trembled from the effort it cost her to restrain herself, yet did not utter a single word in her own defense.

5. - Of her heroic Prudence

In all her manner of acting she was most prudent. She had no aim but the Glory of God. She disposed of nothing without the counsel of her Spiritual Director and of the dear Mother, for whom she held profound veneration. At a mere sign from her, she would undertake any journey, heedless of any effort involved. At home, everything proceeded in order. She was the first at the heaviest tasks, especially those of the laundry, by night and by day.

6. - Of her heroic Temperance

She was temperate in character, always courteous, patient, mortified in touch; she almost never used a bed, contenting herself with a little sleep taken uncomfortably on the altar step, before the Most Holy Sacrament. She mortified her palate, always eating humble, scant food from the kitchen and the like. Not even in times of illness did she allow herself delicate food, unless compelled by Holy Obedience.

7. - Of her heroic Humility

The servant of God showed no esteem for herself. She spoke very little, and accepted deference only out of necessity. She hid from the eyes of others the good she did, content only to please the Lord.

This is what I can attest to of the virtues of the servant of God, Sr. Anna del Salvatore Orsi, over the course of one year. After that, no longer being in the same house, I had no occasion to witness the virtuous acts she performed, either in her final illness or after her precious death.

Of everything I have set forth in this account, I would be ready to swear to it as well, should there be need. May all of this contribute to the glory of the Lord, and to seeing our dear St. Anna del Salvatore venerated by the Church at the Altars.

This is the wish of one who, with confidence, signs

Sister A. Nazaria Provera

18. Report — in the form of memoirs — of Sister Anna Costanza Cenni, of 5 March 1913 (Proc. p. 557).

She highlights the exquisite charity the Servant of God showed towards the sick, her humility and her gracious manner, which she observed while accompanying her on the alms round. She recalls that, when she was about to be expelled from the Institute, the Servant of God declared herself ready for sacrifice, like Isaac, and willing in any case to help the Institute.

The author was also a witness to graces obtained through her intercession.

Memoirs to be kept concerning Sister A. Salvatore Orsi

I certify I observe the following:

In 1874 I first came to know Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi at Sestri Ponente; I, being ill from an operation performed on my throat, can assure you that she showed me great charity, both for my soul and for my body; with her I went several times to keep watch over the sick, and the sick themselves called her "the angel of comfort," and vied with one another over who could have her near their bedside. That little free time she had at night she spent in prayer; with her I went on the alms round, and such was her humility, her gracious manner, that no one dared to refuse her a small offering. One day she came to accompany us for bathing, myself and the Superior. Now it happened that the Superior suddenly lost her balance and fell into the water, in danger of drowning; so great was the charity and heroism of Sister Anna del Salvatore that she at once made as if to throw herself in, dressed as she was, to grab hold of the Superior, but was quickly stopped by the lifeguard, who stepped forward.

With her I was in Florence, and I declare I can attest that I found in that sister a particular drawing towards every virtue, especially love of God, and I can say she communicated it also to others.

I am witness to a humiliation she suffered at the Mother House in Piacenza. She was accused of a grave fault, unknown to me; not seeing her with us as usual, I went looking for where she was, and found her in the dormitory, alone, holding a bundle of letters in her hands; I asked her: "What are you doing here? What are those papers you're holding?" She answered me: "They are letters from Mother General." Well then, I added: "What will you do with these letters?" She, with all gentleness, but greatly pained, said: "I have heard that today they will take off my Holy Veil, and I will hand these letters over to the Mother; I will put up no resistance at all, I will do as Isaac did, who made the sacrifice of his life. I will lay my head on the Mother's knees, as Isaac laid himself on the bundle of wood; let her do as she wishes, I will offer no resistance whatsoever; but if I must leave the Institute, I shall try, in my lowliness, to do as much good as I can for the institute, and if necessary I will even go begging alms to help it." I admired in her a great virtue: not a word in her own defense, not a complaint, but great humility and resignation.

I was witness to many graces received by the simple means of her portrait placed upon the sick, even instant cures, such as, for example: Sr. A. of the Stigmata, declared by the doctor to have lost an eye, was healed when the portrait of Sr. A. del Salvatore was placed on the eye. I declare that I had an operation on my throat, and many years later the illness recurred; before having myself examined, I suffered terribly; it occurred to me to take the portrait of Sr. A. del Salvatore and apply it to the ailment, which was spasmodic; there was no need to have myself seen by doctors, because I was already healed. — I found myself in a Hospital she had opened, where I was sent as Superior; finding myself in certain critical circumstances and not knowing what to do, it occurred to me to turn to her, as in an act of prayer (saying: "You, dear Sr. A. Salvatore, I know for certain it was you who inspired the dear Mother to send me here. You think about it, then; you are the Superior, not I") — I can assure you, with complete truth, that all obstacles, after this prayer, vanished; and things always went from good to better, all to the glory of God.

I heard from a priest in Sicily that, having obtained a handkerchief used by the said Sr. A. Salvatore and a rosary, he used them to place on the sick, and these had great effect; I also heard from the same priest that he obtained many graces through the sister's merits; his name is a certain Father Galliani; I do not know if he is still alive; he was in Palermo; perhaps Sister Rosalba might remember him.

She was most loving of poverty; her obedience and respect for Mother General were extraordinary; simply recalling the dear Mother's name filled her with great joy.

Here is the degree of her humility: when I congratulated her on being made Provincial, she blushed deeply, and, convinced in her heart of what she showed outwardly, answered me: "The dear Mother could not have found a more wretched creature than me. God wishes to humble me; patience." This is the esteem in which she held positions of office. This is the plain truth.

As for her spirit of sacrifice, it reached to heroism; she would have suffered any pain to see her neighbor happy in every respect.

For now I cannot say more; this seems to me the plain and holy truth.

Arena Po, 5 March 1913

Sister A. Costanza Cenni

19. Report of Sister Anna Del Consiglio Chiaramonte, of 5 March 1913 (Proc. p. 559).

She narrates her first encounter with the Servant of God, and what she heard her fellow sisters recount of her union with God and her charity; she then goes on at length to testify about each of the theological, cardinal, and related virtues, and about her supernatural gifts.

Institute of the Sacred Heart of Jesus

Monreale, 5 March 1913

It was in the year 1883 that I had the good fortune to come to know, quite closely, and to be convinced of, the rare virtues with which Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi was adorned; that is, when I was at the Mother House in Piacenza as a novice.

She came from Sicily, from Palermo itself, where she held the office of Provincial Superior, to confer, as was usual, with our Holy Foundress and Mother General Rosa Gattorno; and, at the same time, to gladden a number of Palermo novices with her presence. — One can well imagine that as soon as she appeared in the Novitiate's workroom, a good number of young Sisters surrounded her, besieging her with questions; and she, with all gentleness and kindness, tried to answer every question put to her and to satisfy the fair wishes of each one: to one she gave a smile, to another a word of comfort and encouragement, often punctuating her speech with this lovely phrase — "Let us all become saints, for up there with Him, dear Jesus wants us." And as she said this, her eyes sparkled with holy and purest joy, while her face, flushing with a lively glow, no longer seemed a creature of this earth, but a Seraph who burns and lives only on the love of God.

I, who, I repeat, was present at so compelling a scene, need hardly say whether I stood there entranced, minutely observing the wonderful phenomena that, one after another, followed on that heroine of love's face, and soon a murmur of several voices reached my ear: "Sr. A. del Salvatore is about to be caught up in ecstasy any moment... The Provincial of Sicily is a saint," they added, "yes, everyone says so." No more was needed for me to form, from that hour on, a holy opinion and to nourish a true and solid devotion to the venerated Person of the Servant of God, and not I alone, for I often heard the rare virtues of this seraphic creature praised. Whenever I heard it spoken of, a holy envy came over me; mulling it over in my small and ignorant mind, searching for the reasons why the Servant of God was so holy, and I so full of every imperfection.

I was quite young then, and did not understand that Sr. A. del Salvatore had earned such high perfection through the force of great sacrifices; continual and fervent prayer, nightly vigils, which, as I heard from the Sisters who had the good fortune to live alongside her, never gave the least rest to her weary and emaciated body; she would spend whole nights on her knees praying, melting in acts of love before Jesus in the Sacrament. On the days set aside for the Sisters' laundry, she was the first to take part, and sought every means, with holy pretexts, to send the Sisters away so that she alone could take on all that labor; and often, as I heard from the Sisters, she would get up from the lye and rinse all the clothes left to soak the day before. In the morning, amazed, the Sisters would ask who had done that; she, turning them away from any suspicion, told them it had been St. Anne.

What I have set forth above is a slight showing compared with all that this Soul, enamored of Jesus, hid of what was virtuous and holy; and yet I swear that what I have said is the plain truth; called upon to make a declaration, I would affirm it with a thousand oaths.

Of her heroic Faith

So great was the love the Servant of God bore for her Jesus that one need hardly say whether, at every minute of the day, she gave him thanks for having her born into the bosom of the Church and of Catholic parents. With fearless candor she always showed everyone that she firmly believed in all the articles of the Faith and the most sublime Mysteries. She showed the most tender affection for the Most Holy Virgin, calling on her often during the day by the sweetest and most tender names and titles. She prepared to celebrate feasts with works of piety, and then with fasts and penances. One cannot say with what devotion and recollection she stood before Jesus in the Sacrament. It seemed her heart wished to melt away, so tender and fervent — indeed so ardent — were the acts of love, sorrow, and humility she offered him. Her fervor was immense when she heard Holy Mass and frequented the Sacraments of Penance and the Eucharist. She was most devoted to the Passion of Jesus, and spoke of it with such feeling that it kindled fervor in all who heard her. She instilled devotion in everyone, especially the sick, whom she led to regard their bed as the Cross of Jesus and to offer him their painful illnesses. Very great was the love she bore towards St. Anne, our glorious Mother, and with what devotion, and with what exercises of piety, she prepared every year to celebrate her feast!... She likewise professed great devotion to St. Joseph, to St. Michael, and to the Guardian Angel, and when she instructed children or the unlettered, she urged on them devotion to these dear saints, especially to the Most Holy Virgin.

She was most attached to the laws and precepts of the Holy Church, and therefore held a holy veneration for it; most respectful of the head of the Church, that is, the Supreme Pontiff, of the Bishops and of all priests, whom she regarded as the very person of Jesus Christ. She always wished to gain indulgences, and let no slightest occasion slip to benefit the Souls of the Departed by them. Most zealous, then, for the dignity of God's house, she aimed above all at silence, orderliness, and recollection, and then at the careful tending of the Sacred Vessels and other furnishings.

Of her heroic Hope

The Servant of God always showed that she held a very low opinion of herself, to the point of considering herself a great sinner, yet she firmly hoped to obtain eternal salvation through the infinite merits of our Lord Jesus Christ.

She never worried about nor showed excessive concern for temporal matters; she always hoped in God, even in the most difficult and sudden circumstances, redoubling her prayer and her fervor, and, serene and calm, awaited the happy outcome. She suffered always, and at every time, slanders and persecutions such as would have weakened and terrified souls endowed with solid and vigorous virtue. But the Servant of God never lost her serenity of spirit, nor her peace of conscience; she always showed herself calm and serene, whether in prosperous or adverse circumstances, and always prayed for her fiercest persecutors.

She was often visited by her dear and loving Jesus with quite painful illnesses, but she always bore them with unwavering patience; indeed, she seemed to rejoice in them, for her face was more cheerful than usual. All her desires, every sigh of her heart, were turned towards heaven; so in her conversation there was nothing but God and heaven, kindling such wholesome longings and stirring them even in the hardest hearts. With a manner of life of such great perfection, one can well understand, and it is no wonder, that the Servant of God obtained from her beloved spouse Jesus graces and benefits, and even the gift of miracles; this as a reward for her heroic hope.

Of her heroic Charity towards God

The Servant of God was most observant, indeed most scrupulous in keeping both divine and ecclesiastical law, and one cannot say how much she hated and abhorred sin; indeed she gave all possible and imaginable attention to avoiding even the slightest faults. She never undertook anything without having invoked divine help, and kept her mind always turned to her God; hence it follows that she was always in continual union with her Good, speaking of him always and with such feeling, with such tenderness, as to kindle even the hardest and coldest hearts. — Her prayer was continual, and ever constant and fervent until death.

When the Servant of God heard some rash person blaspheme the Holy Name of God, Sr. A. del Salvatore was horrified, even trembled, and loudly intoned "Blessed be God," etc., and, so that no greater offense be committed against His Divine Majesty, she sought every means to calm the rash offender, and then made reparation for the outrage with exercises of penance and mortifications she inflicted on her exhausted body. Besides the frequent, that is, continual works of devotion she repeated throughout the day, the Servant of God addressed her Jesus with continual and ardent short prayers.

Of her heroic Charity towards her neighbor

The Servant of God was all love and charity towards the poor, especially the sick; she helped them generously, as far as her strength allowed, comforted them, and then recommended them to the wealthy so they might assist them. Immense was the charity she had towards the poor and abandoned sick, especially those with contagious diseases. The servant of God cared for them with love and charity, cleaned them, washed their putrid and gangrenous sores, urged them to patience and resignation, and had them consider their bed as the Cross of Jesus; she had them confess, receive communion, and prepared them for the great passage. She was tireless for the sake of obstinate poor sinners; she left no means untried to convert them and draw them to God. She used the most winning manner to induce them to give up sin; she made them promises of generous gifts, if they were poor; and when that was not enough, she turned to prayer, to penance, punishing her body and mistreating it with fasts, hairshirts, harsh and bloody scourgings. The same exercise of penance she used to pray for the Holy Souls in Purgatory. She always prayed for her enemies, especially for her fiercest persecutors, and never raised the slightest complaint against them.

Of her heroic Prudence

The prudence the Servant of God practiced was quite different from that of worldly people, since her actions were wholly directed towards God, from whom she expected to attain eternal glory. And she sought to attain it with an irreproachable purity of conscience, and so had a great fear of offending God; hence her prayer was continual, as was the scrupulous watch she kept over her senses, subjecting her rebellious flesh to the spirit with never-interrupted scourgings, hairshirts, fasts, and mortifications of every kind. All this she carried out with the order and express obedience of her superiors and spiritual directors, for whom she held untouchable respect and veneration. The Servant of God always fled idleness like the plague, and so always worked, even taking sleep from her own eyes to ease the weariness of the Sisters. Her immense charity could not bear to see her own fellow sisters, who kept watch at night attending the sick, also having to attend to other wearisome tasks by day.

Of her heroic Justice

The Servant of God was most zealous in everything concerning the worship of God. She was submissive, obedient, and respectful of her Superiors to the point of scrupulousness, humble and meek with her equals, kind and charitable with the sick, and the same towards everyone. Her words and her conversation were simple, without the slightest trace of pretense, duplicity, or dissimulation.

Of her heroic Temperance

The Servant of God was never seen upset, for she was of a gentle and meek character. She was most temperate and mortified in her eating, always choosing for herself the coarsest food in small quantity. She allowed her body very little sleep, spending whole nights praying on her knees, or seeing to some task to relieve the Sisters, or else going out to attend to the sick at home.

For her own use she always chose the worn and discarded clothes of the Sisters. She tamed her flesh with harsh penances, scourgings, hairshirts, and mortifications of every kind.

She was most modest in her eyes, keeping them always lowered, especially when conversing with persons of the opposite sex. She always tried to mortify her hearing as well, and in general all her senses, never allowing the slightest relief to her exhausted body.

Of her heroic Fortitude

The Servant of God was always strong in enduring any adversity, both in illness and in the injuries and persecutions that came to her at the hands of wicked men. She was always strong, steadfast, and undaunted on the path of perfection she had undertaken, always showing herself the same both in adverse and in prosperous circumstances.

Of her heroic Humility

The Servant of God never showed any wish to be esteemed, much less praised; and, an enemy of her own esteem, she fled praise as from the infernal serpent. She held a very low opinion of herself and of worldly things, and if she accepted the office of Provincial Superior, it was only to obey her Superiors, who imposed it on her by Holy Obedience.

Of her Supernatural Gifts

A soul so great and enlightened, and which felt such lowliness of herself, one cannot say how many graces and favors, as well as supernatural gifts, she received from her God, whom she loved with immense love.

The Servant of God, who felt such deep abasement of her body as to treat it like a vile beast of burden, deserved, in all justice, to be exalted by God and enriched with supernatural favors and gifts, graces freely given, that is, to heal the sick of incurable diseases by making the sign of the Cross over the affliction and turning to God with a fervent prayer; and to foretell the future to very many people.

Of her reputation for holiness in life and after death.

Although the Servant of God was so modest and reserved in her manner of acting, attributing to God the merit of working miracles, nevertheless people, edified by such rare modesty, need hardly be said to have held her in such high esteem as to call her a saint. People of every class and condition hastened to her for counsel and instruction and to receive heavenly graces and favors. And how many people, from the city of Palermo and from other parts of Sicily, experienced the beneficial effects of the miracles worked in life by the Servant of God!

After the death of the Servant of God, rather striking graces and miracles occurred through her intercession; that is, instant cures by the mere touch of her relics and by simply invoking her dear name. Still today in Sicily, especially in the city of Palermo, it is widely held that Sister Anna del Salvatore was a saint.

Sister A. del Consiglio Chiaramonte

Of the servant of God Sister A. del Salvatore Orsi, I, the undersigned, cannot testify to many things, because I never lived alongside her; only a few times, and for a very brief time, did I have the good fortune to enjoy her company.

21. Report of Sister Anna Irene Carmeli, of 9 March 1913 (Proc. p. 565).

She narrates various episodes she witnessed and highlights the Servant of God's spirit of mortification, her union with God, her charity especially towards the sick sisters, and her gift of discerning hearts. She also recounts the last moments of the Servant of God's life.

News about the life and death of the Servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi.

In 1882 [sic], for the opening of the House of Castelvetrano, I was a companion of the Servant of God, who had already been appointed Provincial by the venerated Foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno.

We were lodged by Fr. Lentini, and there we stayed for a full 12 days. I never once saw the said Sister rest in the bed prepared for her. She kept watch all night long, and when her weary limbs demanded relief, she would lie down on the bare ground. In the morning, as if nothing had happened, she would go to church to hear Holy Mass, feeding on the Bread of Angels, and would remain for a long time as if in ecstasy before Jesus in the Host.

She liked to live on simple herbs, and when by necessity she had to join the daily meals in the company of the priest's family who hosted us, she casually tasted only a little of the food offered to her, but soon returned to her own room, setting aside the rest with unspeakable suffering. This happened every day we remained in Castelvetrano; meanwhile, she concealed her own suffering. During that stay, all who came near her venerated her as a saint, and vied with one another to have her in their own home, even if only for a little while.

The Servant of God, visiting that town's hospital, found there a poor sick woman struggling between life and death. The woman then commended herself to the good Sister, begging her to obtain her healing from God. Sr. A. del Salvatore remained silent a while, then, looking to heaven, added: "Daughter, ask the Lord rather for the salvation of your soul, for there is no hope at all for the health of your body." For two days she did not cease comforting the sick woman, until she convinced her to receive the Most Holy Sacraments. That poor woman died in the grace of God, calm and tranquil. It was later learned that she had not approached the altar in many years.

Sr. A. del Salvatore also exercised charity towards all the needy in general, but was most sensitive towards the sick Sisters, taking care that they lacked nothing necessary, attending to them herself and comforting them to suffer so as to gain merits for paradise.

In 1883, in Palermo, in the Briuccia palace — then the provincial house — the first Daughter of St. Anne, Sr. A. Albina, died the death of the just. Being gathered together, we sisters spoke of the deceased's virtues and her precious death. One of us said: "Sr. A. Albina is truly a saint, she could be venerated." The servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore then exclaimed: "No sister will be venerated at the altars before our foundress is venerated."

Sister Anna Orsi — a sister once told me — in 1881, having to travel from Piacenza to Palermo, always traveled in a third-class compartment, ate once a day, and only bread. Crossing the sea, the sister took a berth, and the Servant of God, promptly putting out the light, lay down on the floor. The Sister, needing to get down from the berth, so as not to disturb her, climbed down in the dark, unintentionally putting her feet on the body of the Provincial Sr. A. del Salvatore, who immediately got up, asked the sister if she had hurt herself, and, embracing her, asked her a thousand pardons.

On approaching the Most Holy Sacraments, especially the tribunal of penance, she wept copiously, saying she was a great sinner. She had the utmost devotion to Our Lady of Lourdes, and I often saw her before the miraculous Virgin, praying and weeping.

One day I was sitting with her, as she lay ill, when a letter arrived from the venerated Mother Gattorno, telling Sr. A. del Salvatore to go to a town in Sicily on important business. The virtuous Sr. A. del Salvatore, though suffering and all swollen, without saying a word, left her bed and departed.

Most grateful for her vocation, she often addressed words of thanksgiving to her Heavenly Spouse for having chosen her as his bride, and uttered them with infinite ardor and great humility, considering herself unworthy of such a lot. In 1880 the Daughters of St. Anne were called to Palermo to carry out their work of charity, caring for the sick at home. Sr. A. del Salvatore was chosen as superior. They settled in the house of St. Mark, a very poor house, lacking everything. That virtuous Superior was not at all discouraged; rather, she encouraged her daughters to trust in Providence, and often, unexpectedly, they were provided with what they needed.

Her death was precious. In her final moments, aware that the end was near, she asked forgiveness of all her fellow sisters; she urged them to observe the Institute's rules, to pray, and to persevere in their vocation. Her devotion and living faith were admirable as she asked for and received the Holy Viaticum and Extreme Unction. Comforted by all the Sacraments of the Church, she crossed her arms over her chest in the form of a cross, remaining for some moments as if caught up in ecstasy... Before dying, she opened her eyes, bade all of us gathered around her bed a final farewell... and peacefully breathed her last.

I confess, in my conscience, that these written accounts of the virtue of the provincial Sr. A. del Salvatore are in accordance with the truth.

Palermo, 9 March 1913

Sister Anna Irene Carmeli

22. Report of Sister Anna Raffaela Ceruti, of 13 March 1913 (Proc. p. 568).

Brief though it is, this is a valid testimony on the theological virtues, the spirit of mortification, the deep humility, and the reputation for sanctity enjoyed by the Servant of God.

Of the Faith of the servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi.

Her faith was most firm on all the articles of our Holy Religion; she was notable for her devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament of the Eucharist, so that, unable because of her duties to spend long hours during the day to satisfy her burning longing, she would remain whole nights without taking any rest.

Her hope rested solely in God; in the most difficult circumstances she was always cheerful and content with whatever God disposed for her; under slander she kept silent and prayed, always the same; threatened with punishment she did not change her ways, but rather, in those difficult moments, seemed to unite herself more closely with God, so much so that it seemed it was not she who suffered such distress; and this convinces me of her innocence, that she suffered it all for love of God and for justice.

Her charity towards her neighbor was boundless; especially in attending the sick at home, she was always first, day and night, never disdaining the humblest tasks, especially among the poor where necessities were lacking, and her charity shone brightest in begging alms from the rich to relieve the misery of others.

With the Sisters her charity stood out even more, relieving them of their labors, taking on herself the heaviest ones; with the sick she exercised every vigilance, so that they were provided with everything that could be useful in relieving them, both morally, with charitable words urging them to suffer everything out of love for God who suffered so much for us, and physically, making sure nothing was lacking for that purpose.

In eating she was most mortified, contenting herself most of the time with eating even the sisters' leftovers, doing this with such ease so as not to be noticed by the Community.

In humility she was singular; she held herself to be the most abject, incapable of discharging the office assigned to her by her Superiors, and she said this with such conviction that it was clearly no affectation, but solid virtue.

With people she often dealt with by reason of her office, if she so much as sensed they valued her virtue, she always tried to hide herself as much as she could; but since virtue makes its own way, however much she tried to conceal herself, the Lord, who exalts the humble, never failed to make shine forth in his servant the virtue most dear to her, to the point of edifying others by her outward bearing; there were those who entrusted themselves to her prayers to obtain graces through her.

Among these are mentioned two Benedictine nun sisters who, their father being old and ill and unwilling to receive the Most Holy Sacraments, dismayed, begged her to commend their father to the Lord for his conversion; she answered that they should rest assured, that the grace would be granted; meanwhile, the servant of God passed on to her eternal rest before the said sick man; one day, finding themselves disappointed, one of them complained of the deceased for not having obtained the grace for her; that night she appeared to her in a dream and told her to rest assured, that the grace was granted; this came to pass, for the sick man received the Most Holy Sacraments with signs of a true Christian; this rewarded the two nuns, who recounted this fact with true conviction that they had received the grace through her.

This is what I can affirm concerning the virtues of the Servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore.

Sister Anna Raffaela Ceruti

Caltanissetta, 13-3-913

24. Report of Mr. Luigi Curà, of 22 March 1913, written in the form of a letter to his brother-in-law don Valentino Orsi (Proc. p. 570).

He sets forth the information gathered from relatives and contemporaries of the Servant of God concerning the period of her youth.

Albareto, 22-3-1913

Dearest brother-in-law,

In reply to your esteemed letter of the 21st of February last, I inform you that I have questioned Messrs. Mussi Lorenzo, Don Tommaso Grilli, parish priest of Albareto, and other contemporaries of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, our cousin, who died in Palermo in 1885, provincial nun, about the qualities, gifts of spirit, character, religion, prayers, and virtues with which she was endowed in the brief time she stayed in Albareto.

They declare and depose, as far as is within their knowledge, that the aforesaid Orsi Marianna was a young woman of good nature, mild character, generous heart, without vanity in her dress or her personal bearing, sincere, cheerful, modest in conversing with her peers, obedient and respectful. With recollection she carried out her daily devotions or prayers, and with devotion frequented the Sacraments.

She never failed to attend novenas and feasts, even devotional ones. She willingly took part in accompanying the Blessed Sacrament when it was carried to the sick. She resigned herself with patience when she lacked something she needed. However, there is no record that Orsi, in Albareto, showed signs of extraordinary gifts or the exercise of special virtues to a heroic degree.

Valentina also asked those of Casa Mazzetta, of the Moie, of Case Mirani and of Costello what they could say about the said Sister Orsi, their companion and peer, and all attest that she was good, kind, cheerful, patient in adversity, and assiduously frequented the Sacraments. They also attest that, if she took part in some amusement in the company of other companions (such as invitations to dances and weddings, etc.), the next day she wept over the mistake she had made.

This is what I can report concerning Sister Anna del Salvatore. In returning the questionnaire sent to me, and wishing you a happy Easter, I send you the most cordial and sincere greetings, also on behalf of my whole family, and remain

Your most affectionate brother-in-law

Curà Luigi

25. Report of don Tommaso Grilli, of 5 April 1913, written in the form of a letter to Sister Anna Fabiana Orsi, sister of the Servant of God (Proc. p. 571).

He attests to the virtues of the Servant of God, above all during the period of her youth.

Madam Sister A. Fabiana Orsi,

I feel the greatest consolation in learning from your letter that the proceedings for the Cause of Beatification of Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, your beloved Sister, are being resumed.

As to her life and conduct during the time she lived in Albareto in her youth, I can attest that she was always of good and religious conduct.

She frequented the Most Holy Sacraments with devotion, said her prayers with devotion; at novenas or feasts, even devotional ones, she came to attend them. When needed, she did not fail to accompany the Holy Viaticum to the sick with a candle, and to accompany the bodies of the dead to their resting place.

This parishioner of mine (I say parishioner because, when she left Albareto, I had already been parish priest for 6 years) was a young woman of mild character, calm disposition, without vanity in her dress or her conduct, sincere, cheerful, but modest in conversing with her companions, obedient, respectful. With commendable patience she bore the lack of things she often needed. Being the firstborn, she helped her own mother, with all care and patience, to raise and look after her little brothers and sisters. In this, surely, the exercise of her charity was always a great relief and benefit to her.

Before entering religious life, she returned to Albareto to say farewell to her relatives and her companions, and had a familiar conversation with Mrs. Bosi Valentina of this parish, her confidante, and told the said lady that she had found a match to marry, and had given him hope; but that afterwards (surely enlightened by a higher grace) she thought it over and resolved to renounce the world, and told the young man that she no longer wished to take a husband, because she had decided to become a nun, wishing thus to choose Jesus as her Spouse, as she later did.

I commend myself to your prayers, and, wishing you every blessing from God, I remain yours

A note on the youthful life of Orsi Marianna, daughter of Angelo and of Mussi Domenica, born in Albareto in February 1842, died in Palermo in June 1885.

Concerning the statement of Bottego Orsolina, daughter of Giuseppe, aged 76, of Albareto. I declare and certify that Orsi was always a very good Christian daughter, always honest and most obedient in everything. She always bore with resignation all the tribulations a person may have, and Orsi was always patient and good with everyone; Orsi, being the firstborn of her family, taught Christian upbringing and doctrine to her dear brothers and accompanied them to the sacrifice of Holy Mass, and raised them in the holy Catholic Religion.

Talking with Orsi, she always told me she wanted to go and keep her innocent and pure life among the sisters.

After 1862 Orsi settled elsewhere, and in the course of her life, to deny herself, she almost always ate legumes, but then had grown so weak she could no longer bear it; so she took to eating poultry food several times as penance, and told me she ate it hidden from her parents.

One day she told me that she could have found a good match to marry, but that however rich he might be she would marry no one; her vocation was always to enter an Institute. Municipality of Albareto di Borgotaro

Mayor's Office

9 August 1913

Better late than never: today a postcard sent some time ago by the Reverend Sister Fabiana Orsi came into my hands, in which she asks me for information about the life of her sister, the Reverend Sister Anna del Salvatore, regarding the time of her youth spent here, who died with a reputation for holiness in Palermo: and here is what I can say.

32. Report of Sister Anna Gregoria Poppelmann, undated, probably from 1913, written in the form of a letter to the secretary general Sister Anna Celsa Speranza (Proc. p. 577).

She highlights the charity of the Servant of God, her union with God, and her spirit of penance.

A. M. F.

Reverend Secretary,

To give greater glory to God and out of a spirit of obedience and truth, I say: I had the good fortune to know fully and to appreciate the heroic and illustrious virtues of the Servant of God Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi. I did not, it is true, see her work miracles in her life; but her existence was a continuous miracle. Endowed as she was with supernatural gifts and freely given graces, one would have seen in her a Seraph of love when, before the Most Holy Sacrament, she spent the long hours of the night and also of the day, when time allowed her, remaining motionless, utterly absorbed in the passage of ecstasy and contemplation. Her heart was a burning furnace, and it was enough to speak with her of matters of perfection to feel one's own heart catch fire with holy affections. She also held a special veneration for priests, regarding in them the very person of Jesus Christ.

Most observant of the Holy Constitutions, all heart and charity towards her subjects, whom she loved as a tender Mother, and she knew how to draw honey even from bitter flowers.

What, then, shall be said of her charity towards the sick Sisters? They were her chosen portion; all the time left to her from her ordinary duties, which were not light, she spent at their bedside, serving them even in the humblest tasks, keeping watch over them at night, preparing them for a good death, and only then leaving them once they had already given up their souls to God; when they breathed their last, she would withdraw at once to the chapel to pray, as though she wished to hand over to God, with her own hand, the victim who had already passed away. — She also went to keep watch at private homes, and when her turn for rest came, she spent the night pumping water, washing linens, and making flowers for the chapel, and when her weary limbs demanded the rest they needed, only then would she prostrate herself at the foot of the altar, giving herself over to the sleep of Love.

For her there was neither a room nor a bed. The Sister in charge of linens, when giving her a change of clothing, left it for her in the sacristy.

Her food was a simple soup of legumes, vegetables, or potatoes, at a single meal, at midday; other foods she could not keep down, for after much suffering she was forced to vomit them.

Her natural temperament was always jovial, always cheerful in mood, and she knew well how to conceal her sufferings, both physical and moral. I never saw her lose her composure, except when she saw an offense against God; then, full of zeal and gravity, she worked until she achieved her purpose, or made some reparation.

Everything I have deposed above were things I observed in the various times I had the good fortune to live in the same Community; and when she was elected Provincial, and I was in other houses of Sicily, her visits gladdened us, and we always saw a model in her because of her heroic virtues.

What I have said is too little, but I have told the truth; my capacity does not allow me more. Sincere respects to you, good Secretary, promising to pray always according to your intention. Bless me

Most humble Subject

Sister A. Gregoria Poppelmann
