35. Report of Sister Anna Maristella Calderone, undated, but probably from 1913 (Proc. p. 580).

She underlines the theological and cardinal virtues practiced by the Servant of God, as well as the related virtues; she highlights in particular her charity towards God and her union with him. She was also witness to an instantaneous healing obtained through the Servant of God's intercession.

Notes on the life of Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi.

The servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore had a most vivid faith, which she showed in her continual professions of attachment to the Church's Dogmas, in the abundant tears she shed whenever she set herself to meditate on some truth or mystery of our holy religion, in the ceaseless thanks she gave to the Lord for having had her born in the bosom of the Church and of pious and most religious parents, in the constant supplications she made for the exaltation of the Church, in her most ardent desire to draw to the truth and to Christian practice the sinners she came into contact with by reason of her office, and in the teachings, both in word and in deed, with which she sought to instill in souls, or revive, the sentiment of piety.

Equal to her faith was her hope, for, detached from all earthly things and entirely distrustful of herself, she put her full trust in her God, whose mercy and help she invoked both for the needs of her soul and for the growth of the Institute, which she loved tenderly. And from this complete confidence in God was born in her that admirable peace of heart and that ready conformity to the divine will.

Love for God overflowed warmly in her soul, often causing her to break into expressions, acts, and deeds that showed the beautiful and great soul she was. She also greatly loved her neighbor in God and for God's sake. There was no class of people she forgot, no physical or moral misery she did not ease; there was no sacrifice, even a heroic one, which she would not take on, merely to dry a tear and console an unhappy soul.

Great too was her prudence, which she showed above all in the good government, first of the communities entrusted to her, and then of Sicily, of which she was Provincial, in the direction of souls and in the wisdom of the counsel she gave. She practiced the virtue of justice in a holy manner, faithfully fulfilling her duties towards God, the Church, and her neighbor.

In temperance the servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore attained to heroism. Content with coarse and poor food, she felt joy when she could feed on nothing but a little hard and moldy bread; and so that this act of hers might not be ascribed to virtue, she used to say that bread was good for her stomach. Her continual and arduous journeys, and the inward mortifications of her spirit, completed the beautiful picture of her temperance.

Sr. A. del Salvatore, walking in the footsteps of the divine Master, loved poverty as if she had found in it her rich treasure. As poor as she was, she was also chaste, keeping watch over herself to flee from anything that might arouse in her soul a thought that was less than pure. She also cultivated obedience; her Superiors always found her submissive, and so much the enemy of her own will as to conquer and mortify her inclinations.

All these virtues shone with an even more splendid beauty, because accompanied by that simple, unaffected humility, free of ostentation, which spiritual masters have always held to be the foundation of holiness.

The chief thought and affection around which the whole life and activity of the servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore gathered was nothing other than God. She spoke of him continually with her fellow sisters, discussed him with the sick she went to attend, meditated on his perfections, and felt his continual presence, which kindled in her heart flames of true charity. Her existence was one continual act of love towards God, to whom she consecrated herself, her labors, and her sorrows.

As if the day were not enough for her to adore and love her God, she devoted the nights to him as well, consuming herself with love before the Most Holy Ciborium. Prayer was her daily food, for, not content with what the Holy Rules prescribed, having obtained permission, she prolonged it much further. We might even say that her very occupations were interwoven with prayer, which never ceased from her lips or her heart. And when she meditated on the Passion of this God made man, on the sublime mysteries that brought him closer to us wretched mortals, then her prayer became something truly moving and sublime.

She held equal veneration for the Eucharist. Enamored of Jesus, she hastened daily to the sacred altars to feed on that bread, and with such reverence that it was at once an act of homage and of repentance: homage owed to a God who, driven by a boundless love, offered his divine flesh as food for souls, and repentance of a heart for the natural flaws that humility made appear fearfully great to her. From all that has been said, it is certain that Sr. A. del Salvatore was regarded by the whole Institute, and by all who knew her, even while she still lived, not merely as a soul most zealous for the glory of God, but even as a saint.

I myself had occasion, on two occasions, to experience that she must have been a great soul, endowed by God with supernatural gifts: the first was the success of my vocation. My parents were opposed to my becoming a sister, and she knew how to persuade them so well that they not only consented, but themselves came to present me to our venerated foundress.

The second was that, while I was still a novice and assigned to attend a sister at the point of death from the illness called the Miserere, when the servant of God, Sr. A. del Salvatore, was invoked, the dying woman was instantly healed.

Everything I have written here, I believe to be the truth, and I would be ready to swear to it as well.

Sister A. Maristella Calderone

36. Report of Sister Anna Aniceta Montanari, undated, probably from 1913 (Proc. p. 582).

Very well articulated and detailed, the narrative follows the order of the theological, cardinal, and related virtues, and of her reputation for sanctity; it particularly highlights the Servant of God's charity towards God and towards the sick, and her humility. It also highlights some healings attributed to her intercession.

Of her heroic Faith

I had the good fortune to be with the dear servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi in 1883, when she, with the great aspiration of a saint, held the office of Provincial of Sicily. I keep a vivid memory of her, one that can make me feel proud of having closely witnessed the deeds of a saint, for everything about her pointed to the grandeur of holiness, which, while trying to conceal itself with humble bearing, shines all the brighter and gives off its fragrance. Perhaps no one more than she blessed having been born into the bosom of the Church and of Catholic parents; as simple in all her belief as she was strong, never did a shadow of doubt seem to cloud the articles of the Faith and the most sublime mysteries. She had a very particular devotion to the Most Holy Sacrament: the altar was her refuge in her tribulations, her rest in the long struggles of life, her haven of peace and her nightly repose. And there, with what liveliness of faith she implored God's help for her needs, and for those that concerned the Community, all of them.

To Jesus in the Sacrament she poured out her griefs and her many sorrows, confidently asking to obtain, and with the trust that only love can give, infinite graces and favors for all who needed them. And how many graces her saintly faith did obtain! And her bed was the steps of the altar, for her night was made for nothing but prayer, before the Tabernacle or at the bedside of the sick, where she often went to keep watch.

She loved the holy Virgin with most tender love: oh, how much fervor her bearing inspired when she prayed before the beautiful little Madonna, still kept in the Provincial house in Palermo! How often, in difficult moments, was she seen prostrate before her, with the strength of an invocation insistently seeking help, light, or courage!

The Mass, that sublime Sacrifice, was deeply felt by her soul, which was lifted up in it, at one with the great Act she profoundly intuited, communing with the Love she clasped to her breast, ardent with fervor, through the Holy Eucharist, on which she fed daily with rapture and devout humility. Often, and with compunction, she also approached the Sacrament of Penance, filled with sorrow for her faults.

She spoke of the Passion with pious recollection, and, reading the little passage of the morning meditation — oh, how one could feel the fervor of a soul that, though still clothed in its bodily veil, flew in the eternal spheres where sorrow finds peace, earthly suffering glory. And so she caught fire speaking of our Lord's sufferings, and with inspired words sought to instill in the souls of her listeners devotion to the Mysteries of the Cross, which are the ascent to Heaven. — And the saint often stirred in our hearts a surge of affection, an infinite desire to resemble her at least in her ardor for Jesus Christ.

Among the saints, she loved with particular devotion the Patriarch St. Joseph, and this could be sensed from her invoking him in difficult moments, and sometimes also in prosperous ones, whether asking or giving thanks. The house of the Lord, also her own dwelling, she loved tenderly, and took its dignity to heart, instilling respect for it in all those under her: her face would immediately darken if the smallest act betrayed to her the slightest transgression, and in this she was strict, with zealous love.

In the Supreme Pontiff she venerated the Vicar of Christ, and respected his laws and his word with love; she respected the Ministers of God, and never was the slightest word heard from her lips that pointed out a fault in any of them.

Of her heroic Hope

Sr. A. del Salvatore's Hope shone forth often, with the surges of her heart attached to the Eternal Good, in every little trial the Lord was pleased to send her: it is not said here that she firmly hoped for eternal salvation through the merits of Our Lord — rather, in temporal matters, in the most difficult or sudden cases, she referred everything to the foot of the Sacrament, and then, to her living Faith, the sweet Hope of a swift answer responded.

In 1882 influenza was raging in Palermo, an epidemic that reaped many lives; the poor Provincial was called on for many acts of care, and meanwhile the Sisters were all stricken by the fierce illness. One anguished evening she went to the Most Holy Sacrament, and, not knowing that in a corner of the church the sister sacristan was present, spoke to her Jesus thus, almost as to a living person who should answer her or make amends for a wrong done to her: "My Sisters are all sick, and if You permit this much, how much do You yourself ask of me in service to my neighbor? Ah, You wish it so, and so be it! But I will leave You without my attendance if You do not make my Sisters recover tomorrow!" A miracle! The next day all the Sisters rose, and strong enough to go to the duties they were called to. — And to the sister who had witnessed this and had told it to her fellow sisters, she gave a gentle reproach and enjoined silence.

If some need pressed on her, if some sorrow touched her most sensitive heart, she never despaired; strong in prayer, she placed in it all her trust, and, hoping, the smile never left her lips, just as calm never fled her heart; she laid before her Master all the cares her office never failed to give her daily, and, though inwardly she suffered for it, she never shared her sorrows with anyone; but always cheerful, always calm, she never lost her composure nor grew discouraged, hoping for everything from the Divine Source.

Of delicate constitution, she never consented to have her body treated with the care it needed, and in her illnesses she never once complained; nor did I, in the year I spent near her, ever hear from her lips that she did not feel well. And how many times, with her eyes glistening with fever, with the weakness of an illness she disregarded, she traveled by day and by night, to go wherever her work or her presence was urgently needed.

O holy soul, give us a gleam of your hope to sparkle in our hearts, as when you spoke of your longing for Heaven; give us the smile that, whatever happens, lets us rest at peace in the bosom of the One from whom you yourself hoped for everything!

Of her heroic Charity towards God.

This virtue was a field of sublime elevation for our Servant of God; but I, being obliged to live apart from her almost the whole day, since she herself assigned me to carry out my work alongside a poor madwoman who lived outside the city, in the countryside, could not closely observe the heroism our Saint showed in this virtue. Often, however, I heard her consider herself the greatest sinner, and I received some exhortation to flee sin, that monster of hell, a grave offense against the Crucified Love, and I could observe in her how, in the smallest things, she sought to avoid even the slightest faults.

Her union with God was evident the moment one came near her: her very bearing, her walk, everything spoke of a soul that had a real intimacy with God; and when necessity led us to address her, she always had Jesus as her example on her lips and in her heart, with the sweetness of counsel and instruction.

Heroic Charity towards her neighbor

The poor! For our heroine they were truly the person of Christ himself; on them she lavished her care with the fervor of one who wishes to please her beloved, to them her pure and comforting smiles, to them her caresses and the cheerful help that never humiliated, and all flocked to her, the needy and the afflicted alike, and received, as needed, bodily comfort and relief of soul, when, oppressed by anguish, they went to pour it out upon that heart which, understanding them, shared the sorrows of poor mortals, and knew how to dry bitter tears, lifting hearts to God. To the wealthy she bound the cause of the poor, whenever she herself could not supply all their needs, making them understand the lofty mission God had given them on earth, making them stewards of the poor.

For the sick, then, she had a true vocation of love: to them she gave her work with the rapture of one who intuits the good, exalts it, makes it beautiful. For the poorest she had a greater predilection, and never failed to join to bodily comfort the strength of spirit that often falters at the great moment of passing. Then, like a true athlete, she offered her fortitude to souls that needed it, and, with a good spirit, administered the sweetness of the life to come, thus sharpening the desire for rest in God's bosom in a soul that, shortly before, had perhaps felt a great fear of that God as judge, of its earthly end.

Of her heroic Prudence

Of our Sister's heroic Prudence I can affirm that she showed continual self-denial; she never considered herself before hastening to wherever her work was needed, and, at the cost of any sacrifice, was ready to ease any physical or moral pain; and so, always solicitous for the good of her neighbor, for the growth of the Institute, intent on nothing but tireless activity, she fled idleness, showing herself an example of virtue and of work.

Of her heroic Justice

Towards her Superiors she had the respectful submission of the humble person who finds herself placed in a high office only by others' goodness; faithful to their wishes, she wanted everyone to find the yoke sweet; towards her subjects she was, more than a Superior, a Mother in the dealings of her office, which knew no commanding, and in her humility she held herself lower than the Sisters themselves. Of her it could truly be said that she had no place to seek rest in the hours following the weariness of long labors; and while she took great care that the Sisters lacked nothing, she allowed herself to lack a bed, a nightstand, in short, the bare necessities. I could never accuse her, as far as I saw, of duplicity or pretense in her dealings; rather, simple in word as in deed, she treated us as a good Sister who lives on love and, with its rays, kindly lights up all around her.

Of her heroic Temperance

Gentle in word, in manner, she was the living example of meekness; nor do I recall, in the little time I spent near her, her ever raising her voice at any adversity, small or great, that befell her. In spontaneous mortification, in the necessary relief of the body — eating, drinking, sleeping — she was most exceedingly temperate.

One day, finding myself with her and seeing her eat barely a salad, and knowing she suffered from her stomach, I dared say to the cook: "But give the Superior something substantial!" And the sister cook, who understood the Superior's holy ways, answered me smiling: "Oh, don't worry, this is enough for the Superior!" I never saw her drink wine. And I can say her food was limited, during Lent, to raw vegetables alone, and outside that time to just a little pasta, as she, because of her penances, did not follow the Community's nourishing diet.

To her fasting from food corresponded, as I said, fasting from sleep: I have already said she had no bed, her place of rest being the holy Tabernacle, and this alone shows how watchful that exhausted body remained over the senses, subjecting them to the strength of spirit that made our athlete of the faith so great. Her plain dress never set her apart from the lowliest Sister in the house; simple and neat without refinement, she loved nothing but to enrich the heart beneath the poverty of the wool that clothed her. Sparing in her speech, she was edifying in her brief remarks, in which divine teaching was always distilled; nor did pride or vanity ever touch her word as she spoke. In her gentle laughter she was inspired, and she inspired the serenity of the good during common recreations, where her spirit shone, giving relief to the body, tempering the spirit of the Sisters in the shadow of her illustrious and holy example.

Of her heroic Fortitude

Of her fortitude in adversity I can say little, for my acquaintance with the saint was not intimate; I can speak only of her fortitude in illness. For her, nothing was too much when it concerned her body's discomfort, and, always unchanging, disregarding sickness, as I have said, she carried out with the same strength the most exhausting tasks, to which, with a saint's delight, she submitted with love.

I always saw her face in a serene bearing: always gentle and cheerful, whatever happened to her, she never clouded over with adversities nor rejoiced too much at good fortune. A saint in deep feeling — what could disturb or alter her, when the Strength of God so greatly held sway over her?

Of her heroic Humility

I never heard her speak of herself except to show her own smallness, for I often heard her repeat that she was good for nothing. And if ever some event revealed traits of her virtue, or the Sisters spoke of some benefit obtained for someone through the Sister's intercession, and she heard it, she was right there, ready, with the humility that seeks to efface itself, to cut the conversation off right in the middle, but so gently, without affectation, with the indifference of one who finds easy the success of an enterprise that seems difficult.

Of her reputation for Holiness in life and after death

Of Sr. A. del Salvatore's reputation for holiness an echo of admiration still resounds in Palermo: whoever knew her truly loved her as saints are loved and venerated, and even today, when it falls to me to speak of her with those who admired her virtues closely, I feel proud to belong to the Family of a gentle saint, as they called her, a saint in feeling and in word.

And her holiness is not merely the fragrant perfume of virtue she spread around herself while living: no, with her fragrances she wished to embalm the very air for her Sisters, who still seek her even after her death — she who, as a tender Mother, loved us on earth, and, departing for Heaven, was purified while her tenderness only deepened, and from her dwelling of peace sends us the rays of her pure love. And a ray of her love is the following event, which I now set out to tell.

In 1887 I was a simple subject at the Porrazzi Asylum in Palermo, and performed the duty of attending to Sr. A. Placentina Domaneschi, who for two years had lain in bed with continual hemorrhaging. That year the Holy Memory of our dear Mother Rosa was coming to Palermo, and in the spring the bones of Sr. A. del Salvatore, buried for two years in the cemetery of St. Ursula, were to be exhumed.

The fine day came, and I was among the fortunate Sisters who were to go to the cemetery. Before leaving the Asylum, I went up to the bed of Sr. A. Placentina, still ill, and, half tenderly, half jokingly, asked her: "Sr. A. Placentina, don't you want me to bring you anything? We're going to Sr. A. del Salvatore." The Sister answered me with interest: "Oh yes, bring me something!" We went. Present at the exhumation of the body, along with the Foundress Mother, were the then Secretary Sr. A. Benedetta Carrega, many Superiors and Sisters, and various ecclesiastical authorities, among them Monsignor Zuccaro. Opening the coffin, the body was found detached at every joint, but all surrounded as if by a kind of mold, which, observed closely, was nothing other than a mass of countless tiny worms, of which, on taking them in hand, only thin skins remained. I had the happy idea of taking a small handful home, and, taking a scrap of paper, I placed these little worm-casings in it. When I was home, I showed them to the Sisters, including Sr. A. Placentina. She, with a burst of truly ardent faith, took one of these little worms and, after looking at it, put it at once into her mouth and swallowed it. A miracle! The next day she left her bed, completely recovered. Even today, thinking back on this event, a shiver of gratitude and affection touches my heart, and the Sister, who is still alive, after twenty-six years, agrees to share with me the joys of an enthusiasm that cannot end.

Nor is this the only smile of grace our most dear friend has given me. In 1891 I was appointed to the office of Superior in that same Asylum, but I was afflicted with a painful illness I had contracted during the cholera of 1885, which for six years had tortured me bitterly; an illness produced by the strong disinfectants used that year to drive off the fatal infection. Despite the illness, overcoming the reluctance this office caused me, I accepted. But the illness made me unable to carry it out well; weighed down by the longing to be healed, I was overcome by a repugnance towards having myself examined by the doctor: a great sense of shame made me swallow bitter tears of suffering rather than show myself to the doctor as I needed to. I spoke of this with filial affection to the good Mother Gattorno, when in December of that same year, 1891, precisely on business of my new office, I was forced to go to Rome, to draw strength and receive light from that holy Mother, who was tender and generous. From her, to whom with trusting love I revealed the harsh sufferings of my illness, which often did not even let me walk because of the spasms I suffered, I received these words of counsel: "Do you know, daughter, what you must do? You must commend yourself to Sr. A. del Salvatore. She's a saint, you know? And she will be able to heal you. Go to her tomb as soon as you are in Palermo, and ask her for everything you need."

The Mother's inspiration found faith in my heart, and as soon as I was in Palermo, though suffering, I dragged myself to the holy Sister's tomb. At that tomb I prayed with all my heart; then, before leaving, I gathered some of the grasses growing around it and took them home. I boiled them, and with the water I made baths. I was healed. Now I feel the traces of the illness, but not the sufferings that invoking a saint took from me; and, as though in continual recollection of the favor received, there remains in me the faint trace that makes me feel the protection of the saint I venerate with love, with complete and immense gratitude.

In 1892 I returned to Rome, where the 25th Anniversary of the Institute's Foundation was being celebrated, and Sr. A. del Salvatore, who had loved it so much in life, rejoiced from heaven at its being celebrated over time. She rejoiced, taking part with the sweetness of an interest to which she had sacrificed herself for its good. And here is how she made herself felt as near at that time.

One day I went out with Sr. A. Pellegrina Blanchichi and other Sisters, and we were riding in a carriage to visit the city. Suddenly Sr. A. Pellegrina asks: "What devotion do you have? I don't know what strange thing is happening to me. I had a pain that for a long time tortured my left arm, and I don't know by what divine power I now feel free of it." I thought at once that I was wearing the ribbons of Sr. A. del Salvatore, which I had kept with me when, in 1887, at the exhumation of the body, we had divided her garments among us. So it was the Saint's ribbons that had spoken of divine power even without being asked! It was, then, the touch of a single object that had belonged to her that gave off that hidden fragrance, that revealing power. And the wonder of the ribbons, since I have not forgotten it, I am moved to include in this report, so that all may know of my faith in the Holy Sister, who has many times been my light in darkness, comfort in sorrow, protection in danger.

Sr. A. Aniceta Montanari

37. Report of Sister Anna Anastasia Cecconi, undated, but probably from 1913 (Proc. p. 589).

The narrative of the Servant of God's virtuous life is the fruit of the direct testimony of the writer, who lived with her in Florence. It especially underscores her ardent charity towards God, her trust in Providence, her charity towards the sick, her kindness, her gentleness with everyone, and her spirit of mortification.

Placed in the presence of God, this is what I can attest to the heroism of the venerated Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who was my Superior for two full years, in 1876 and '77.

Of her heroic Faith

1. — She always gave thanks to the Lord for having had her born in the bosom of the Holy Church and of Catholic parents; speaking with us when we could gather during recreation she would say: "Sisters, how good the Lord has been to us; he could have had us born of heretics, and instead he gave us the privilege of being born of Catholic parents, and moreover chose us as his brides."

She believed all the most sublime articles of the faith, and often said to Jesus Crucified: "How much you have suffered for me, and what am I doing for you?" and she had bursts of affection; she showed a particular devotion to the little Madonna of graces, who seemed to speak to her, and likewise to the image of Mother St. Anne. If she had a little time, she spent it before the Most Holy Sacrament, for she was found many, many times, both by day and by night, her face to the ground on the step or behind the altar, praying, and she looked like a seraph; she prayed as much as she could, heard Mass with such devotion that it made me say to myself many times: "But why, Lord, do you not let me feel those feelings she feels?" She went to confession every eight days, and when she needed to seek advice about something she went more often, saying: "Jesus must enlighten me to do my duty well"; such was her faith in confession.

When she approached Holy Communion, which was daily, she would remain as though in ecstasy, all joyful; one could see in her face that she was speaking with the Lord; sometimes I would ask her: "Superior, how do you manage to pray with such fervor after Holy Communion?" She would answer me (baccicì): "How would you put it, if you had to ask favors and graces of your father and mother? Surely with complete trust; well, Jesus is a father in our heart, so long as we do not drive him away with our faults"; and she wished that everyone would love Jesus; many times I was her companion in attending the sick, and, speaking with the families, she always spoke of matters of religion; she would say: "The Supreme Pontiff must be respected as the person of the Lord," and she showed this in many ways; she wished to gain every indulgence she could; she respected the church, and when she was in the chapel she would not allow anyone to speak of anything; she would say: "If you need something, call me outside, but not in the chapel, because that is a lack of respect for Jesus."

Of her heroic Hope

2. — She firmly hoped for eternal salvation; she would say: "By my own merits I would deserve to be forever lost, but by the merits of the Lord's Most Precious Blood I hope to become a saint," for she said: "we religious must say: to make ourselves saints; we have consecrated ourselves to the Lord for this purpose." She always sought to fulfill her duty; when even the necessities were lacking for the community, she always trusted in divine providence; how many times I myself saw how distressing it was to see what need the house in Florence was in, with 22 sisters to support and the house rent to pay; she would say: "Lord, you must see to this"; one day in 1876 she had to pay a large sum (I no longer recall the amount), she told me: "Let's go out," and we went to the church of Santa Maria Novella; she set herself fervently to pray before the Most Holy Sacrament; what passed between her and the Lord I do not know; suddenly an unknown lady comes in, presents herself to her and says: "Take this note"; she, not knowing her, says: "Excuse me, I cannot take it, come to the house"; but the lady told her: "You are the Superior, you may take it"; she asks her where she lives so as to go thank her, and the lady tells her: "There's no need, the person who sends me does not want me to tell you"; we then wanted to follow her to see where she went, but the unknown lady disappeared; she opened the envelope and found the sum of money she urgently needed to pay; she gives endless thanks to the Lord and says: "That was truly little old St. Anne." Other times too, finding herself in such circumstances, there would always appear a lady dressed in black with a veil over her forehead, always doing the same thing, presenting the envelope containing whatever was truly needed, and vanishing. When necessities were lacking she always said: "God will provide."

She had immense difficulties, even from her own superiors, especially a certain Father Andreotti of Florence, to the point of slandering her, saying she was working against the Foundress Mother, when I can say in good conscience that she held her in the veneration she deserved; the poor woman bore all these terrible difficulties to the point where she was nearly to be stripped of her habit, but she, with the utmost resignation, always trusted that God would never let her go without it. In that same year she was struck several times by hemoptysis, to the point of coughing up basins of blood, and yet she wanted neither doctors nor medicines; barely a little recovered and revived with the scantest food, she carried on with her usual tasks, such as spending nights at the bedside of the dear sick who called for her care; she was always the first to go; she would say: "How beautiful it is to attend to Jesus"; she always hoped for eternal life from the Lord, and to see the dear institute always thriving so as to do good to her neighbor.

Of her heroic Charity towards God

3. — Most observant of the law of the Lord, she abhorred sin and sought to avoid even the slightest faults; one always saw in her actions her union with God, of whom she spoke frequently and with fervor, always content; she was heroic in the exercise of prayer; when she heard worldly talk, and on other occasions some obscene word or blasphemy, and whenever she saw an offense against God, she was grieved; if she could prevent it by her own involvement, she did so, or resorted to prayer and short invocations such as: "My Jesus, mercy, enlighten and forgive them," etc.; if they were poor, she even gave them alms so that they would stop offending God; many times she said: "If it were possible, I would make any sacrifice and penance, only to be allowed to prevent such a sin."

Of her heroic Charity towards her neighbor

4. — She loved the poor as the very person of Jesus; indeed, in her care she preferred the poorest and most needy; she consoled them with such sweetness that she always left them content and amazed; she also brought them alms meant for this purpose and devotional objects they liked; many times she asked acquainted ladies to send the doctor free of charge, and the medicines too; she herself then combed their hair, made the beds, swept the rooms, etc.; and she urged us to do the same, saying that what we do for the poor little ones we do for Jesus.

She used the scourge and wore the hairshirt; she did not want to be discovered, but even I found her so a few times, when out of necessity I went to her room. She was most devoted to the souls in purgatory and mortified herself for them; her enemies were the first to whom she did good.

Of her heroic Prudence

5. — Her prudence was truly for the Lord, and the sole aim of all her actions was to attain eternal glory; her life was one continual labor and prayer, an enemy of idleness; indeed, passing nights to spare the Sisters and to gain merit secretly, she washed the dirtiest linens and pumped the water for the laundry, which in the morning was found already done, although she was of most delicate health.

Of her heroic Justice

6. — Most zealous for everything concerning the worship of God, most humble and most ready to any sign from her superiors, provided there was not the slightest offense against charity, as she showed with me when, in the current year, I was persuaded — not by her, but by others — and forced to go to my family on account of health.

I, believing, as a certain Father Andreotti had persuaded me, that I would go and then come back healed, instead found the cure to be very slow, as I was afflicted with scrofula; I understood the aim was for me to stay away forever; then, trusting in my superior Sr. A. del Salvatore, I came back alone a few days later; prostrate at her feet, I said to her: "Dear Superior, dead, throw me out whenever you want, but alive, no"; she was moved to such compassion and charity that she kept me upstairs in a room until she obtained the grace of my reinstatement from the dear Foundress Mother Rosa Gattorno; to her I owe my religious life, because on my account she had to suffer many difficulties.

Of her heroic Temperance

7. — Most meek and patient of character towards everyone, she grew angry only when she saw an offense against God; she ate but once a day for the whole time we were together, and, if she could choose, she chose the worst for herself; she always showed on her face a cheerful and contented look towards everyone.

Of her heroic Fortitude

8. — Most strong in bearing adversities and illnesses; moreover, though sick, if a command of obedience came from her superiors, she would even rise from bed, saying: "God commands me, and I must obey"; courageous in the Lord's life, she always showed herself the same both in adversity and in prosperity.

Of her heroic Humility

9. — She always held herself the vilest of creatures, and sought to keep her virtues and merits hidden, both from her fellow sisters and from everyone else.

Of her reputation for sanctity in life and after death.

10. — While she lived she was held by most to be a saint; to speak with her was a paradise; each one grieved at having to part from her, as I too did when, by obedience, I was assigned at the end of 1877 to go to the hospital of Spello; my tears were inconsolable, and she said to me: "Come now, Sister A. Anastasia, do the Lord's will, do not doubt that I have always protected you and will always protect you in life and also after death, if God permits me," as came to pass in July 1892, when I found myself at Campi Salentina, sunk in sorrow over a great difficulty.

There was a woman who had been sick for 22 years, whom everyone truly regarded as a chosen soul, and I often visited her, bringing her the alms the chairman allowed me; while I was most distressed, one night Sr. A. del Salvatore appeared to this sick woman, asking her if she prayed for the dear institute; since she was accompanied by a sister who had died in that house of Campi Salentina, the sick woman asked her: "Who are you? I don't know you"; then Sr. A. del Salvatore answered her: "You don't know me, I am Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, I beg you to pray for Superior Anastasia, pray, pray a great deal, the poor thing" (her own words); the sick woman said that Superior Anastasia is a little saint, she doesn't need my prayers; the same del Salvatore answered her: "Yes, but I beg you to pray for her"; the next day I went to visit her, and hearing the account I could do nothing but burst into tears, thinking of the promise made to me to protect me even after death if God permitted it; and indeed only a few days passed before I was summoned by the dear Superior General Sr. A. Rosa Gattorno, on the day of her silver jubilee, who filled me with filial [maternal] affection.

In 1897 I was at the clinic in Palermo, operated on by Professor Tanzini for a floating kidney, right and left, in two surgeries; the first operation resulted in a declaration of intestinal occlusion, caused by adhesions from the surgery undergone, so grave that I received the Viaticum.

The poor Provincial Battistina had grown truly gravely worried, to the point that one night she did not want to leave me, believing herself certain that I would not last until morning; she left two sisters at my bedside; I, however, told them: St. Anna del Salvatore has promised me her protection, and in this circumstance she must protect me and will not allow me to die outside the religious house, promising her that the first visit I would make would be to her tomb; when everything was prepared for reopening the surgery, to see what had happened, they found the intestine functioning perfectly, to the amazement of all the professors and assistants.

In faith, I sign myself

Sr. A. Anastasia Cecconi

38. Report of Sister Anna Amante La Barbera, undated, but probably from 1913 (Proc. p. 594).

A detailed account of her own religious vocation, attributed to the Servant of God, and of the wondrous signs she performed. Her protection after death is evident.

A. M. F.

In homage to the truth, and out of a duty of gratitude, and because of the veneration I have always had for the Servant of God Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, since the moment I had the good fortune to know her; I, the undersigned, Sr. A. Amante La Barbera, Daughter of St. Anne, depose the following, and this will always make better known how great her virtue was, and how dear to the Lord this beloved servant of his was.

The events I am about to tell, which can rightly be called prodigious, I saw myself, or, to put it better, concern me directly. After God, it is to her that I owe it, if I am clothed in this holy habit of the Daughters of St. Anne, and if I belong to this worthy and holy Institute, which I love so much, and which, with the Lord's help, I shall love and serve until the end of my life. And here is how I came to know the dear Servant of God, how my vocation came about, and how the events I am about to narrate took place.

It was the year 1881 [1882], and the Servant of God, Sr. A. del Salvatore, had for some time been in Palermo, my native town, as Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne, at the Briuccia House. At that time I was engaged to a young man from Palermo, whom I loved dearly and by whom I was loved with equal affection, and we were hastening with longing towards the moment of our union. My parents were happy about it, but the young man's were not, and so there was great discord between the two families; and this grieved us greatly, because it delayed and hindered our union. I prayed, I prayed hard for this discord to vanish, but in vain; I was in despair!... In the meantime I heard talk of this Servant of God, who was said to be a saint; then the thought came to me to turn to her, so that she might pray to the Lord to grant my wishes, thinking that the Lord could deny nothing to a holy soul; and so resolved, I went to her at once, and she received me most kindly.

From that first meeting she inspired in me a great trust. I told her the reason for my visit, and I begged her, begged her earnestly to intercede with the Lord for the grace I so longed for. She listened to me with great charity, and, as she bade me farewell, said to me: "Yes, yes, I will pray, I will pray," and said nothing more.

I went home more at ease, hoping in her prayers; but more days passed and nothing changed. Then, in despair, I went back to her, and again I begged and implored her to obtain the grace for me, and that I hoped for everything from her prayers, and that I wanted it at all costs. She then looked at me with a look I would call inspired, and said to me: "No, you will not marry that young man; the Lord wants you for himself, he wants you to be a Sister." How I was left at such words I cannot describe; and, disconcerted, I answered: "Me, a sister? It's impossible!... I will never be a sister; I have never had this vocation; it's impossible that this should happen!..." And she repeated: "Yes, you will be a sister, the Lord wills it"; and I, still repeating: it's impossible, it will never be; I took my leave in the grip of the greatest agitation, the greatest distress, for I felt not the least call to religious life; and, still so agitated, that evening I finally went to get some rest.

While I slept I had a dream I could call mysterious. I saw the Sorrowful Virgin appear to me; she held her arms crossed over her breast; suddenly she unfolds her arms, and, matching her words with the gesture of her hand, says to me: "No, I do not give you what you want, but I give you my Son." At that instant I awoke, and, still struck by that vision, by those words, as though beside myself, I began to cry: "No, no, I don't want Jesus!... I don't want him!..." My family, frightened by that cry, thought I had gone mad, and did everything they could to calm me.

The next day I went again to Sr. A. del Salvatore and told her the dream I had had, and she, with great calm but resolute, told me: "Yes, the Lord wants you for himself: that young man you will not marry, neither you nor any other" (and indeed he died two years later, that is, in 1884) "and if you go against the will of God, who wants you in the religious state, you will have greatly to repent of it." But it was useless, she could not persuade me, for I felt the repugnance towards that state rather growing in me, and I said: perhaps if I see some miracle that makes me know this will of the Lord more clearly, perhaps then I might bring myself to embrace this state.

Meanwhile the good servant of God comforted me, urged calm and prayer upon me, and assured me that she too would pray much for me, but always remained firm in telling me that my state was the religious state; and I, though she would not consent to my wishes, still felt drawn to her, and from time to time went to see her; her company was most pleasing to me. One day, when as usual I went to visit her, after keeping me a little while in holy conversation, she told me: "Tonight at 8:45 come here, for tonight we must pray together in our little chapel," and so I did.

I went to her at the appointed hour, and, when the Sisters had already retired to rest, she led me into the chapel, before the altar on which stood a statue of Our Lady of Lourdes, and we prayed, prayed a great deal, close to one another; she then prayed with a fervor I cannot describe; she seemed absorbed! When all at once I saw her rise slowly from the ground, and while I, astonished, watched her and almost tried to hold her back, I see that she has reached the statue and, in sweet ecstasy, was close to the dear Madonna!... I, by an instinctive gesture, held back, fearing she might fall upon me, and I watched her and called out!... After a little while, very slowly, she descends to the ground, and, as if awakened, looks at me and says: "Did you see? The Lord allowed this for your sake, to convince you that he wants you for himself; are you convinced of it now? But take care, take care that not a word of what you have seen should escape you!..."

Astonished, confused, I answered: Yes, I am convinced, I will do what the Lord wants; with his help I hope to overcome every difficulty; and in the morning I went home, bewildered, stunned by what I had seen, resolved to do God's will, however much I felt within me a great struggle, a great conflict.

The difficulties that arose to obstruct this plan of the Lord concerning me were without number. Besides the struggle I waged with myself, there was added the opposition of my parents and of the young man, my betrothed, who in no way wished to give up our union and grew furious and made threats!... What my state of mind was can well be imagined. I turned to the dear Superior Sr. A. del Salvatore for comfort and help through her prayers.

She suggested that I do some mortification, some fasting; but meanwhile, although I was resolved to do what she told me was God's will, I could not bring myself to decide, and I kept putting off from one day to the next the fulfillment of what the Lord required of me, and so struggling I came to Lent of 1882. The dear servant of God prayed, and I believe also undertook great mortifications, to obtain for me from the Lord the strength and resolve I needed to break through every obstacle; and to obtain it the better, she suggested that I too undertake, that Lent, the strictest fast, living on bread and water alone; and I submitted to it all willingly; but still the indecision continued: my God, what struggles!...

We were at the end of May of that same year, and the good Superior told me, in a most resolute tone: "If by the last Saturday of May you have not come here, resolved to break through every obstacle, you will have irreparable cause to repent; do you understand?" What was I to do? Those such resolute words shook me, made me think!... I struggled!... I prayed!... At last I decided to put an end to it!...

On the morning of the last Saturday of May, without the knowledge of any of my relatives, I fled from my father's house, resolved never to return, and ran, ran to the dear Superior, who welcomed me with signs of the deepest affection, of the greatest joy!... The first step was taken!... I will not describe the protests, the rage, the threats of my family and of the one who was to have been the companion of my life; but nothing availed to shake me from the resolve I had taken, and however fiercely the struggle within myself continued, still, with the Lord's help, with the encouragement, the prayers, the comfort of her whom I loved so much and already venerated as a saint, I prevailed!...

She kept me with her the whole month of June; during this time I was able to admire still more the spirit of mortification, of prayer, of sacrifice of that dear soul! She spent most of the night in prayer or at the bedside of the poor sick, whom she served with admirable charity; she did not use a bed; she ate very poorly and in very scant quantity, and only once a day; she usually fed on the Sisters' leftovers, the crumbs and little pieces of bread they left over; she never ate meat or other good things, only vegetables, and the worst of these, such as cabbage stalks, etc., and she hid these mortifications of hers by assuring the Sisters that these things pleased her greatly, and that they were the food suited to her stomach, and that her stomach could not retain the better foods, and so on... The Sisters, so as not to go against her, did not offer much resistance to this manner of eating, but, not giving credit to her claims, attributed it to a spirit of mortification rather than to a need of her stomach to feed on those poor scraps, and they remained edified both by her spirit of penance and by her great humility and by the care she took to hide her mortifications, which one could never finish enumerating, and besides, who could ever know them all?

If, however, she was most mortified with herself, she nonetheless wanted the Sisters to be properly fed, as the Holy Rule prescribed, and she had for them truly maternal care, and saw to it that they lacked nothing necessary, whether for their sustenance or their clothing, etc., always, however, within the bounds of the Holy Rule.

During this time of my stay with her, I witnessed two wondrous events, which occurred, I believe, to confirm ever more in me that it was truly the Lord's will that I embrace the religious state, and to strengthen me in the struggles that still lasted within my spirit.

One day she calls me and says: "Carmelina, let's go to the sacristy"; once there, she says: "I ought to write an urgent letter to Mother," and takes up pen, paper, and inkwell; she sits down at a little table and begins to write: "Dearest Mother"; then she stops, sets down the pen and says: "How sleepy I feel! I should write this letter, and it's urgent too, but I feel I can't manage it," and, saying this, leans her head on my shoulder — I was sitting next to her — closes her eyes and peacefully fell asleep, or so I thought. I, for fear of waking her, did not dare move, and remained motionless, waiting for her to wake up; when my eyes came to rest on the sheet lying there on the little table, where she had written that first line, and I see — oh, surprise!... I see that the sheet is filling with writing done by an invisible hand!... I cannot describe how astonished I was... I would say almost frightened... I can't describe it; I could no longer contain myself, and, between fright and astonishment, I cried out: "Superior!... Superior!..." She started and said to me: "What is it?" And I: "Superior!... look!... look at that paper!... it's written on!... I don't know who wrote it!..." Then she looks at it, takes it, reads it!... and, with an immense burst of joy: "Thanks be to God!... thank you!" she says, "exactly what I was supposed to write!... oh, what a grace! what a grace!" and, saying this, she kissed and kissed again that sheet, so miraculously inscribed, and then said to me: "Did you see? This too is a proof from the good God; he wanted to let you see this too, to better convince you of his will; tell me, do you still doubt? Are you persuaded? But for charity's sake, don't let a single word escape you about what you have seen; take care if you speak of it!" I, meanwhile, felt a certain change in myself, a new strength, and I exclaimed: "Yes, yes, I am convinced; I want to love only Jesus, him alone, and forever."

Meanwhile the moment of my departure for Piacenza was drawing near; there I was to take the Holy Habit of the Daughters of St. Anne; only a few days remained, we were at the end of June, and one morning the Superior told me: "In a few days we shall leave, so I want to take you to say goodbye to your aunt Teresa Ferrara," and without further ado we went to her, who received us most cordially; we spent a while in friendly conversation, and although she was not against this resolve of mine to become a religious, she doubted my vocation very much, and kept saying: "Superior, I don't believe Carmelina will persevere, you'll see she'll soon come back home"; and the Superior told her: "No, no, you'll see that Carmelina will be steadfast, I have no doubt of it, I'm sure of it."

The good aunt would not let us leave without giving us some gift, and handed the Superior a sealed envelope; we thanked her warmly and parted. On reaching the door, we climbed into the carriage the good aunt had arranged for us, and, as we made our way home, the Superior said to me: "Did you see? She wanted to give us a gift, oh good! good!... let's see how much there is; let's open the envelope, let's count the money": it was 70 lire. "Oh!" said the Superior, "if only it had been 200!... for I truly have great need of such a sum at this moment; but let us content ourselves meanwhile with this, and let us thank the Lord." I then said to her: "And why didn't you tell me you needed that sum? I would have told my aunt, and I'm sure she would have given me more, at least 100 lire." "No, no, do you think so? Let's be content with this; the Lord will see to the rest." Meanwhile we reached home; it was about 11 in the morning; she took me to the chapel, and, after a fervent prayer, took the envelope and set it on the altar behind a card-stand, and told me: "Stay here and pray, don't go away," and went out. I remained there before the altar praying. The Sisters came to say their common prayers; when these were finished they went out to go to lunch; I remained firmly in my place; after not too long the Superior returned, and, seeing me still there, said to me: "What, you're still here?" "Yes, Superior, I was waiting for you." "Good, good," she said to me, "you did well, and... tell me, is that envelope still there?" "Yes, Superior, I haven't touched it." "Well then, let's take it and look." She takes it, looks at it, and — oh, marvel!... no longer just 70 lire were found there, but 200 lire!!... How can I describe my astonishment, my wonder, the dear Superior's joy? It's impossible!... she did not stop thanking the Lord with outbursts of the tenderest gratitude. "Did you see, Carmelina," she said to me, "did you see how good the Lord is!... but don't let a word escape you about what has happened; don't speak of it, understand?" I promised.

At last the day of my departure came; I say nothing of my family's protests and threats; finally they consented to my leaving, hoping I would soon return, all of them doubting the stability of my vocation. I, however, though the struggle was not over, remained resolved and firm in my decision; I trusted in the Lord's help, which had given me so many proofs that this was his will, and in the efficacy of the prayers of that guardian angel of mine whom the Lord had given me to carry out his designs for me. Yes, after God, I owe everything to that holy soul!...

I arrived in Piacenza in the early days of July of this year, 1882. The good Superior, Sr. A. del Salvatore, accompanied me herself. How can I describe the pain I felt at having to part from that dear person whom I loved so much and venerated as a saint? It is impossible to describe!

How many beautiful things she said to me! how many recommendations she gave me! she comforted me, encouraged me; she told me that the struggles, the temptations would still continue, but that I would overcome and surmount everything, and that she would not abandon me; but that she would always, always pray for me. At last we had to part; I remained in Piacenza to prepare for the clothing ceremony, which took place on the 20th of July, and I was given the name Amante, because the dear Sr. A. del Salvatore wished me to be called so, and made this wish of hers known to Mother, and she returned to her house in Palermo.

Six months had passed since I had taken the habit of the Daughters of St. Anne, and I found myself at the House of Siena; when one day I saw, to my great joy, Sr. A. del Salvatore arrive; what happiness was mine to see her again... to embrace her again!... She had come to take me to Palermo. My family, not seeing me return as they had hoped, were up in arms, threatening, and wanted at all costs to see me again, and, since I was still a minor, it was necessary to satisfy them, otherwise who knows what they would have done. The good Superior went to Piacenza, laid the matter before the Reverend Mother General, who agreed I might go for a little while to Palermo to satisfy my family, and so she came to Siena to fetch me and take me there.

During the journey she told me: "On arriving in Palermo, you will have a great shock." I, almost terrified, said to her: "What's going to happen to me, Superior? My God! Will I lose my vocation, perhaps?" "No, no, that won't happen, be calm, you'll see what it will be," and she said nothing more about it.

Having arrived in Palermo and disembarked from the steamer, we took a carriage to take us to the Superior's house; on reaching Via Maqueda, I meet that young man I was to have married; he looks at me, recognizes me!... My God, what an impression that gave me! "Superior," I say, "Superior; did you see that young man? It's him!..." "I had already told you that you'd have a shock, but be calm, don't be afraid."

We arrived home; a few hours pass, and my father appears at the door, telling the doorkeeper: "Carmelina has arrived, hasn't she? I want to see her." The doorkeeper immediately informs the Superior, who comes before him and says to him: "Who told you your daughter is here?" "Who told me," answered my father, "it was that young man who met her just now and came right away to tell me."

He saw me, he did, he said everything he could to shake me from my resolve, but it was all in vain, and so, seeing every effort useless, without raising further obstacles, they allowed me to remain in the state to which God called me, and shortly after I set off again for my house in Siena. The dear Superior told me that perhaps I would never see her again, and so it was.

Two other things she foretold me during my journey to Palermo, which have come true exactly. One was that I would soon be a Superior, and this came true a little more than a year after my clothing, when I was appointed by Mother General to be Superior at the House of Prato. She told me that I would then be in that house where she had suffered so much!... this too came true a little more than three years after I had been at the House of Prato: Mother sent me as Superior to the House of Florence, where I have now been for 25 years. This was the house where she had truly suffered so much and shed so many tears. Not without some fear did I go there, lest the same fate befall me, but instead I must confess that, up to now, I have found many consolations there.

From my journey to Palermo, which I have told above, I never again saw that dear and holy woman, and much, much did I weep over her departure from this earth; but if I no longer had the consolation of seeing her again on this earth, her memory, however, will never be erased from my mind; and just as she was my guardian angel while she lived, from Heaven, where she enjoys the beatific vision of that God whom she loved so much and whom she strove with all her might to make me love and consecrate myself to — from heaven, I say, her protection over me continues, and oh, how many, how many times have I experienced its beneficial effects!...

I note here one or two things that will serve to confirm this. In the early years I was at the house in Florence, it happened once that I found myself without anything and without money. Our Venerated Foundress Mother was due to arrive to stay there a few days. It is true that for her little expense was needed, since, like Sr. A. del Salvatore, she was most mortified in everything, but it displeased me that she should find the house so destitute and without a penny; I did not even have enough to pay for the carriage that was to take her from the station to the house, and all those few necessary provisions I had to buy on credit. Let everyone imagine my dismay, and furthermore I did not feel the courage to reveal my situation to Mother; what was I to do? What course to take? I resort to prayer, I resort to Sr. A. del Salvatore.

Mother had arrived; it was evening, and she had retired to her room; all the Sisters too had retired for their usual rest; I, seized by the greatest dismay, withdrew to the chapel, and there, at the feet of Jesus in the Sacrament, poured out, poured out with weeping my sorrow, and I begged and implored that help might come to me, and I begged and implored the dear Sr. A. del Salvatore to go herself to Mother and reveal to her the situation I was in, for I, I repeat, had not the courage to do so myself, and so I spent nearly the whole night weeping and praying. In the morning, before Mass began, I see Mother turning her head a little, as if looking for someone; I go up to her and say: "Mother, what is it you want?" "I was looking to see if you were in the chapel"; and as she went to the altar to receive Holy Communion, she touched me lightly on the arm, as if to say: "Come," I follow her and kneel down near her. While the priest held up the Sacred Host, I say: "My Jesus, this is the moment; send Sr. A. Salvatore to Mother, and let her tell her of my need," and I received communion beside Mother.

When Holy Mass was over, Mother withdraws to her room, and shortly after sends for me. I go at once, and as soon as she sees me she says: "Well done, well done indeed! Is this the trust you have in your Mother?" "What, Mother," I answer, "do I perhaps not have trust in you?" "Yes," she answers me, "because instead of coming to me, you go bothering people from the other world?" I then, at once: "Tell me, Mother, did Sr. A. del Salvatore come, perhaps? Did you see her?" "Yes, I saw her, and she told me you had cried all night and that you need money." And I then: "And when you took Communion, did you see her?" "Yes, then I became convinced of the truth: well then, daughter, take these 500 lire, and another time have more trust in your Mother, do you understand? And hush now, you know, about what has happened, don't speak of it with anyone, understand?"

Another time, Mother, while I was in Rome, where I had gone to visit her, saw Sr. A. del Salvatore close by me; I, however, did not see her, as indeed I never have; she protected me and still protects me, but she has never let herself be seen by me!... And here is how she saw her.

I was alone in the office with my work in my hands; Mother, who had been there with me shortly before, had to go out; after a little while, she comes back, and no sooner is she in the room than I hear her say, smiling: "Well now, truly well, how much Sr. A. Amante is loved!..." I, surprised at such words, look around and see no one, and say: "Who is it, Mother? Who is it?" And she: "Sr. A. del Salvatore, don't you see she's right beside you?" I saw nothing; and meanwhile, with the gesture of her hand, she seemed to be caressing someone. "See how much she loves you," she told me, "she came to keep you company while you were alone." I then, in a burst of affection and veneration, kissed the floor at the spot where she told me the dear servant of God was standing. This event has convinced me ever more of her continual care and protection over me.

Oh, how many, how many times, I repeat, have I been able to experience this predilection of hers for me, and my veneration, my affection for her will not cease even when life ceases, for I hope one day, as she has promised me, to be near her feet, in the blessed dwelling of the elect, and together with her to praise and exalt the goodness of Him who, in so admirable a way, called me to follow and serve him in holy religion, in this holy Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

What I have set forth here is the plain truth, and I am always ready to swear to it should I be asked.

Sr. A. Amante La Barbera

39. Report of Sister Anna Paolina Viani, undated, but probably from 1913 (Proc. p. 602).

She highlights the charity, humility, and spirit of sacrifice and mortification of the Servant of God, and also narrates her final illness and death.

A. M. F.

Having had the good fortune to know the Servant of God, Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, and to have been with her for some years in various houses, I had during this time occasion to admire her heroic virtues, the holiness of her life, and so, out of a duty of conscience, affection, and veneration towards her, I briefly depose what I was able to observe in her regarding her manner of life, which was in every way most exemplary.

The first time I knew her was between the end of 1871 and the beginning of '72. I was then at the House of Genoa (opened at that time), and she was at the house of Sampierdarena; and, because of the closeness of the two places, it was easy for us to see each other. Even then the Sisters spoke of this good sister's exemplary conduct, a conduct that, however, had nothing singular about it. One admired in her a great humility, obedience, charity towards all, scrupulous exactness in fulfilling her duties, in observing the Holy Rule; she was, in short, a great edification.

Not long after, she was moved from the house of Sampierdarena and sent to the house of Genoa, where I was, and it was then that I too was able to admire her virtues, her spirit of sacrifice, of mortification, and her great humility and charity towards everyone. All the Sisters loved and esteemed her, and were glad whenever they could have her as a companion in their duties.

We used to go to attend the sick at home, and we always went two by two. It was a joy for me whenever the Superior assigned me as her companion for this care. In her company the hours passed more quickly, one felt neither the tiredness nor the sacrifice too much!... everything was forgotten merely by seeing with what love and charity she served those poor sick people, who blessed the Lord for having her near them and would always have wanted to keep her close, and their regret was great when, in the morning, she took her leave of them. Towards us too, who were given to her as companions and helpers, she showed great charity, and wanted us to rest, especially when there was no great need for both of us to be attending them at the same time; she, however, was tireless and never wanted to rest, and when the sick woman did not need continual attendance, in those intervals of time she prayed, and oh, with what fervor!

She served everyone with equal charity, rich and poor, for she was truly convinced that she was serving Jesus in the person of those unfortunate ones; but her preferences, however, were for the poorest and for those with the most repulsive illnesses; when it fell to her to serve these, her joy reached its height!...

Once we were assigned to care for a poor woman sick with cancer; she suffered terribly. One night, after she had lavished on her the care the case required, the patient seemed to calm a little, and happened to rest her head on the shoulder of the good Sr. A. del Salvatore, who was standing beside her. The good sister did not pull away, but let the poor woman try whether, in that position, she could find some rest, and indeed she found it and fell peacefully asleep, and slept for a good two hours. The good sister, during all this time, remained there motionless, without the slightest movement, for fear of waking her, and I could not take her place in that pious task because she would not allow it, for the poor woman would have woken; I was edified by that stillness and charity of hers, and by the joy that showed in her face as she endured that discomfort.

All the sick, once they had had the good fortune of having her as their nurse, would have wanted to keep her always near them, such was her charity and the relief they felt in seeing her and being served by her.

She was most mortified in everything; she never complained of anything, however much discomfort or pain it caused her; she bore everything with great calm, and I would say indifference, for she let nothing show; she was always of a pleasant and cheerful mood.

After we had been together for a while at the house of Genoa, for some years I did not see her, as we were sent to different houses; and I came to be with her again when she opened the house of the Boccone del Povero in Palermo, which was, I believe, in 1879 or in '80. I went with her to open this house; she was Superior; our duty, here too, was caring for the sick at home. From that time I remained with her until her precious death, which occurred in June 1885. In these years I was able to admire how her holiness grew day by day!... and it would take too long if I noted down all her mortifications, her penances, and her practice of every virtue to a heroic degree.

Her Faith, Hope, and Charity were very great; in practicing the other virtues too she distinguished herself admirably, as well as in the spirit of mortification, penance, prayer, and union with God. She made it a study, however, to hide from others' eyes the practice of all these virtues to so eminent a degree. She did not use her bed for resting, and spent her nights in prayer or at the bedside of the poor sick; she hid, however, this mortification of not using the bed, especially when she slept in the common dormitory, making it seem she was going to rest, but in reality it was not so, for I myself, driven by curiosity, observed her, without, however, letting her notice, when she had her bed near mine, and I always saw her on her knees in fervent prayer; and if she was ever forced to use it, it was plain this cost her a great deal.

She ate very poorly, and usually leftovers and the worst vegetables, and only once a day; she never ate meat or other good things; she concealed her mortification by saying that her stomach could not retain delicate foods, meat, etc., and that, on the contrary, it was these poor scraps that agreed with her stomach; we remained in admiration of her mortification and her humility in hiding her penances. That she truly suffered in eating these better foods, when she was forced to it by necessity, so as not to seem singular, she showed several times, among which was this one occasion. When, invited by Fr. Briuccia, our benefactor, to his country place for an outing, she was obliged to sit at table with him and with all of us. Some most delicious macaroni was brought; she, poor thing, looked at it and did not know how to go about tasting it, so great was the repugnance she felt; we, who knew her manner of eating, watched her, while she tried to draw out the conversation with the priest, now about one thing, now another, without tasting it; but finally the priest noticed she was not eating and asked her to eat; and she then, without saying anything, put a few forkfuls of that macaroni into her mouth; but after a few minutes she had to ask leave to rise, and was not seen again until the meal was over; her stomach could not retain it.

She bore the physical ills that tormented her with unalterable patience, saying nothing; we became aware of her sufferings from the change in color of her face, but from her one never learned anything; she was always of a cheerful mood.

Towards her fellow sisters she had a truly maternal heart; she was most mortified with herself, but wanted the Sisters to lack nothing necessary, whether for food or for clothing, etc., and she was tenderly loved by them in return.

Her delight was to be at the feet of Jesus in the Sacrament whenever her duties and the exercise of charity did not prevent her, and oh, with what fervor she prayed! An offense against God saddened her immensely, and there is no telling what she would have done to prevent one. She loved everyone with equal affection; offended, slandered, she forgave generously, and prayed for those who offended her. Even when she was Superior, she occupied herself in the humblest tasks of the house, including with the laundry, especially when she could not be seen, and so the work was found already done.

In her final illness she gave the greatest example of admirable patience and conformity to the Lord's will. She also gave a last example of blind and prompt obedience to the command of her superiors. She had for some days been gravely ill, with a burning fever and little hope of recovery, when a telegram arrived from Mother General, who perhaps knew nothing of the serious state she was in, ordering her to go at once to Trapani, where her presence was needed; the good Superior, without delay, asked for her clothes to dress and leave, and our protests, given the very grave state she was in, were of no avail, and she told us: "Mother commands me this, I must obey." She left; a few days later she returned, took to her bed again, and after a few days gave up her beautiful soul to the Creator.

It is impossible to describe our grief at such a loss; we were inconsolable; the thought of never again seeing on this earth our beloved Superior, who had given us so many and such sublime examples of holiness, was heartbreaking; our only comfort was to know her in Heaven, enjoying the Supreme Good, the reward of her heroic virtues; we commended ourselves to her intercession and prayed that from above she would protect us and pray for us.

Not only we, but the whole city of Palermo was moved and wept at her passing, and proclaimed her a saint, and they turned and still turn to her intercession in their needs.

My affection and veneration for her have never diminished, and I cannot recall her without being moved, and it is my living wish that she may soon be enrolled by the Holy Church among the Blessed, for Sr. A. del Salvatore is truly a saint, and was declared so by all who knew her.

What I have here briefly deposed is the plain truth, always ready to confirm it under oath should I be asked to do so.

Sr. A. Paolina Viani

Piazza Armerina, 3/28/27

Most Reverend and dear Mother,

I have received the circular, and I am glad to set myself to write what I know and have learned of our venerated Provincial Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi. I can, however, tell you very little, as I did not have the good fortune to be close to her.

Sent to Sicily by obedience in 1883, I was assigned to Linguaglossa, to the Carmine house, as a municipal schoolteacher. Passing through Palermo, the Sisters of the Provincial house praised their Superior, who was a saint, humble, affectionate; who ate nothing but ordinary food; who did penances; who never slept and had neither room nor bed, and who spent every night in prayer before Jesus in the Sacrament and doing household chores, such as washing all the community's linens, sweeping the whole house, washing the floors, etc., and all this always while the Sisters were in bed.

One day, while I was at Linguaglossa, she came to us, with all the Sisters of the Castiglione orphanage, to give them a diversion; I could note that, at table, her food was little bread, and whatever was set before her she divided among this Sister and that. During the two nights she stayed with us, which seemed like two minutes, so welcome and comforting was her presence, the bed was not touched, and we knew it because we set markers. She listened to all of us: her words were few, but seasoned with such sweetness and charity that each one was left [moved].

About six years later I moved to Patti, as teacher and Superior, and I had with me Sr. A. Gemma, of Cremona, of happy memory. She had had the good fortune to be under the Provincial for several years, and, seeing her rare virtues, wished to imitate her. She told me that every night, once the community was already in bed, she, Gemma, would slip very quietly out from under her curtain and go to spy behind the church door, and, seeing the Superior prostrate at the feet of Jesus in the Sacrament, would have liked to remain, but did not lie down, staying on the floor under her own bed the whole night. God's will, however, was not in this for Sister Gemma: with these mortifications she brought on herself a bad cold with a cough that never left her, and little by little she wasted away and it brought her to the grave. In all the six or seven years she was with me, her talk was nothing other than recounting the virtues and mortifications of her Superior.

Many of them have slipped from my memory; I recall her saying that she ate almost always raw greens, and rejected — she gave this very order to the cook Pelagia — if ever a little bit of minced meat were put in among the vegetables so as not to be seen, as soon as she tasted it she would set it aside, with such suffering.

She told how, when the Reverend Mother came to Sicily on a canonical visitation, she one day sharply reproved the Superior for taking her coffee black, without milk, and not as the community did; she called her scandalous for being singular, etc., and made her take what her Sisters took. The Superior and Provincial obeyed blindly, without a word, but as many mornings as she took it, just as many times she rejected it again, until the Reverend Mother became convinced that this was not God's will.

For obedience and for charity she would have given her life. Indeed, once she was ill with a fever of forty degrees, when a telegram arrived from the Reverend Mother telling her to go to such-and-such a house; she got up and left at once. Another time she arrived at a house around eleven at night; certainly all were in bed, all the more since they had not been told of her arrival; so as not to disturb the community, she spent the whole night behind the door, even though it was wintertime.

The Sisters of the house vied with one another to see who could get closest to her and hear her holy words. One night, while the whole community was in bed, a Sister stayed up to speak with the Provincial; she goes into the office where she was writing, kneels before her. The good Provincial stopped writing, listened to her, and gave her counsel. After a while the Provincial fell silent: she had dozed off. The Sister waited for her to wake, but hesitated, uncertain whether it would be better to leave or to stay. After about half an hour the Superior started and said: "Oh, I must send this urgent letter to Rome," and, without looking at it, folds it and puts it into an envelope addressed to the Reverend Mother. The letter had been completed by an invisible hand, and I do not recall whether the Sister told me it had come out written in letters of gold.

She also told how, at the Provincial house, two Sisters died only a few days apart. The Provincial, on the day of the retreat, while urging the Sisters to blind obedience and exact observance of the Holy Rule, told them that she had seen Sister B. (I don't recall the names) go up to heaven a quarter of an hour after she expired, and Sister C. after half an hour. "They did nothing extraordinary," the Provincial said, "they spent so little time in purgatory only because of their exact observance of the Holy Rule."

Dear Mother, here is what I can depose about the dear and venerated Provincial Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi. I was assigned far from Palermo, and so did not have the good fortune to be close to her and see her often. Forgive the scrawl; I write it in several sittings for lack of time, and also while speaking it aloud, so it is written plainly and with some mistakes, but time does not allow me to redo it; so please excuse me. Hoping always to have your excellent news, I offer you my respects and ask you to bless me, together with the Community.

Your ever most affectionate daughter

Sr. A. Bianchina Andreoli
