Loreto, 7/20/1960

Most Reverend Provincial Superior,

at your request, by obedience, I depose in writing what I recounted verbally at Siena, in your presence and that of the Sisters, on the occasion of the "Local Superiors" meeting of June 22, 1960.

Sr. A. Giulitta Ciuti, of happy memory and my Superior, told me of an episode that happened to her personally while she was at the Generalate House in Rome, Via Merulana 177, where she had been summoned by the Superior General.

The Sister in question resided in Bevagna (Perugia) as Superior. She was a native of Florence and still had her mother, a pious and good old woman, wholly devoted to her family and concerned solely with instilling in her children's hearts sound religious sentiments.

Sr. A. Giulitta Ciuti was then carrying out her work at the house in Bevagna, when she was urgently summoned by her family to come to her dying mother's bedside. With the permission of the Major Superiors she left for Florence, accompanied by a Sister of the same Community, whose name I do not know.

The mother's agony was long, and the nights followed one another, for the children, without respite at their mother's bedside, since they did not have the heart to leave the patient. Sr. A. Giulitta too kept watch over the dear old woman, but one evening her sister-in-law insisted that she go rest, and offered her own room, where the marriage bed was, since it was next to the dying woman's room. At the pressing invitation, Sr. A. Giulitta agreed, begging her family to call her at once should her mother's condition worsen. She withdrew to her sister-in-law's room and, still dressed, lay down on the bed; but she could not fall asleep.

The brother, worn out and weighed down by the approaching catastrophe, went into the room where his sister, Sr. A. Giulitta, was, and, sitting at the foot of the bed, leaned against it, being in need of rest. At a late hour, the door opened, and the accompanying Sister appeared, who apologized and withdrew at once, despite her Superior's invitation to stay. After the mother's death occurred, Sr. A. Giulitta Ciuti and her companion returned to Bevagna.

A short time later a letter from Mother General summoned her to Rome. Sr. A. Giulitta, an obedient daughter, left at once; but what was her astonishment when she learned of the accusation against her! She had been slandered by the very Sister who had accompanied her, on the grounds that, on that fateful night, she had surprised her in the room together with her brother. She was ordered by the Major Superiors never to return to Bevagna. Sr. A. Giulitta spent agonizing hours and shed copious tears, for she was conscious of her innocence. In this state of mind she was assailed by a strong temptation that she wished, at all costs, to carry out. She was now resolved to flee, crossing a little sitting room to the right of the entrance gate of the Generalate house, whose door, at that time, was always open, because in a room above it lived the Sister who was the shoemaker. Her escape was made easier by a second door that gave access to the outer church.

One afternoon, as she was slowly making her way towards that exit, the crucifix she wore at her side caught on the fringe of the rug covering a small table. Sr. A. Giulitta, agitated, tried quickly to free the crucifix, but what was her surprise when she saw before her a Sister she did not know! The Sister said to her most kindly: "Be calm, take heart, for we shall pray together at the tomb of Sr. A. del Salvatore."

Sr. A. Giulitta, filled with confusion (for she supposed the Sister to be an office worker in the secretariat), was about to apologize, when she noticed that the Sister had vanished. Then, more downcast than ever, for fear that her flight had been discovered, she returned home still sadder, and, at the foot of the Tabernacle, raised her anguished prayer. She was called again by Mother General, who told her of her coming departure for Sicily. She was to go to the Provincial house in Palermo, and from there reach her new post.

Having arrived in Palermo, after a brief rest, the Reverend Provincial invited Sr. A. Giulitta Ciuti to go to the cemetery to visit the tomb of Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi. In the company of a Sister she went to the cemetery, and, while she was praying at the tomb of Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, she noticed that another Sister of our Congregation was kneeling in front of them. She asked her companion who it was, but the Sister, whom no one else could see, gave no answer. Sr. A. Giulitta looked at her again, but what was her surprise on recognizing her as the very same Sister she had seen in Rome, when she had wanted to carry out her flight! She rose to approach the mysterious Sister, but she, for the second time, vanished. But Sr. A. Giulitta's astonishment was enormous when, looking at the photograph of Sr. A. del Salvatore Orsi, she had to admit that it bore the very features of the unknown Sister who had appeared to her on two occasions. In faith.

most affectionate sister

Sr. A. Cesarina Costantini

1. On the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne. Obituary, in "La Sicilia Cattolica," year XVIII, no. 129, June 12, 1885, signed with the initial "M." (Proc. p. 486).

A moving remembrance of the Servant of God, who had just passed away; the author briefly traces her life and highlights her heroic virtues: humility, charity, kindness, gentleness, a spirit of penance.

On the death of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne

A grave opened on the evening of June 7 to receive the mortal remains of a soul dear to God, a model of the perfect religious, an honor to the worthy Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, superior of the nurses' house and Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily, on the 7th of this month at 11 p.m., breathed out her beautiful soul in the smile of the Angels and in God's embrace; and while the grieving Sisters, gathered around the precious remains, poured out their irreparable loss in copious tears, the sorrowful news, spread through our city, filled with grief all who had had the good fortune to know and approach so rare a woman and so perfect a religious, and to appreciate her extraordinary virtues. "She was an angel! She was a saint! She was a woman of charity! She was a model of virtue!" is heard repeated from every mouth; nor do such expressions arise from hearts biased by affection, but it is the irresistible force of truth and virtue that imposes itself even on the most depraved consciences, and wrings confession and praise even from tongues accustomed to infamy and slander. So it happens with a soul in which the Lord has stamped, in mysterious signs, the discernible mark of predestination, and whom he destined to shine like a luminous star of virtue amid the darkness of a corrupt age.

And such did Sister Anna del Salvatore truly show herself to be, by which she made herself dear and admirable to all, just as today her departure has become painful to all.

Nor is this the place to trace the rare virtues that, like fragrant flowers, adorned the springtime of her precious life, it being known besides that, from girlhood, she was so devoted to the things of God, and so loving of Christian mortification, as to show herself always beyond her years and favored by the Lord's grace. And it was indeed the Lord who shaped and schooled that virgin heart in the exquisite sentiments of piety and the lofty senses of the spiritual life, so that she, matured by grace and formed by heavenly love, was later to shine in the holy Institute, to which she was luster and honor, and which today mourns her loss bitterly.

She was scarcely twenty; and already her Beloved was calling her, with a sweet and irresistible voice, to consecrate herself wholly to his love and to charity towards her neighbor in the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

This beneficial and providential institution was barely three years old, and it seemed as though the Lord had inspired it just for her. The life spent in charity and sacrifice that forms that institute's program, the desire to make fruitful and effective the love she felt for her neighbor, and the heroic virtues of that noble, no less than pious, lady who, with a generous outpouring of charity, divested herself of all her possessions to found the charitable institute, were such motives to the heart of our twenty-year-old young woman that she did not delay an instant in faithfully answering God's call, and became a Daughter of St. Anne.

And oh, how true it is that religious institutes are chosen gardens, watered by God's grace and made fruitful by the eternal sun, where pious souls, like vigorous plants, flourish wonderfully and brace themselves for ever harder virtue; and it was here that the lamented Sister Anna del Salvatore, like a fruitful tree, rooted in faith, watered by a greater abundance of heavenly grace, spread her beneficent branches, and appeared rich in precious fruits of virtue. Ah! She was such that at the mere approach to her one remained spellbound, not knowing which to admire first in her, her profound humility or her dignified bearing; her gentleness of manner or her sober restraint; the strength of a lion or the meekness of a lamb; the zeal that consumes or the charity that has compassion. She was one of those beings who shine with a light clear, beautiful, consoling, yet at the same time mysterious and indefinable like the very light of God; what shall one say of her charity towards the sick? Ah! "Why doesn't the Superior come?" the sisters were often heard to repeat; "when she comes we feel better." And indeed the mere sight of her cheered the souls of the poor sick, and the spirit of God instilled in her such depths of compassion for those who suffered that she would have crushed and worn herself away, if only to bring comfort and relief to the wretched who languished.

Her humility caused confusion, nor was there ever an occasion on which anyone managed, in word or in deed, to wrest from her the coveted primacy of the last place. Ah! "When shall I convert? Ah, I have not yet converted!" she was often heard to exclaim, so it is no wonder that she hated herself to the point of declaring pitiless war on her body and her senses, giving herself over to the most laborious and austere life for love of that God who drew her to himself and united her to him. Enormous labors, tireless activity, continuous travels, countless hardships wore down a life that could be said to have been consumed for God and for the benefit of her neighbor. But what were her austerities, what her prayers, what her outpourings of love for God? What was her food, what her bed, how did she spend her nights, how did she fill her days?

Who can lift this veil but those who, by virtue of spiritual direction, were granted to know the little that could escape the ingenious and inviolable secrecy with which this woman of God was wont to conceal her rare virtues?

Were it not so, all the efforts of the most profound humility would prove useless to prevent, amid the darkness of a hidden life, some flash of light from at times revealing the secret workings of grace, and bringing to light the poorly hidden virtues.

It is thus no wonder that eminent persons, ladies of quality, and noble dames made it a point of pride to seek out and approach the humble Daughter of St. Anne, to ask her comfort, to request her prayers, to obtain her counsel, to pour out in her charitable heart their sorrows and their anguish; and let the noble and pious Princess of Fitalia stand for all, who more than anyone dealt with her closely, admired her virtues, attended her agony, and wept at her sorrowful loss.

And what wonder is it, when persons who, out of notorious impiety and a systematic hatred of anything bearing the mark of religion, felt drawn to her beautiful virtues, and were moved to benevolence towards her holy Institute?

But alas! So precious a life was to decline so soon towards its setting. Who would not have sought to hold still on the horizon this luminous star of virtue? But she, who had barely passed her fourth lustrum, was already rich in merit and ripe for heaven.

It was indeed in the last days of last April that a fatal illness struck her, from which she was never to recover. With difficulty, and once nature had been overcome by the illness, she had to take to her bed, where she lay like a little flame that quivers all around as it tries to break free from the earth and be lost in the vast fields of heaven.

And it was in those final moments that she was suddenly to revive and give new displays of virtue before being extinguished.

She had been ill no more than three or four days when a telegram arrived from Mother General ordering her to go to Trapani, where a new house of the Institute had been opened. The poor sick woman grieves, but does not care for herself; she gathers the last strength remaining to her, and for Jesus Christ, for obedience, and for her dear Institute finishes spending it; she leaves and goes where obedience calls her, but after a few days returns in the worst state: her sacrifice was already consummated: God had already accepted it and was hastening to call her to her crown. Oh, what examples of heroic patience, of inner calm, she gave to whoever had the good fortune to witness her final agony! What sweet perfumes of virtue breathed from that deathbed! What air of Paradise filled that room! Having received the last Sacraments, she now expects nothing more from this earth; her thoughts turn to Heaven, where she longs for the yearned-for wedding; her bed is surrounded by four priests and by the desolate Sisters, who can scarcely hold back the anguish of their hearts, and she turned on all a sweet gaze, a kind word, an angelic smile, as if to say: I am leaving for heaven; I am flying to paradise. And the moment had come. The clock struck half past ten, and, feeling herself failing, she calls her spiritual father, and: "Father," she says to him, "commend my soul." These were her final words, resembling those spoken by Jesus on the cross, and having said this, she breathed her last.

Blessed soul! You flew to heaven, and delight in your God; to us you left the fragrance of your virtues and the longing for you.

Ah! Pray now that you are in the bosom of blessedness; pray for us, who sail the stormy sea of the world; pray for your holy Institute and for your sisters, while we, imploring from God eternal rest for you, offer this tribute of heartfelt praise to your sweet and holy memory.

M.

2. Funeral oration delivered at the solemn obsequies of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, Provincial Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne in Sicily, by Fr. Gaetano Gabriele (cf. above, p. 302), Beneficiary canon of the Metropolitan Cathedral of Palermo, member of the Palermo Catholic Academy and of the Society for the History of the Homeland (Armonia Press, Palermo 1885) (Proc. p. 490).

No other office could prove to me, at once, more welcome and more painful than this one, which your kind goodness has today chosen to entrust to my weak powers. The reverent and sincere affection that binds me to the venerated Provincial Superior of this Central House of the Daughters of St. Anne leads me, with lively satisfaction of spirit, to speak of her merits, her life, her great soul; but, my heart torn by her death, the more I speak of her, the more painfully I grasp the loss, and the more wretched our common misfortune proves to be431. On the one hand, the gentle, lovable, and holy figure of Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who has left behind her a precious legacy of noble examples, of distinguished virtues, of Christian heroism, consoles and gladdens us; on the other, the thought that we shall no longer see her moving among us, a loving dispenser of graces and peace, of comfort and blessing, grieves us, wounds our hearts.

Is it then left to virtue only to show itself to the earth, and swiftly return, there whence it came to us, to heaven? Was it, then, among the incomprehensible designs of the Divinity, that so good a Superior, so good a mother, so wise and prudent a leader, should be lost in the full vigor of her years, when her presence was most keenly needed? Has cruel death then suddenly extinguished that noble and religious life, which for all was a most lofty school of piety, of self-denial, of charity, of prudence? Has the tomb forever stolen from our eyes that angelic, serene, sincerely pious face? Has the grave devoured that gentleness of manner, that serene cheerfulness of spirit, which showed itself in her features, in her gesture, in her whole person, that holiness of deeds and words? Has that soul, in which a sweet harmony of all virtues formed the good, the experienced, the prudent superior, taken flight towards another heaven, towards regions incomparably better than our own?

It is indeed so, alas, gentlemen! It is now seven days since the mother left her daughters, since paradise called back its angel, since this Central House, this Sicilian province, the whole Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne have been draped in mourning, have suffered a grave and irreparable loss!

It is now seven days since Sister Anna del Salvatore's spirit returned to heaven, and do not doubt it for an instant: many more seasons must pass to their setting before, in us, in you, O Sisters, in this province and beyond it, the longing, the memory, shall fade.

But what have I said, forget her, let our longing fade? I would do injury to the whole pious Institute, to the majority of our people and to the ladies of our nobility, if I could for an instant fear that the veneration, the sincere devotion to so great a woman, could ever, like dust in the wind, vanish from our hearts. I would pronounce dishonor and condemnation upon my homeland, were I to tell you that the name of Sister Anna del Salvatore, before which even the indifferent, whom nothing stirs or moves, had words of praise, of heartfelt gratitude, could ever, among later generations, fall into forgetfulness and ignorance. No! The name of Sister Anna del Salvatore speaks to us of humility, of gentleness, of charity, in short, of virtue, which the tomb shall show all the more luminous; for, alas, it shall make understood all the better her heroism, her efficacy.

There shone in her, indeed, a humility, an incomparable modesty, a tireless activity, an unceasing love of suffering, a gentleness that won every heart, a charity that consumed itself for everyone.

Giving herself wholly to all, forgetting only herself, she embodied in herself the spirit of the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne in the most admirable and simple way, the most virtuous and holy: an Institute whose program lies wholly in sacrifice and self-denial, in love for suffering humanity: an Institute that is the very embodiment of the evangelical counsels.

But of the many virtues that so beautifully adorned our Superior's soul, which shall I take as the theme of my unadorned oration, such as will portray her entirely to our gaze, and let us picture her in that air, in that bearing which were most truly hers and most naturally show her?

The Holy Spirit points me to the Book of Wisdom, a book that formed men after the heart of God, and puts in my mouth the words the Wise Man addresses to the just: Placens Deo, factus est dilectus (Wis. 4:10). Yes, Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi pleased God by the virtue that reigns above all others — humility, I mean — and by all the others that form its noble and necessary retinue. She pleased God by the modest regard she always held of herself; she pleased God by the charity that inflamed her towards heaven and towards the poor sick; she pleased God because she became a model of the perfect religious in the practice of every virtue; and, so pleasing God, she has become an object of veneration and love among men. And if it is true that glory will accompany the humble in spirit — Humilem spiritu suscipiet gloria (Prov. 29:23) — the lamented Sister Anna del Salvatore cannot lack such glory, for, humble in spirit, she mirrored her life on the divine and perfect model, Jesus Christ, the humble, the meek of heart.

Part one

The ways of the Lord are not the ways of men, nor are his judgments comprehensible by the measure of earthly minds. Men believe they add to their greatness, gain the pinnacle of glory, by putting down the small, with the arrogance of pride, with the noise of the press, which is called public opinion; whereas the great ones of the Church come to us out of humility of spirit, simplicity of life, disregard for self. And so Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi, who was to shine so brightly with every chosen virtue like a most brilliant star in the sky of the Catholic Church, and to stand out like a flower breathing the ambrosia of paradise in the new Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne, came to us from a small and unknown place in Upper Italy.

She came into the world in 1843 [1842] at Albareto, a small village of Borgotaro in the area of Parma, born of Angelo Orsi and Domenica Musso [Mussi], pious, well-off, and distinguished parents, who at Baptism gave her the name Maria Anna. That first fruit of their holy marriage they took care to raise and bring up for God in holiness.

The Christian upbringing of her parents, strengthened by good example, found in her little heart ground so sweet and ready that, even then, it ripened lovely fruits and gave lovely hope for the future.

Observe her as a child. Will her innocent soul, possessed by God, fear perhaps the arrows that the enemy of the human family will strive to hurl at her? Never. God had gone before her with his grace, with his gifts; and she breathes of God, speaks of God, consecrates to God the tenderest affections of her heart, the dearest aspirations of her soul. Her parents beheld a tender devotion, a filial piety towards Jesus and Mary, an ardent charity towards heaven and everything concerning religion, and they were not mistaken in esteeming that they possessed not an earthly child, but an angel who, descended from heaven, had come to increase their domestic peace, the harmony of their well-born hearts.

She had scarcely reached her fifth year, and our little Marianna was already showing what she would become once grown. At that tender and unknowing age she frequently practiced fasting and penance, during Lent eating with strict abstinence, and choosing for her meals the plainest and most insipid foods. As a child she treated her body like a slave; and, as though mindful of the saying of the Apostle Paul: Qui Christi sunt, carnem suam crucifixerunt... (to the Galatians 5:24), shunning entirely the comforts and conveniences of life that her family's prosperous condition offered her, she was often found asleep on the bare ground. At that childish age one observed in her an innate tendency to solitude, to withdrawal; and, in the remote corners of the house, pouring out in the secrecy of her heart the affections of her soul for God, who in baptism had infused in her the habit of sanctifying grace, she showed, by clear signs, that God would call her to the religious and perfect life. And a religious life she lived in the house of her father and of three paternal uncles, priests, who vied with one another to keep her with them so as to form her spirit towards that perfection to which she aspired, to complete in her that civil and truly Christian upbringing which forms the illustrious ornament of souls well born and gentle.

Oh, how beautiful is this flower as it first opens on its stem! How it spreads a fragrance of virtue, able to enchant all who have the good fortune to draw near her!

When the Lord is pleased to choose a creature for his noble ends, he furnishes her with those graces, those gifts which are as the seed of great things; he watches her attentively, fences her heart about, curbing the passions, purifying the affections, and gently guides her whole towards virtue. Our little Maria Anna entrusted her childhood to God, and no sooner had she set the foot of her youth on the difficult and rugged path of virtue than she walked it bold and strong, rejoicing like a giant running his course. Exultavit ut gigas ad currendam viam suam (Psalm 18). Yes, God himself was preparing her for a most noble end, God who, enraptured by that young girl's candor and simplicity, meant to make of her a model of the perfect religious, one who would join to the contemplative life a tireless activity for the comfort of troubled and suffering humanity.

Now, since virtues will not stand firm unless cemented upon their one foundation, holy humility, God infused in that candid soul so great a love for the virtue of humility, such care to keep herself hidden, such effort to seem of little worth, that her whole life can above all be summed up in a mass of facts revealing how highly she held the virtue that so pleases God, humility. Discite a me quia mitis sum et humilis corde, the divine Savior had said (St. Matthew 11:29), and the disciple of Jesus Christ, having heeded that sublime precept, became a faithful imitator of her divine Master in humility, in a humble and despised life. Already that soul, so humble, so passionate for Jesus, so penitent, hears the voice of her Beloved, a voice known to her ear, accustomed to the higher illuminations of grace, a voice that, piercing her soul, comes seeking her sweetly, even into the inmost fibers of her heart.

The Lord's voice calls her to become part of the religious family of the Daughters of St. Anne: she listens to it, knows its mysteries, appreciates its purposes, and, humbling herself before so great a condescension of God, answers, with the Bride of the Canticles: my Beloved is mine. Dilectus meus mihi (Canticles 2:16): and what can I do for you, my God, in return for what you have chosen to work upon me, your unworthy servant? One thing alone I ask of you, O Jesus: to dwell in your house all the days of my life, and at the same time to consecrate myself to the service of the forsaken and troubled members of your mystical body, of suffering humanity, of my brothers and sisters who lack a mother, a sister.

With such sentiments she reveals to her family the most vivid desire that set her whole soul alight, to become a religious of the Daughters of St. Anne. For love of the truth, let us say that her parents, though grieved at such a vocation, did not oppose it, but, resigned, offered God the sacrifice of the first fruits of their chaste marriage. But opposition, gentlemen, is the touchstone that distinguishes great souls from common ones; opposition ripens great undertakings, and it was not lacking to our Marianna.

Her priest uncles, who perhaps thought that the newly founded Institute promised nothing for the future, opposed her strongly, raising before her the gravest and most serious difficulties. To them was added her spiritual director, he too showing her the obstacles that, in his view, kept her from following the wishes of her heart. But what edification did he take when he saw all the difficulties dissolve that he raised, so as better to test her vocation? He suggested to her observations about the austerities of the life she was to begin — better to have said continue; and she answered: "Father, I hope to hold out, and am ready even to shed my blood." And he: "But you are not capable, given your body's frailty, of leading so active a life, so full of sacrifices." To which she: "When I cannot hold out in body, I shall hold out in spirit." Yes, our Marianna will be a religious, will be a Daughter of St. Anne; and when the austerities of the rule, and still more the voluntary mortifications with which her life flourished, shall have overcome her body, her spirit, ever victorious and strong, will not succumb, but, full of good works, will present itself before him who formed the object of her love, to bind about her temples the crown of justice that the eternal Judge had prepared for her.

Faced with such firm resolve, with such enlightened answers, both the priest uncles and the confessor had to be convinced that God was calling her to religious life, and, with the blessing of her parents and of everyone, she obtains leave to enter the Institute of the Daughters of St. Anne.

How many souls, gentlemen, by not heeding the voice of God who calls them to one state sooner than to another, how many souls, I say, clinging to the world, closing, seduced by its flattering and deceitful allurements, the ears of the mind so as not to hear the divine calls, and, their first step thus taken amiss, plunge miserably into the abyss of perdition, with infinite affront to virtue and holiness, because one abyss calls to another?

But fear nothing of all this, gentlemen; God leads our young woman by the hand, and she, a docile little lamb, lets herself be led by Providence into the Institute of Sister A. Rosa Gattorno.

The beneficial and wholesome institution of the Daughters of St. Anne was barely three years old, and it seemed as though the Lord had inspired it precisely for her432. The life spent in charity and sacrifice, which forms that Institute's program, the desire to be of use to her neighbor, the humility that inclined her to hide herself before the world, with a heroic surge of virtue strip her of everything and everyone, and, at barely twenty, Orsi is a novice of the Institute of the Poor Nurses.

What God had said to Abraham he seems to have repeated to Orsi: Egredere de terra tua, et de cognatione tua, et de domo patris tui, et veni in terram quam monstrabo tibi et benedicam tibi: Leave your land, your kindred, your father's house, and come into the land that I will show you, and I will bless you, and you shall be blessed (Genesis 12).

She, then, abandoned her parents, her relatives, her homeland; she gave herself wholly to God in the religious family of St. Anne, solely to satisfy her heart's burning longing: to consecrate herself as the bride of Jesus, and to devote herself to the service of the poor sick.

Religious institutes are indeed so many oases scattered here and there in the dreadful and barren desert of the great world, sown and tended by a wise and pious husbandman, and watered by the ever-flowing waters of heavenly grace. And there, gentlemen, in the novitiate of Piacenza, what a morning star shone out in distinguished virtues amid the clouds of corruption of present-day society, by whose stench the very heavens are still offended and tainted. There she devoted herself to the exact observance of the Institute's rules, its prescriptions, its counsels, showing well before her time what type of perfect religious she would give to the world. There, in that training ground of true spiritual progress, on that road which adds to Christian perfection, she gave the most beautiful proofs of living blameless and pure in obedience, in poverty, in angelic virginity.

Stripped of everything, and especially of that one possession that remains even to a man disinherited by fortune — the will, I mean — she never showed any wish for one thing rather than another; rather, convinced that in the voice of her superiors God's own voice was made manifest, she does not argue, does not examine, does not hesitate, but promptly and most willingly obeys, always choosing for herself the humblest and most lowly tasks — that is, of cook and of laundress of the community.

What shall one say of the beautiful virtue of virginal innocence that adorned the great soul of this illustrious departed one? She knows full well that such a virtue makes men like angels, and that virgins, marked by a mysterious seal upon the brow, form the honor guard of the Immaculate Lamb, and follow him wherever he goes, and sing a mysterious song that only they are allowed to sing. And she, zealous to keep this priceless pearl of heaven unspotted, not unaware of the burden of Adam that falls upon whoever is born of woman, although she had always lived most innocently, nonetheless wished to build around herself a kind of hedge that would make her invulnerable to the attacks of the world, the flesh, and the devil: a hedge woven of the voluntary mortifications that, for love of her God, she liked to add to the austerities of the rule, to the precepts of the Institute.

But of these and of the above-mentioned virtues, allow me, gentlemen, to pass on here, since a better occasion to speak of them will present itself later, when we shall see this luminous star shine under the fair sky of our Palermo, scatter its beneficent rays upon sick and forsaken humanity, the firstborn daughter of the charity of Jesus Christ.

Truly great soul! What a treasure of holiness gathers in you, a novice of the Institute yet seasoned in virtue, making you an object of delight to the Lord: Placens Deo!

Having finished her training with praise, she had scarcely passed twenty years, that age at which one frolics carefree, dreaming of a future crowned with roses; our young girl buries a smiling earthly future in the humble following of the evangelical counsels, and is deemed worthy to profess in the pious Institute, which now mourns her premature loss with resigned but intense grief.

In 1865 [1869], upon pronouncing her vows, she took the name Sister Anna del Salvatore, to show that she wished to be animated by the humility and charity of him who came to blot out sin and save souls. This name, gentlemen, sums up her religious life: namely, to sacrifice herself for others, to people heaven with souls who cost the Savior the shedding of his blood, the labors of his life, his ignominious death on the cross.

And now, daughter of St. Anne, Sister A. del Salvatore, we are given to admire her at the bedside of the wretched sick, a consoling angel, a bearer of peace, of comfort, of blessing. But who can follow the sublime outpourings of her heart, so passionate for Jesus and for those brothers dearest to his heart, the poor sick?

Many places in Italy had the good fortune to welcome her, admire her, and love her. Genoa, Milan, Florence, Macerata, Naples, Rome saw this good Daughter of St. Anne remain fearless, patient, kind, at the bedside of the poor dying, comforting them, sweetening their sorrows, purifying their souls, and strengthening them with the inventions of divine charity, which is ever ingenious for the good of one's neighbor. Many other places in Italy likewise saw and admired good Sister A. del Salvatore give herself wholly to all, forget herself, consume herself, sacrifice herself for her brothers and sisters.

And to us too it was given to admire her closely, for, having come among us five years ago, she edified with the fragrance of her virtues all who had the happy fortune to deal with her closely, to see her even once.

Part two

With the political upheavals that followed 1860, the Catholic Church began to suffer great harm, towards whose ruin the modern reformers of Italy secretly labored. From this came the subtle and hypocritical war on the regular and secular clergy, from this the favor shown to impiety, to the evil customs invading every order of society. In order to achieve such perfidious designs — that is, to bring Italy back to paganism — the religious Orders were suppressed, ecclesiastical goods seized and squandered, the Churches' revenues decimated or rather reduced to nothing; to weaken and starve their ministers, with what grave harm to the poor there is no one who has not seen, for it is ever true that in robbing the Church, bread is taken from the mouth of the people, and they are left to die of hunger and despair.

But Providence, which lovingly watches over the good of its Church, came to the aid of civil society with the institution of other Orders, which greatly conform to the needs of the people, remedying the ills that grieve the human family. Among the new and many institutions by which the Church's inexhaustible vitality is shown is the religious family of the Daughters of St. Anne, which, as I have said, spreads its beneficent influence where the boastful philanthropy of the age does not reach, bringing comfort to every sorrow, balm to every wound, help to every need.

Could, then, the pious Institute in question remain a stranger to our native land? Could Sicily, before such heroism of charity and self-denial as the Daughters of St. Anne display, could it, I say, call itself indifferent? Will the homeland that gave the world and heaven its Agathas, its Lucys, its Silvias, its Rosalias, not make it a sacred duty to welcome into its bosom the worthy nurses of St. Anne, if only to find in them relief for the ills that grieve suffering humanity, the whole human family? You know well how, through the agency of a worthy son of this land of faith and sublime impulses, through the agency of an illustrious and pious prelate of the Church of Palermo, this blessing of God came down to us, and the Institute of the Poor Nurses was established and spread throughout all Sicily.

Well then, the first to set foot in this land of sacred memories and glorious traditions was our Sister Anna del Salvatore, whom, as Superior, Mother General Sister A. Rosa Gattorno sent to us. And now, gentlemen, what a vast field of action opens before our good Superior! Her virtues soon made her popular and esteemed by every class of person: and though her particular care was to hide and conceal the Lord's gifts, we very soon realized how much holiness adorned her, how many virtues made her an incomparable teacher to us. Oh, how dear she became to us! How we treasured her in our hearts, precisely because she strove to seem — without showing the contrivance — strove to seem and to be thought full of sins, of faults, of imperfections?

If she gave splendid proof of the evangelical virtues, she became most admirable for the virtue that reigns above all others, humility, which she possessed and practiced in heroic degree.

It seems at first sight that humility should be a virtue proper only to sinners; prostrate under the weight of their iniquities, nearly annihilated by the sense of offended divine justice, they have too much reason to descend into the dust, not to raise their eyes towards heaven, and to say with the Prophet: Bonum mihi quia humiliasti me (Psalm 118). But humility is, by better right, the endowment of the saints. If it is a true awareness of our own nothingness and of God's greatness; if it alone can bring us near to him, because it detaches us from ourselves, which of the saints will not be humble, and which of the truly humble will not be a saint? Ah! Why is it not given to me to show you Sister Anna del Salvatore, who opened herself with confidence and full of holy sorrow to the directors of her spirit, while in her own eyes she believed herself a sinner? Wholly indifferent to earthly glory, intent only on the things of heaven, of the soul, of Jesus, of the poor sick, of the Sisters entrusted to her tender care, with a lowered face, a composed bearing, she seems to say: "Pay me no heed: Familia mea infima est in Manasse," and I am the least in my Father's house (In the Book of Judges, 6:15).

Ah! Why am I not granted to show you the holy cheerfulness with which she knew how to fulfill the Institute's duties; the sweet serenity of spirit that she knew how to instill in the sick; and above all that low estimation of herself, and the way she knew how to deftly turn aside the talk made in her praise, and the ridiculous words that came from her mouth to confirm in others that she was a woman of little worth and a sinner, deserving of nothing but pity and commiseration?

Grateful for the smallest favor done to her, she overwhelmed, with her gracious manners animated by the most vivid gratitude, all those who had helped the growth of her Institute; generous in piety, comfort, compassion, and love towards whomever it might be: who then could fail to love one who had become an object of delight before God? Placens Deo.

I shall not enumerate all she did for the growth of the Institute in the service of troubled humanity. San Martino delle Scale, Termini Imerese, Sciacca, Sambuca, Aci, Sant'Antonio, Girgenti, Linguaglossa, Castiglione, Adernò, Trapani all admired the wonder of charity and humility combined that lay hidden in the great soul of Sister Anna del Salvatore. Hospitals, asylums, orphanages, educational institutes, houses of correction and reform were all witnesses to the heroic exercise of her duties, her wise and prudent governance, her kindness towards all.

Who could enumerate all the labors she sustained for the growth of her Institute? Suffice it to say that to her labors, her gracious manner, her charity is owed the fact that it is spread throughout all Sicily, to the infinite delight of the good, to the ineffable consolation of the sick, the orphans, the children. And who then could resist the power of her attracting virtues? Placens Deo, pleasing God, she made herself worthy of the love and reverence of men.

What shall one say of her care for the sick? She was sought everywhere as a consoling angel of peace. Oh! "When the Superior comes," was the sufferers' common saying, "we feel better." Before her the complaints on the lips of the sick ceased as if by enchantment. Does she then possess some amulet that drives away anguish and pain? She possesses, gentlemen, the charity of Jesus Christ, and with it she works wonders. I myself was many times a witness of the tenderness, the solicitude, with which she tended her ill Sisters, and of how she, especially at night, never left their bedside, with a charity that was a sharing in that of Jesus Christ, and so she spent herself for all.

What shall I tell you of her continual vigils, her unbroken fasts, her austerities, by which she wasted her innocent flesh, offering herself a willing victim of love to her beloved Jesus — austerities that would seem impossible, were they not true? If in the world our Sister Anna del Salvatore chose for herself common foods, and practiced fasting and penance, in religious life she carried her austerities to such a degree that she amazed even the most austere scourgers of human lusts in Nubia and Egypt. She, by the testimony of those few who could evade her watchfulness in hiding herself, fed herself only on greens, with the greatest nonchalance of this world: hiding even from them the penitential motive that led her to this, and giving the impression that her physical constitution was gladly content with it, being unable, on the contrary, to bear substantial and rich food.

What could I add about her continual likeness to the suffering Jesus, she who was in pain, and in considerable pain, from the ills that tormented her body, while outwardly, through her habitual cheerfulness, she showed enviable health?

What shall one say of her ardent prayers, her outpourings of love for her God, her Institute, her Daughters, the sick? What of her filial devotion to the Most Holy Virgin, to Mother St. Anne, to St. Joachim, to St. Joseph? She loved them with the purest and holiest love, copying their virtues in herself, imitating them in a humble, despised, penitent life.

It was and is a mystery when she rested her weary limbs; by day, always on her feet, in motion, either tending the sick or governing the Central House and this Sicilian Province433. By night, whoever had need of her need only go to the chapel. There she would spend the long hours of the night praying, pouring out the fullness of her affections before Jesus in the Sacrament. But, great God! Is she a woman, or rather an angel, able to do without bed and rest? And yet Sister Anna del Salvatore, for fifteen years, never once saw a bed, treating her body as a fierce enemy that had to be fought unceasingly.

And so, when sleep suddenly overcame her, and for a brief hour she dozed in that uncomfortable kneeling position, on waking she tormented and distressed herself, judging that she had shown little respect to Jesus for that very brief rest taken in the chapel, against her own will.

To the labors inherent in the office, which she filled so holily, she added others, which it is worth relating.

She, as you well know, did not rest at night, but remained before the tabernacle of the Living God, keeping watch over the King of her heart. Now, when she noticed that weariness might overcome her into sleep, she would rise from prayer and, on tiptoe, so as not to let the good Daughters of St. Anne notice her vigils, would go to the laundry and do the community's washing. And if by chance she were caught at this task by some religious, who naturally showed displeasure at such labor and at such an hour, she would smile and answer that this occupation caused her no trouble at all, but rather untold contentment and happiness. Skilled in women's work, by night, always by night, she made cloth flowers to form bouquets to adorn the altar, or sewed the community's habits, or made lace for use in the chapel.

A lover of the worship of the Lord, she desired and obtained that the Most Holy Sacrament be frequently exposed, regarding the day of exposition as a day of paradise, for then she could better linger in sweet conversation with blessed Jesus434.

Intelligent as far as her sex's station allowed, but wise and versed in the philosophy of the saints, confidently entrusting herself to Providence, she overcame the obstacles that in any way hindered the good, acted virtuously, and supplied the Institute's needs with the means in which Providence is rich.

A teacher of evangelical perfection, she taught her Religious detachment from earthly things, from self-will, always instilling obedience, and teaching more by example than by words, through a life of the perfect religious. When she had to correct in another some negligence or fault in the practice of the duties of the pious Institute, whoever could have penetrated that soul would have observed the dreadful torment that was wrought within her heart, believing herself the cause of those faults. And, correcting as her duty required, she did so with such dear and humble sentiments that it was impossible to resist her, to disobey her. Who, then, could fail to love, to obey, to anticipate the holy wishes of so good and humble a superior?

But I mean to let you witness, gentlemen, a scene that, while on the one hand it shows the virtue of her soul, on the other reveals to us how she was mistress of hearts, and at will managed them so as to purify them even of the smallest faults. A sister of this house fell mortally ill, and, at the height of the illness, said: "I don't want the broth, but something else." At this somewhat imperious remark, the Superior was deeply grieved at heart: and, "Sister," she answered her, "a religious must never say 'I want this or that,' but rather will say: 'would you do me the favor, the kindness...'" At this gentle reproof, the sister, confused at having caused pain to her good mother, joining both hands in an attitude of prayer: "Superior," she says to her, "how good you are to me, I will not do it again, forgive me." And the Superior kissed her on the forehead and pressed her to her breast, with an affection and a tenderness that drew furtive tears from those present.

Illuminated by a light from above, she foretold the day of her death, and foretold other things that events fully confirmed435.

What wonder, then, if great was the esteem with which Mother General holily honored her? She had need of graces, of heavenly favors, to provide for the needs of a religious family whose members are scattered even to the furthest Americas: and to her she turned, trusting to obtain by her prayers the graces she needed. Sister A. del Salvatore, most humble as she was, not suspecting that through her the grace was being sought, effectively urged the Sisters to pray. "Pray," she would say, "to the good Jesus; Mother needs graces." The Sisters prayed, and she too prayed through the long hours of the night; and the, so to speak, omnipotence of her intercession, the immense force of that warm torrent of tears, rose to the throne of God like a most pleasing perfume of choice incense: and the grace had already been granted; and, informed of this by Mother, she would urge the Sisters to thank the Lord: "Thank blessed Jesus," she would add, "Mother has obtained the grace."

Most obedient in everything, she carried out, by Mother's wish, continual, distant journeys, within the island and on the mainland, quite uncomfortable ones, given the inward sufferings that were slowly consuming her, without her noticing, without anyone being able to foresee so sudden a catastrophe, so much did the thorns of her penances blossom into roses.

Part three

God has spoken, and proclaimed through the mouth of the royal Prophet, that he knows his saints and calls them from the earth with a death that should not be called punishment, but rather reward and prize; for the death by which the saints complete their fleeting course on earth is precious in his sight, enviable among men; it being the beginning of a life that will never see its end, the beginning of a life in the full possession of God, the inexhaustible source of happiness and glory.

Now, that God who has numbered the days of each of us had already numbered those of our good Superior.

So holy, so precious a life was therefore soon to be extinguished! So luminous a star in the sky of the Catholic Church was, alas, very soon to turn towards its setting.

She had barely passed her fortieth year, and, rich in merit, in good works, she was found ripe for heaven. In the last days of last April, indeed, a fatal illness struck her. And here, gentlemen, is where it is best shown how dear she was to God. Placens Deo.

Her doctor having ordered her to stay in bed, most obedient as she was, she lay down. After four days of illness, Mother, unaware of our good Superior's grave condition, ordered her by telegram to go to Trapani, where a new house of the Institute had been opened. The fever burning within her had sapped her strength. But she did not fear to fail in obedience; she was too accustomed to that virtue. With a heroic effort of will she rallies her exhausted strength, rises from bed, sets out, goes to Trapani, and returns after a day in the worst condition. Her sacrifice was already accomplished; God had already accepted it and was hastening to call her to the unfading crown of eternal glory.

She who, in religious life, had never tasted meat or other substantial foods, since her daily sustenance consisted of greens alone, in her final illness took what the doctor prescribed, but wished that the blessing be given over all her food and medicines.

It was June 3, and as the illness advanced by great strides along the road to dissolution, a telegram arrived from Mother, who, knowing the grave danger of death our Superior was in, wished once more to test in her, in a wholly extraordinary way, the virtue of holy obedience. Mother ordered her to leave her bed and receive Communion in the chapel: and our good Superior, have no doubt of it, rises, receives Communion in the chapel, and then returns to sit in the room assigned to her. And it took the doctor's express order for her to go back to bed, feeling a painful thorn in her heart for not having been able to remain out of bed, as Mother wished436.

But the illness grew worse before their eyes: and on the morning of June 7 she was given Communion as Viaticum, and on the evening of that same day Extreme Unction, which she ardently desired. And now she was quite joyful and smiled on everyone, for, death soon freeing her from the bonds of the body, her soul would celebrate her espousal with the Immaculate Lamb. Many priests gathered round her bed, and I tell you, they were edified to see with what resignation, or rather serenity of spirit, she bore the pains that tore at her insides, as if it were nothing. Never a complaint came from the mouth of that strong soul! Asked how she felt: with a smile that habitually touched her lips: "As the Lord wills," she would answer. Asked by her confessor if she believed herself resigned to doing God's will: "Yes," she would answer, "whatever the Lord wills," and very often she pressed warm kisses on the image of the Crucifix that she always held tightly in her hand.

It is now a quarter past ten at night, and the Sisters, who realized they were about to lose their good Superior, who had loved them with the tenderest affection, kneel around their mother's bed and, with stifled sobs and with tears, beg her to bless them and forgive them the sorrows they might have caused her. The Superior, who had already lost the strength to speak, overcoming her inner emotion, makes a sign to the confessor, and he blesses, he absolves.

And, the confessor suggesting she leave the Daughters some remembrance, she, making a supreme effort, pronounces in an intelligible voice: "Be good and obedient." Behold, O Sisters, the last will of her who had for you a mother's heart, behold her inheritance; you shall be good and obedient: you have been, you are, and you shall be, by the grace of God, and of you heaven and earth will say: behold the worthy heirs of Sister Anna del Salvatore.

A little later, feeling death draw near, she asks the confessor to commend her soul; and, keeping her unmoving eyes fixed on heaven, amid the sweet names of Jesus, Mary, and St. Anne, her great soul takes flight to the eternal regions of glory, and she falls peacefully asleep in the Lord, leaving her dear Daughters orphaned of an affectionate mother, and plunged into mourning and grief.

Has the good, lovable, and holy Superior of the Daughters of St. Anne then died? And why, then, O just God, deprive us so soon of so clear a model of perfection? But since your inscrutable judgments are just, we adore them in profound silence.

Her death was received with lively and general sorrow, and her coffin was bathed in noble and sincere tears. And these solemn obsequies, and the unbloody sacrifices offered to God for her soul, tell us, in the eloquent language of facts, that true glory will accompany Sister Anna del Salvatore, because she was humble in spirit. Humilem Spiritu suscipiet gloria.

In this way Sister Anna del Salvatore Orsi made herself dear to Jesus Christ, her Heavenly Spouse, the foremost object of her ardent love; she made herself dear, esteemed, and honored by men, for whose benefit she always labored, offering the world the spectacle of a religious life virtuously led, generously spent. Placens Deo.
